talks.title: Szilárd Pfeiffer - TOTP is not a Silver Bullet
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Szilárd Pfeiffer - TOTP is not a Silver Bullet.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Szilárd Pfeiffer challenges the belief that enabling TOTP solves authentication, drawing on decades of crypto work including the D-Heat Attack and Cryptolizer.

## Limitations of TOTP
TOTP is not a true second factor when login and code generation happen on the same compromised mobile device. Short code lifetimes provide natural rate limiting, but clock skew forces servers to accept previous, current, and next time windows—widening attack surface.

## Implementation Pitfalls
He surveyed popular providers: roughly 25% use validity windows under 120 seconds contrary to RFC guidance. Lower digit counts (e.g., four digits) ease brute force. Eight-digit codes reduce usability.

## Takeaways
TOTP improves security only with sound deployment—separate factors, conservative time windows, and awareness that client-side secret storage on phones remains a weak point.

talks.title: How to find rootkits in the linux kernel
talks.teaser: Shows how a Volatility plugin cross-checks kernel module structures in memory to expose hidden Linux rootkits.
talks.summary:
Roland Nagy of the CrySyS Lab presents a method for finding kernel rootkits in Linux memory dumps. Rootkits hide processes, files and network connections, and kernel-level variants usually live in loadable kernel modules, so the talk focuses on those. The approach uses the Volatility memory forensics framework and a custom plugin, modextref, that applies cross-view detection: it collects module structures from seven kernel data sources and flags modules that appear in some sources but not others. The speaker goes through each source, from the module list and the sysfs kset to the module layout tree, vmalloc areas, the bug list and ftrace mappings, and notes which kernel versions each one applies to.

In a live demo, the plugin reports hidden modules in three infected memory dumps from older and newer kernels. When cross-view checks find nothing, the plugin lists modules with external-build taints and examines their dependencies, which led to a suspicious module with hook-related symbol names. That module was dumped to a file and opened in Ghidra for disassembly.

The evaluation covered 55 rootkits: 35 open-source samples built from GitHub and 20 samples from VirusTotal. The original Volatility check found 13 of the 35 open-source rootkits and 10 of the 20 wild ones, while the new plugin found all of them. The speaker closes by sharing the plugin, the dataset and an accompanying paper. The practical takeaway is that comparing several kernel data structures catches hidden modules that a single list-based check misses, although a rootkit that hides from every source remains undetected.

talks.title: AI in Adversarial hands
talks.teaser: Explores how adversaries can manipulate AI systems through poisoned documents, fake data, deepfakes and influence campaigns.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how artificial intelligence could be turned to adversarial use, drawing on live exercises the speakers ran recently. A dealership chatbot could be talked into an absurd deal, and a single malicious instruction hidden in one document can spread through retrieval-based systems. The speakers also describe seeding the web with fake professional profiles so that large AI systems ingest false information as fact.

They cover failures and abuse in practice. A researcher registered a package matching a name that models kept hallucinating for a Hugging Face command line tool, and it was downloaded over 30,000 times before it was shown to be harmless. Pickled model files were described as a way to get a shell on an AI machine, and Hugging Face has begun scanning for them. The speakers found AI penetration testing tools overhyped, noted that real-time voice and face deepfakes are now easy to run, and said generated content can be fingerprinted even after fine-tuning. They then moved to influence: AI personas posing as influencers, and content tailored to individuals using behavioural data.

The closing section covers monitoring and control, including workplace assistant dashboards that summarise what staff did, face recognition and plate scanning in public, and the concentration of model control in a few providers. Media authentication such as C2PA was presented as one possible counter. The main takeaway is that audiences should think critically about what they share with AI systems, and that the people who shape models and narratives are the ones to watch.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // Examining the Explanatory Factors of Malicious Hacking Behaviors
talks.teaser: Survey research in Portugal identifies peer association as the strongest predictor of malicious hacking among young IT professionals.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames malicious hacking as unauthorized access to others’ systems and contrasts black, white, and gray hat roles before focusing empirical work on deliberate harmful behavior. In Portugal, where comparable work was scarce, the speaker surveyed 680 people in information technology—students, teachers, and professionals—with an average age near 28. Participants reported lifetime and past-year involvement across five behaviors ordered by severity, from password guessing to creating damaging malware.

Lifetime prevalence reached about sixty percent for at least one behavior, while recent activity was lower. Password guessing dominated; rarer acts such as malware creation appeared in only a few percent of responses. Compared with non-offenders, those reporting malicious hacking tended to be younger, more often male, less formally educated yet confident in computing skills, more impulsive, and holding beliefs favorable to rule-breaking. Deviant friendships and peer reinforcement scored higher as well. A combined logistic model explained roughly half the variance; male sex and low self-control roughly doubled odds, younger age increased risk, and associating with friends who hack raised likelihood about sevenfold—the standout predictor—while social-learning measures accounted for the largest explanatory share among variable groups.

The speaker ties findings to international criminology literature and argues the results support preventive planning: awareness in schools, hiring defensive talent inside organizations, and continued research to cover the unexplained portion of the model.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // AI Security
talks.teaser: Gives security practitioners a broad overview of generative AI, its risks like prompt injection, and practical uses in daily work.
talks.summary:
The talk starts for people who have not followed AI developments closely, placing machine learning inside a wider AI field. The speaker covers how quickly ChatGPT grew, studies reporting faster writing and coding with AI assistance, and why hosted models can give different results over time, which makes reproducible security decisions hard. Image generation is shown along with its limits, such as garbled text, and the risk that deepfakes and fabricated media will make fraud and phishing harder to spot.

The middle section explains that an AI system is more than its model. The speaker walks through the surrounding pipeline, including training data collection and cleaning, where poisoning or exposed datasets create risk, and agent loops that execute generated commands and therefore need sandboxing. Other risks discussed are model stealing through large volumes of queries, bias, and misaligned goals, with a call for security people to join AI red teams.

The final section shows applied examples: having a model explain password strength to users, turning WHOIS output into JSON, building a small glossary website, writing Burp Suite BChecks, and generating a script that finds the minimum set of cookies a site needs. The takeaway is to check and challenge AI output through repeated rounds rather than accept the first answer, and to test vendor claims before relying on them.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // It Was Harder to Sniff Bluetooth Through My Mask During the Pandemic…
talks.teaser: Shows how passive Bluetooth sniffing reveals device vendors, chips and trackable addresses, from hotel locks to medical devices.
talks.summary:
The talk shows what cheap passive Bluetooth sniffing can reveal about nearby devices. The speaker logged advertisements with Raspberry Pi boards running simple Linux scripts over several days in cities, casinos, hotels and cars. The aim was to learn which Bluetooth chip a device uses, since certain chip families have known over-the-air firmware flaws and nobody knows where those chips are deployed.

Public addresses embed a manufacturer prefix and never change, and static random addresses are trackable too. Vendor prefixes, module makers and FCC filing photos helped pin down chips in several cases: a TV box sold in only a few countries, pay-by-Bluetooth vending dongles, casino card readers, and scooters that advertised their chip maker. Car models, Nest cameras with sequential names, and Fitbit devices identified through 128-bit UUIDs were also covered. Hotel door locks in Charlotte hotels, tied by the speaker to a 2010 assassination, showed how the same risk reaches physical security. Other examples included OBD-II dongles, police body cams, glucose monitors and CPAP machines.

The closing point was that Bluetooth tooling is immature and that knowing the chip is the first step toward judging whether a known over-the-air exploit applies. Passive scanning exposes trackable people and assets, and the speaker said more active fingerprinting results would follow.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // Roundtable Discussion about NIS2 Directive (in Hungarian)
talks.teaser: Regulator and industry panelists explain how Hungary's NIS2 rules change deadlines, audits, fines and supplier obligations.
talks.summary:
This Hungarian-language roundtable brings together officials from a national supervisory authority and a cybersecurity industry panel to discuss the NIS2 directive and the Hungarian law that transposes it. The discussion opens by comparing NIS2 with its predecessor. The first directive left each member state to write its own rules, which produced very uneven results, so NIS2 raises the baseline and widens the scope to sectors such as manufacturing, healthcare and chemicals, including suppliers along the chain.

The timeline comes next. The directive was published in late 2022 and the Hungarian law followed in 2023. Organisations must self-register from 1 January 2024 within a six-month window, and the new obligations apply from 18 October, when the earlier rules are repealed. Audits must be repeated every two years and can be carried out by private firms on a list of qualified vulnerability assessors. Fines are set in implementing decrees and can reach a share of annual turnover or up to 10 million euros. A roadshow with the chamber of commerce reached more than 2,500 companies, many of which had not known they were covered.

The final part looks at preparation. Speakers urged organisations to start early, map their supply chains and appoint an internal security lead rather than relying only on outside consultants. They also noted that management bodies must take part in awareness training, a requirement the panel said is still hard to picture in practice. Listeners were invited to send questions to the authority's cybersecurity mailbox.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // Pwning into Power System Center
talks.teaser: Recounts a red team engagement against a utility's grid control server, from captured credentials to API privilege escalation.
talks.summary:
This talk walks through an authorized red team engagement against a national electricity provider. The goal was to see whether substations could be disrupted. The control product sat behind a firewall, so the team first had to reach the isolated network. Initial access came from a tool that answers name-resolution queries on a corporate Wi-Fi, then from a crafted email with a mistyped share link that a user clicked, leaking a password hash. Brute forcing recovered a low-privilege Windows credential, which was replayed inside the isolated network. A payload had to be re-encoded to get past endpoint antivirus, and a watching blue team blocked most attempts.

Once inside, a scan found a web interface for the control product that accepted only Windows authentication and gave the account read-only rights. Vendor documentation pointed to API endpoints that could be called directly, and that route allowed escalation from read-only to super admin. The team then reached device terminals and changed substation data.

Findings went to the utility and vendor, with advisories still pending. The closing defensive points covered gap analysis across people, process and technology, layered controls with trust-but-verify access, awareness for users who click lures, email authentication policies, and regular pentests before production releases.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // SIEM Slam: Tricking Modern SIEMs with Fake Logs and Confusing Blue Teams
talks.teaser: Shows how an attacker with root on a Splunk forwarder can intercept and rewrite log traffic to mislead blue teams.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a red team scenario: after gaining root or SYSTEM on a host, an attacker has little time before defenders respond, so simply killing the SIEM agent may draw attention. The speaker argues that changing what the SIEM records can buy more time. Splunk is used as the example, with forwarders sending data to an indexer, and the speaker notes that this traffic is plain text by default.

Using an iptables NFQUEUE rule, the research intercepts outgoing forwarder packets, parses them, and rewrites fields such as host name, IP address and executed command before reinjecting them. A companion tool watches live traffic while harmless commands run on the compromised host, so matching events are altered or new ones are generated. In the demo, a made-up host appears in the Splunk web interface running a download and execute sequence that never happened there. On Windows, the speaker says Echo Mirage can inject into the Splunk process for the same effect.

For defenders, the main advice is to encrypt forwarder-to-indexer traffic with TLS and manage certificates carefully, despite some latency and expiry risk. Splunk's default certificates are shared across installations, so custom ones are needed. The speaker also suggests protected process light as a hardening step. Planned work includes a Cobalt Strike module. The takeaway is that SIEM data should not be trusted blindly.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // Supply Chain Attacks
talks.teaser: Follows supply chain attacks from registry abuse to a token-leaking SQL injection in an artifact server.
talks.summary:
The talk defines the software supply chain as everything touching an application across its development lifecycle, including third-party code, build tools and infrastructure. It cites a prediction that 45% of organizations will face a supply chain attack by 2025. Entry points covered include typosquatting, dependency confusion, repojacking after a repository is renamed, and recent package manager flaws such as RubyGems guessing attacks and npm manifest confusion.

The main case study is a bug-bounty chain against an artifact storage product. A user-enumeration bug let the researcher pick targets for a phishing campaign sent from a trusted company domain, and about 30,000 exposed servers were observed, averaging 10 users each. After gaining a foothold, an LLM helped rank decompiled attack-surface paths, and a blind boolean SQL injection in a proprietary query language was found through a sort parameter. Leaking the forgot-password token bit by bit, a UUIDv4 with a timestamp valid for half an hour, let the researcher reset the default admin password and escalate a medium-severity bug to critical.

The closing section covers detecting malicious code through static rules, anomaly signals such as off-hours pushes, and machine learning clustering. Comparing published binaries with source is hard for compiled languages, and reproducible builds are impractical at scale, so binary-to-source comparison via reverse engineering was offered as one option. The takeaway: attackers can reach a build through any dependency, transitive ones included, so CI/CD systems need protection.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // How to Hack and Defend (Your) Open Source?
talks.teaser: Explains how attackers abuse open source dependencies and self-hosted CI runners, and how to defend sourcing, builds and SBOMs.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through how open source software gets attacked and how to defend it. It opens with recent incidents: automated pull requests that mimicked a dependency bot but carried code to steal developer credentials, a look-alike tool that delivered malware, and npm packages impersonating well-known brands that sent personal data to a command-and-control server. The speaker argues that most organisations depend on open source and should focus on the risks most likely to target them.

The attack section covers dependency confusion, typosquatting, fake AI models, package and repository hijacking, and exposed credentials. The main case study looks at self-hosted CI runners that are not ephemeral. A contributor who can open a pull request to a public repository can push a malicious workflow that runs on an internal runner, which can then be used to reach the internal network and contact an attacker server. Defences include isolating runners in a DMZ, using ephemeral runners, branch protection and code owners, stopping automation from approving pull requests, and scanning binaries and infrastructure-as-code.

For sourcing and builds, the talk recommends checking repository health with tools such as OpenSSF Scorecards, enabling native platform security features, and curating critical components internally. It presents SBOMs as the basis for quickly assessing exposure when a vulnerability is disclosed, with VEX to share status, and describes SLSA levels and reproducible builds for build integrity. The takeaway is to verify every step, follow common frameworks, and automate and oversee pipelines.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // That’s Just a Tool - Not Good Nor Bad. That Part is Up to YOU
talks.teaser: A session frames Windows living-off-the-land remote tools as neutral, then demos attacks and cheap mitigations for both sides.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with the idea that remote management and lateral movement on Windows look identical to defenders; only context and intent separate administrators from attackers. The talk surveys living-off-the-land channels starting with RPC and SMB-named-pipe interprocess communication, including one-liner command execution and remote command-and-control over port 445 without opening new firewall holes, plus detection options such as mini-filter drivers, noisy handle events, Sysmon pipe rules, and remote SMB pipe prefixes.

Recorded and live demos cover RDP risks: man-in-the-middle credential capture with downgrade and forged certificates, terminal-server shadowing of disconnected sessions via elevated local access, and corresponding group-policy mitigations that are only partial. WinRM and PowerShell remoting are presented as powerful admin tooling that attackers can mirror, alongside JEA session configurations that constrain commands. A credential-exposure segment compares vendor guidance with hands-on tests showing full TGT theft from WinRM network logons via process-token duplication, and how virtual-account session configurations block that until an attacker tampers with local config files.

Closing guidance favors a living-off-the-land mindset, skepticism toward vendor tables, disabling PowerShell v2, monitoring remoting drift, and a simple Active Directory “log on to workstations” restriction to block lateral movement without commercial jump boxes—while noting forged tickets can undermine even that. Slides, scripts, and tools are pointed to on the speaker’s GitHub and the event Discord.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // The Power of Coercion Techniques in Windows Environments
talks.teaser: A consultant walks through Windows coercion, NTLM relay chains, and the legacy mitigations that actually blunt domain takeover paths.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames coercion as tricking a Windows system—often a domain controller—into initiating outbound authentication so an attacker can capture or relay it. He positions the topic as long-known offensive tradecraft rather than new research, drawing on penetration testing experience where small misconfigurations compound into full domain compromise.

Several coercion paths are outlined, including PetitPotam-style EFS RPC abuse, PrinterBug over the print system protocol, and brief mentions of Shadow Coercion and DFS coercion, plus tooling that tries multiple methods. Live lab work shows a domain controller authenticating to an attacker host, relay scenarios toward ADCS (ESC8-style certificate issuance), and abuse where one machine account holds local administrator rights on another—linked to common Configuration Manager deployment patterns. A further chain uses unconstrained Kerberos delegation: coerce the domain controller, harvest forwardable tickets, and escalate toward krbtgt and persistent domain administrator access.

The closing emphasis is defensive: Microsoft is unlikely to eliminate coercion as a class, so practitioners should harden relay prerequisites. Priority measures include SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, replacing unconstrained delegation with tightly scoped constrained delegation, auditing excessive local administrator rights (for example with BloodHound), and network segregation—most of which are well-documented but still inconsistently deployed.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // Reality or Myth: Unhackable Application (Using Zero Trust)
talks.teaser: Shows how building zero trust into application code through an SDK can hide services from the open internet, with a live demo.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether an application can be made unhackable with zero trust. The speaker notes that nothing is truly unhackable, so the aim is to secure an application as far as possible. Zero trust rests on verifying every party explicitly, granting least privilege, and assuming the network is already compromised, backed by strong identity and end-to-end encryption. It is compared at three levels: network access, host access through an agent or sidecar, and application access, where zero trust is built into the code through an SDK.

To show the application-level approach, a small Go server with hello and add endpoints was adapted. Its standard listener was swapped for a zero trust listener from the SDK, which places the service on an overlay mesh secured with mutual TLS. The service then exposes no listening ports and needs no firewall holes. In a live demo, an identity was enrolled with a token that produced a JSON identity file, then three examples ran over the overlay: a reflect service that echoed messages, a math example that returned a result, and a curl request that reached a server hosted in AWS.

The closing point was that application-level zero trust is the most secured of the three levels. Attendees were pointed to the open-source project site, a public sample repository and its community forum.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // Carved in Stone: Malware [ab]use of the Bitcoin Blockchain
talks.teaser: Explains how Bitcoin blockchain analysis uncovers malware command-and-control signaling and ransomware key releases.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how criminals use the Bitcoin blockchain beyond simple payments, both to store data and to move money for ransomware and other schemes. Because transactions are public and permanent, they can be used for command-and-control signaling in botnets, where a malware family publishes an encrypted domain or an IP address in an OP_RETURN output that bots read through public blockchain explorers.

The research team built a platform that follows the flow of funds. It combines tags for known addresses, a trained exchange classifier and heuristics that cut graphs at likely ownership changes. Forward tracing is a known method, but the speaker showed that tracing backwards can reveal exchanges depositing money into an operation, which can serve as attribution points. Using classifiers called oracles, the team found previously unknown signaling addresses for several botnets, including Pony and Skidmap, where one case showed that anyone able to send deposits could redirect a botnet.

For the DeadBolt ransomware, the attackers published decryption keys on-chain after payment. Scanner data surfaced 66 payments, which expanded to about 2,400 addresses when the key-release pattern was searched. Scanning the whole chain over two years matched the 155 keys recovered by the Dutch police and raised the revenue estimate from 2.8 to 98.3 Bitcoins. Most operations are likely invisible to traditional methods. Clustering by multi-input transactions was also discussed as a probabilistic aid, not proof that addresses share one owner.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2023 // Get Deception In Your Environment Now!
talks.teaser: Shows how free deception tools like Canary Tokens and honey accounts can expose attackers inside your environment.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that predictable defenses make life easy for well-resourced attackers, since many organizations run the same firewalls, EDR and SIEM products. The speaker presents cyber deception as one part of the answer, pointing to the MITRE Engage framework for planning it. He is skeptical of threat intelligence feeds built on IP addresses and domains, because attackers change infrastructure quickly and those indicators are often stale.

Most of the session is a live demonstration of free tools, mainly Canary Tokens. Planted items include AWS keys in a code repository, a spreadsheet named passwords on a file share, and a token in cloned login-page code that reports who copies a website before a phishing run. Honey user accounts in Active Directory, set with no logon hours, raise an alert when an attacker sprays passwords. Other examples include a decoy Kerberoastable service account, Word documents with embedded content that calls back to reveal where they were opened, and a honey share built with Impacket that captures authentication attempts. The speaker also shows that IP-based geolocation is unreliable and that tracing to the ISP edge router gives a closer fix.

The core takeaway is that deception is cheap, quick to deploy, and can change attacker behavior, since adversaries who fear being caught may back off. The speaker closes by pointing to free online labs for practicing these techniques and a free card game about the attack lifecycle.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // The History of Hacking AI Systems
talks.teaser: Traces how adversarial machine learning developed and surveys real attacks on AI systems, with guidance for defenders.
talks.summary:
Eugene, CTO of Adversa AI, walks through the history and current state of adversarial machine learning. He begins with his own experience in 2016, when a threat detection product his team built with machine learning turned out to be easy to bypass. A smart application firewall fell to altered payload parameters and new encodings, and a user behavior anomaly detector could be taught slowly to treat attacker activity as normal.

The talk then places the field in context. Drawing on an archive of research papers, he describes more than two decades of work, with a sharp rise after adversarial examples appeared in 2014 and heavy government and defense funding from 2018. Computer vision is the most attacked domain, yet he argues that less-studied applications are not safer. Attacks are grouped into manipulation, infection and exfiltration, and real incidents include a 2016 Microsoft chatbot poisoned by online communities and a reported case of fake identities used to fool a national facial recognition system.

He closes with predictions: AI bug bounties, classic attacks such as software supply chain compromises applied to AI, and more documented incidents. He says there are no patch-style defenses for models, that traditional firewalls and antimalware cannot catch these attacks, and that securing AI is mainly operational. His practical advice is to inventory the AI systems in your organization, share the threats with colleagues, and run basic security tests with available tools.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // 4 Weird Google VRP Bugs in 40 Minutes
talks.teaser: Four Google VRP cases show voice-session hijacks, OAuth referer leaks, Apps Script side channels, and Classroom copy abuse.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through four distinct vulnerabilities reported through Google’s vulnerability reward program, each tied to a different product surface. The first chain starts on a malicious web page that deep-links into Google Assistant so the victim starts an authenticated listening session; attacker-controlled audio or text-to-speech then issues commands as the signed-in user, with demos ranging from sharing location via SMS to smart-home actions, plus a later bypass when microphone contention checks were weakened by playing background music.

The second issue targets Sign in with Google during OAuth consent. Clicking the app’s privacy policy or terms links sent the attacker’s site a Referer header containing the full accounts.google.com URL, including flow state and scope-approval parameters. By rewriting approved scopes before redirecting the victim back, an attacker could mark permissions as checked even after the user denied them, still hinging on the victim continuing without noticing tab or UI changes. Google rated the impact similarly to cross-site scripting and paid a substantial bounty.

The third and fourth bugs abuse authorization logic in Google Apps Script triggers and Google Classroom assignment attachments. Swapping document IDs in intercepted requests let an attacker infer when a victim opened a private document via trigger disablement, or force copies of a student’s private Drive file into a teacher-accessible shared folder—including follow-on template edits that needed extra user interaction. Across the set, the speaker stresses not trusting microphone input for authenticated actions, tightening referrer policy on sensitive flows, and ensuring third parties cannot initiate privileged operations on another user’s behalf.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Hackers Deserve Rights
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding #Hacktivity2021 // Hackers Deserve Rights.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Chloe Madji, co-founder of Hacking is Not a Crime, delivers a passionate talk on securing rights and protections for ethical hackers. She argues that public perception conflates hackers (security researchers) with attackers (malicious actors), a dangerous misunderstanding perpetuated by media, outdated legislation, and socially constructed beliefs that undermines both hacker safety and organizational security.

## Key Topics

**Hacker vs. Attacker Distinction**
Madji establishes that hackers use their skills to keep systems secure, stay within scope, and exploit only with permission—unlike attackers who use identical skills to harm, extort, exploit without permission, and act with criminal intent. This terminology distinction is foundational to the entire talk, as public conflation of the two groups drives the crisis.

**Socially Constructed Beliefs and Human Behavior**
Drawing from cognitive science, Madji explains how beliefs form through media exposure (movies, news, social media) and how the amygdala generates threat responses while the prefrontal cortex makes conscious decisions. She uses a metaphor of people with pink hair being stereotyped as dangerous to illustrate how face-to-face conversations and alternative narratives can challenge ingrained biases. The research evidence presented shows that personal video testimonies from advocates are effective tools for shifting perception.

**The Kevin Case and DJI Bug Bounty Failure**
Madji recounts a real case where Kevin found a serious bug in DJI's bug bounty program. Despite staying in scope and receiving a 30k USD award offer, the contract provided no legal protection. When Kevin expressed concerns and DJI's internal communications (calling him a PR threat) were accidentally included in emails, he was effectively threatened with litigation under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Kevin publicly released all correspondence, forcing DJI to withdraw the lawsuit—illustrating both the danger hackers face and the power of transparency.

**Media and Terminology Problems**
Madji demonstrates how even searches for "ethical hacker" vs. "criminal hacker" return identical imagery: hoodies, basements, darkness. She provides examples of harmful headlines misusing "hacker" when they mean "attacker" (e.g., "Hacker Starting to Leak Patient Therapy Notes"). She recommends kindly correcting journalists via direct messages or comments, sending letters to copy desks, and providing feedback to marketing teams that misuse terminology.

**Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) Critique**
Madji details the CFAA's severe problems: passed in 1984 before the internet existed, written with extreme vagueness allowing prosecutorial misuse, containing redundancies enabling repeated charges for the same act, and never involving hacker community representation during its creation. She emphasizes the law was born from fear—specifically Ronald Reagan's reaction to the movie WarGames—rather than thoughtful policy. While the CFAA hasn't been used federally against hackers recently, state and local governments and private companies still wield it as a weapon.

**The Aaron Schwarz Case**
Madji recounts the 2011 case where US attorney Carmen Ortez prosecuted Aaron Schwarz for downloading millions of scholarly articles from JSTOR via MIT's network as civil disobedience—arguing taxpayer-funded research should be accessible. He faced 35 years in prison and $1 million in fines (compared to 25 years for second-degree murder). After a 17-month legal battle with no end in sight, Schwarz died by suicide at age 26; his family attributed his death to the prosecutorial charges. Madji uses this as the prime example of why the CFAA must change.

**Vulnerability Disclosure Policies (VDP) as Critical Infrastructure**
Madji states 94% of Forbes Global 2000 companies lack VDPs, and 1 in 4 hackers do not report vulnerabilities due to lack of protection. Effective VDPs must include: clear in-scope vs. out-of-scope definitions (written for English learners, not attorneys); direct security team contact information; dedicated personnel managing submissions; and timely communication. She names BugCrowd, HackerOne, and disclose.tv as resources, emphasizing VDPs reduce breaches and allow diverse hackers to find bugs security teams miss.

## Technical Details

**Cognitive Science Foundation**
The amygdala operates subconsciously to flag potential threats based on learned associations, while the prefrontal cortex consciously evaluates whether to act on that threat. Socially constructed beliefs feed the amygdala's threat database; challenging these requires conscious deliberation and exposure to counter-narratives.

**CFAA Specifics**
Passed in 1984, the Act predates modern internet infrastructure and was never updated. Its vagueness allows prosecutors to stack charges; a single hack can be charged multiple times under different CFAA clauses, compounding penalties drastically.

**Quantified Problems**
- 94% of Forbes Global 2000 have no vulnerability disclosure policies
- 25% of hackers don't report vulnerabilities (likely due to fear and lack of protection)
- Aaron Schwarz: 35-year sentence vs. 25 years for second-degree murder (non-violent act)

## Takeaways

**Immediate Actions**
1. **Contact media:** Politely correct terminology in press articles and social media; send letters to copy desk editors requesting consistent hacker/attacker distinction
2. **Challenge visual stereotypes:** When appearing publicly about hacking, avoid hoodies and dark basement imagery; present hackers as ordinary professionals
3. **Know your representatives:** Vote and contact local legislators about outdated anti-hacking laws; Hacking is Not a Crime offers support for these conversations
4. **Check VDPs:** Use disclose.tv to audit organizations; advocate for comprehensive disclosure policies wherever you work or engage
5. **Volunteer:** Support organizations like EFF, Cavalry, C3 CTI League, Disclosed.io, and Hacking is Not a Crime
6. **Share stories:** Submit video testimonies to Hacking is Not a Crime's advocacy project to humanize ethical hackers

**Systemic Change**
The speaker argues that improving legislation (especially CFAA reform), ensuring hacker representation in policy discussions, implementing universal vulnerability disclosure policies, and shifting media narratives will reduce both breaches and prosecutions of ethical researchers. Protection and belonging convert would-be malicious actors into ethical participants.

**Core Message**
Change begins with individual action: empathetic outreach to journalists, engaging local representatives, volunteering time to advocacy, and challenging one's own biases about hackers. "Change starts with you and me."

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // A Common Bypass Pattern to Exploit Modern Web Apps
talks.teaser: Shows how altering data after sanitization undoes protections, using XSS and RCE chains in Zimbra, WordPress and Magento.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a way to find web vulnerabilities by looking for places where data is changed after it has been sanitized. As mitigations and secure-by-default frameworks close off whole bug classes, researchers have to look for gaps elsewhere, and the speaker argues that post-sanitization modification is an under-examined one. The model orders a data flow as input, sanitization, transformation, normalization and usage, and shows that when the later steps run after sanitization, the protection can be negated.

Three case studies follow. In Zimbra, the server-side allow-list HTML sanitizer held, but client-side calendar-invite code assigned the sanitized HTML to innerHTML, which decoded entities, and a regex then inserted a form tag that unbalanced quotes and produced XSS in Chrome. Chained with SSRF, a single email could expose cloud provider credentials. In WordPress, comments were sanitized, yet the code rebuilding the rel attribute wrapped values in double quotes without re-encoding them, letting injected event handlers run. Combined with a cross-site request to an administrator, this led to plugin upload and code execution on default settings. In Magento 2, a sitemap file name was checked for an XML extension, but a 32-character database column truncated it afterwards, so a crafted name ending in .php became a file write leading to remote code execution.

The takeaway is that sanitization should be the final step before data is used. Where that is not possible, sanitizing again after transformation is a safer fallback. For auditors, hunting for code that modifies sanitized values can be quicker than trying to bypass a well-tested sanitizer directly, and that code may sit in a different component or repository from the sanitizer itself.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Mobile App Security Testing is Also Essential
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP top 10 mobile risks with real-world app examples and mitigation advice for developers.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that mobile apps need dedicated security testing. It starts with market scale: about 6.3 billion smartphones in use and 28 billion apps downloaded from the Play Store in a year, with major apps from large vendors all having had vulnerabilities. The speaker then goes through the OWASP mobile top 10, pairing each risk with an example and mitigations.

Early items cover platform misuse and insecure storage. A work mail app could be opened without valid credentials because of flawed touch ID handling, so developers should follow platform guidance and request only needed permissions. An authenticator app stored secrets in an SQLite database without a proper key store, so the advice is to store less and encrypt what remains. A child-tracking smartwatch let eavesdroppers intercept traffic and change geofencing, which led to recommendations on certificate pinning and interception testing.

Later items include authentication and cryptography. The Grab app allowed brute-forcing of a four-digit second-factor code because there was no attempt limit, so inactivity timeouts and re-verification for new fingerprints were suggested. The Ola app's cryptographic keys were recovered after a third-party scan, prompting advice to use current algorithms and rotate keys through app updates. A remote car app showed insecure authorization, which calls for role-based testing. The talk closed with code quality, code tampering and reverse engineering, recommending obfuscation and avoiding rooted devices.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Security Awareness in Development
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #Hacktivity2021 // Security Awareness in Development.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Ákos Chilling, a manager at Bosch leading automotive security testing, discusses how large organizations can build security awareness among developers and engineers. He frames security as an essential product quality attribute and describes Bosch's multi-faceted approach to embedding security awareness across a 73,000-person R&D organization.

## Bosch's Security Context
Bosch develops physical products (automotive components, power tools, home appliances, e-bikes, trucks) rather than purely software systems. This introduces unique security challenges: physical supply chains, owner motivation to modify vehicles (tuning), unlimited attacker physical access, and public accessibility of devices. These factors necessitate cross-functional security involvement beyond software engineers—hardware engineers, system engineers, functional safety specialists, testers, and managers must all understand security risks.

## Technical Example: Relay Attack on Car Remotes
Chilling illustrates interdisciplinary security needs with a relay/replay attack on car remote controls. When a user presses the remote, a signal with a secret key opens the vehicle. While the key uses a random number generator that changes each time (making prediction difficult), an attacker can jam the signal during transmission, capture it, and replay it later. The car accepts a buffer of subsequent keys to handle legitimate delayed presses, enabling this attack. This published attack was reproduced in Bosch labs and exemplifies how hardware, software, and system design must collaborate on security.

## Bosch's Security Framework
Bosch maintains an incident response team and published vulnerability disclosure program (accessible via product security links on Bosch websites, though many products carry third-party branding and cannot be disclosed directly). Security is integrated into a risk-based engineering process covering the full product lifecycle, with defined customer and supplier interfaces based on dialogue rather than fixed frameworks.

## Shift-Left Testing and Security Testing
Chilling emphasizes the testing principle of "shift left"—finding bugs early reduces fix costs. Rather than waterfall development followed by testing, Bosch uses a V-model where specification review and test design begin immediately. Unit testing and code review are heavily emphasized. Applied to security, vulnerability testing and penetration testing occur before production, but designing for security from initial concept—and making developers security-aware from day one—is even more effective. This led Bosch to launch "Hack Like a Bosch," an internal CTF (Capture The Flag) gamification event.

## Hack Like a Bosch: Gamification for Awareness
The event was designed to raise security awareness among non-security developers before they begin projects. Key design choices included: gamification (CTF format rather than traditional training), beginner-level focus, inclusion of non-software security challenges (reflecting physical product security), and internal hosting on the corporate network for privacy and security compliance (no external access, no hacking tools, only company-approved software permitted). Bosch partnered with external provider Israelit Lab, with internal domain experts reviewing challenges for relevance. The event was conducted entirely online in English and scaled globally across Bosch.

## Event Results and Challenges
The event featured 30 challenges (11 non-software) and attracted nearly 500 players in teams. Nine teams completed all challenges, primarily existing security experts and software professionals. However, the event proved more difficult than intended and more software-focused than desired. Formulating engaging non-software challenges within a game environment remained unsolved; some required manual review instead of automated flag generation. Despite this, participants—especially those already working on security processes—reported gaining practical experience (e.g., buffer overflow exploitation) for the first time.

## Takeaways
Cybersecurity is essential product quality requiring awareness across all developers; it is not solely a software problem but involves hardware, systems, and architecture. Internal gamification events are useful and enjoyable. Cross-domain collaboration is critical. Chilling noted limited feedback on whether participants applied security thinking in subsequent projects, suggesting the need for better impact measurement. Bosch plans to repeat the event.

## Questions
Discussion covered technical details of the replay attack (including the buffer of acceptable keys and user behavior when the first unlock fails) and measured success (primarily reaching the security community rather than transforming general-population awareness). The event required six months and roughly ten people working in flexible time alongside their day jobs, with reasonable external budget for game development.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Cloud Security Monitoring and Evasion Techniques
talks.teaser: Shows how stolen cloud credentials can blind AWS CloudTrail and S3-based logs, and how to harden logging.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how cloud activity is monitored and how an attacker with leaked or stolen API keys might stay hidden. It explains why short-lived workloads make log collection harder than on traditional servers, then compares the main logging services of AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. Retention varies: CloudTrail keeps 90 days of events by default, Azure activity logs also keep 90 days, and Google Cloud audit logs keep 30 days, with some admin logs kept for 400 days.

The attack section focuses on AWS and shows several ways to hide activity. One demo deletes an S3 bucket that holds logs. The speaker also turns a trail off, or edits it so it skips multi-region and global service events, leaving IAM activity unrecorded. In another demo, the bucket policy is edited to remove the write permission CloudTrail needs, after which access is denied for that service. A custom Lambda function could also filter events before they are stored.

For defenders, the answer is tamper-resistant logging: a dedicated logging account that collects logs from every AWS account, locked-down buckets, and AWS Config to catch risky changes. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode makes stored logs write-once, so even the root account cannot change or delete them. The closing message is that a cloud can be either secure or insecure, depending on setup, and that following provider guidance keeps logging intact.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Vulnerabilities: When Securing Your Own Environment is No Longer Enough
talks.teaser: Explains how Exchange and SolarWinds compromises spread through supply chains, and how to reduce third-party exposure.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing supply chain attacks as a long-running concern rather than a new one, pointing to earlier government guidance and technical reports before turning to recent incidents. The first part covers unpatched software. The presenters describe Microsoft Exchange zero-days in March 2021 that affected around 30,000 organisations, and a September 2021 MSHTML vulnerability that ransomware groups used to deliver Cobalt Strike loaders. Their advice is to know which products you run, follow vulnerability news, and maintain a prioritised patching process that deploys fixes as quickly as testing allows.

The second part addresses trusted access and third-party breaches. A SolarWinds API authentication bypass gave attackers trusted connections into many organisations, and suppliers of directly exposed firms were exposed too. The speakers link stolen credentials to the Colonial Pipeline intrusion and recommend moving away from passwords toward multi-factor authentication. Practical steps include listing third parties and how they connect to your network, avoiding blanket trust for third-party links, watching those suppliers for compromise, and using contractual audit rights.

The final section covers software supply chain compromises, using a case where an altered script sat in a vendor's repository from January to April before disclosure and then reached customers' CI pipelines. The recommendations are to map dependencies, refuse untrusted sources and containers, and audit private repositories. The closing recap is to monitor what you can, avoid trusting what you cannot watch, keep a prioritised view of assets, and read the news. The Q&A touched on auditing vendors and treating cyber risk as part of operational risk.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Millions for Nothing and Clicks for Free
talks.teaser: Examines Android ad-fraud rings, their evasion tricks, and how security researchers tracked and dismantled major operations.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames mobile and connected-TV advertising as a massive fraud economy where civil enforcement and obscured money flows make abuse unusually attractive compared with payment or banking crime. The speaker walks through historical large-scale schemes such as Methbot and Eve, including a long multinational investigation that led to arrests, then pivots to how operators shifted from classic botnets toward Play Store apps that monetize through out-of-context ads, hidden web views, and background clicking.

Several named campaigns illustrate escalating tradecraft: intent receivers tied to everyday phone events, fake home-screen shortcuts that survive uninstall attempts, sandbox and vendor evasion, publisher SDKs pitched to legitimate game developers, accelerometer-aware click timing, and monkey patching of Google SDK methods to trap users in full ad views. Terracotta and Rainbow Mix show coupon lures, Firebase-hosted payloads, packers, and large fleets of look-alike applications spoofing trusted brands to dilute detection.

The climax is a connected-TV-focused operation that allegedly drove a large share of CTV traffic by faking server-side ad impressions with a huge Android click farm, cloned games, rotating C2 tasks, and a custom TLS stack mimicking devices such as Roku until investigators mapped infrastructure and took it offline. Practitioners should expect ad fraud to behave like agile, low-friction malware business lines that abuse platform APIs and measurement trust rather than relying on traditional criminal statutes alone.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // C2Centipede: APT Level C2 Communications for Common Reverse HTTP Shell Tools
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #Hacktivity2021 // C2Centipede: APT Level C2 Communications for Common Reverse HTTP Shell Tools.
talks.summary: Jose introduces C2Centipede, a client-server shim that wraps Metasploit meterpreter beacons to evade Rita-style network beaconing detection. He contrasts bind and reverse shells, explains why HTTP egress blends in, and shows how default interpreter polling creates obvious ten-second patterns Rita scores highly. Centipede encrypts Troian traffic, rotates through thousands of open FRP and localtunnel reverse proxies or domain-fronted hosts, fakes idle responses to stretch intervals, and even tunnels commands over SMB file drops. Live demos suppress Handler noise, add proxies on the fly, and scatter beacons across many destinations so defenders cannot rely on single-pair interval analysis alone.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // GALILEO: In GPS We Trust?
talks.teaser: Explores civilian GPS spoofing risks and how Galileo's OSNMA layer authenticates navigation data with hybrid cryptography.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by comparing major GNSS providers and why civilian GPS lacks strong anti-spoofing guarantees, while Galileo adds open-service navigation message authentication using both symmetric and asymmetric cryptography. The speaker surveys roughly a decade of spoofing incidents—from a captured drone and a hijacked yacht to mobile games, maritime disruptions, smuggling at Shanghai, and trivial Android store apps that falsify location without rooting—and notes that fused Wi‑Fi or cell hints did not block a software-only spoof in his test.

The core technical section walks through OSNMA verification at frame and subframe granularity: only forty bits per page force receivers to assemble fifteen pages across about thirty seconds before checking an HMAC tied to a time slice, then validate a hash-linked Tesla-style MAC key chain backward to a root, and finally confirm that root against Galileo's published public key with tools such as OpenSSL. Captured traffic came from a Xiaomi Mi 8. Limits include OSNMA still being in an official testing phase despite production availability, uneven chipset support (Broadcom devices fared better), and Android GNSS API behavior that mixed components the team had to correct.

Practitioners whose business logic depends on geolocation—for geofenced access control in government, banking, or healthcare, future highly automated vehicles, or authenticated photo metadata—are urged to treat ordinary GPS as untrusted and evaluate whether Galileo OSNMA meets their authenticity needs, while weighing latency, hardware coverage, and maturity.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Investigating the Exploitability of Trusted Execution Environments
talks.teaser: Shows how to extract, emulate and fuzz an ARM TrustZone trustlet to reach a hidden key-returning branch.
talks.summary:
Trusted execution environments keep keys and sensitive data in a secure world that ordinary applications on the normal operating system cannot read directly. The talk focuses on ARM TrustZone, where one physical core switches context between the two worlds. Trusted applications, called trustlets, often sit on the regular file system, carry a signature, and are loaded into the secure world when needed.

To study one, the speaker builds a test setup with OP-TEE on a Raspberry Pi 3B+ connected through a UART adapter. A trustlet is extracted from its container with binwalk, and the embedded ELF is opened in Ghidra. The command handler there returns one of several public keys or a private developer key, depending on a parameter value, and one of those branches appears unreachable at first. The handler is then emulated in Qiling, with trace functions hooked and implemented in Python. AFL++ is used to fuzz the parameter until it reaches the hidden branch, and the crashing input C8C8 is replayed in the emulator and then on the bare-metal device, where it reaches the same branch.

The root cause is a type mismatch: the parameter is checked as a signed 16-bit integer but used as an unsigned 8-bit value, so 51,400 wraps to 200 and lands in the hidden branch. The speaker concludes that emulating and fuzzing simple trustlets is now approachable with short Python scripts. Deeper nested functions and fuzzing speed are the harder parts and will take the most time. The tools are linked on the final slide for anyone who wants to try them.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // Mount(ain) of Bugs
talks.teaser: It connects macOS mount callouts to MAC policy checks and shows how snapshot and arbitration tricks bypass TCC or reach root.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by positioning the Mandatory Access Control framework in the kernel, with hundreds of system-call hooks that aggregate the strictest policy decision. It follows the mount path from user space through VFS and mount_common, including snapshot-mount checks, and explains why the root, unsandboxed Disk Arbitration Service is attractive yet guarded by caller sandbox checks and mount-point ownership validation.

Two public 2017 cases anchor the middle: sniffing authorization references written for privileged SecurityAgent workflows, and a disk arbitration time-of-check-time-of-use race that remounted over root-owned paths and was chained to root in Pwn2Own. The speaker then describes personal findings—snapshot mounts that expose protected folders without full-disk access tied per app, overlaying a crafted TCC database via mount, abusing app translocation and LSD entitlements to read private data, and turning a FortiClient installer temp-directory write into root through periodic maintenance scripts and a prepared disk image.

Apple’s mitigations (new snapshot MAC hooks, file-descriptor and sandbox hardening on translocation) are noted alongside unresolved concerns such as cross-user full-disk access on shared Macs. Practitioners should treat mount and arbitration as high-value primitives for privacy bypass and privilege escalation, and expect further issues in the same vein.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2021 // GhostEmperor: From ProxyLogon to Kernel Mode, Story of a Modern Day Rootkit
talks.teaser: Traces a stealthy APT campaign from web server and Exchange footholds to a signed-driver loaded kernel rootkit.
talks.summary:
The talk presents GhostEmperor, a previously undocumented cluster the presenters describe as an advanced persistent threat aimed at government and telecommunications targets. Initial access came through compromised web-facing servers, and one infection on an Exchange server appeared around the ProxyLogon disclosure. A batch file ran a PowerShell script that needed a key to decrypt its embedded content, then created a service to load later stages.

Two service variants were seen: a C++ build with a key stored in its code, and a .NET build whose decryption key came from the victim's machine GUID, so it only worked on one system. The implant communicated using a malleable C2 profile that imitated Amazon traffic and prefixed data with fake JPEG or WAV headers. A rootkit was loaded by abusing a signed Cheat Engine driver to place an unsigned kernel component in memory. That rootkit, called Demodex, hid files, registry keys and TCP connections, and used zeroed PE headers and a patched pci.sys to obscure its origin.

Post-compromise activity used built-in Windows utilities, open-source scanners and WinRAR, with searches for Office documents and PST mail archives. The speakers attributed the activity to a Chinese-speaking actor based on shared tools, a key tied to a GitHub account and similarities with an older rootkit, while noting the links are not conclusive. Their closing point is that rootkits remain relevant despite recent Windows hardening.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Fault Injection (FI) Attacks Against Embedded Systems by András Kabai
talks.teaser: Shows how voltage glitching and electromagnetic pulses bypass read protection on a crypto wallet and an automotive diagnostic ECU.
talks.summary:
Fault injection deliberately pushes a chip outside its specified operating range, for example with a brief voltage drop or an electromagnetic pulse, so that a precisely timed disturbance can skip an instruction or flip a bit. The talk explains why this matters for software security: checks such as signature verification or authentication can be bypassed when the weakness sits in the hardware underneath them. Affordable DIY kits and FPGA-based timers are enough to build a working setup.

The first demo targets a Trezor One hardware wallet, whose microcontroller uses read data protection levels. The speaker removes decoupling capacitors to expose the core voltage, then times glitches from the reset line against the window in which the boot ROM reads option bytes and flash. After many automated attempts, a glitch downgrades protection from level 2 to level 1, restoring debug access and allowing memory to be dumped. The wallet's current firmware held no sensitive data in that dump, but the same weakness could expose secrets on other products built on this microcontroller.

The second demo uses electromagnetic fault injection against an automotive ECU in a car-hacking training setup. The attacker sends authentication attempts with a wrong key over the diagnostic protocol and fires a pulse at the chip to skip the result check. Once the glitch lands, the ECU accepts the session and a privileged routine opens a simulated door lock. The takeaway is that software-only defences fail when the underlying hardware is vulnerable. Redundant checks and stored complemented values can make such faults easier to detect, but they do not protect the boot code or silicon itself.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // DDoS Testing Your Infrastructure, including IPv6 SYN floods by Henrik Kramselund
talks.teaser: Walks through structured DDoS stress tests of your own internet-facing network, covering IPv6 floods and firewall limits.
talks.summary:
The presenter argues that every internet-connected network is scanned constantly, and that firewalls, routers and servers all rely on limited resources such as CPU, interrupt handling, memory and session tables. Any of these can become a denial-of-service bottleneck, so the talk proposes testing your own infrastructure in a controlled, structured way rather than waiting for a real attack. The first step is mapping open services with nmap, then confirming a stable baseline with monitoring before any load is applied.

The attack phase uses packet generators such as hping3 and t50, plus a Lua-based MoonGen script the presenter built to add IPv6 support. Tests start at low packet rates and step up while device behaviour and logs are watched, with each run lasting at least five minutes and sometimes up to fifteen, because some state tables fill slowly. One customer firewall failed at 50 000 packets per second but handled millions after its configuration was changed. Spoofed sources and unfinished IP fragments were also shown as ways to exhaust firewall state, and a probe-monitoring tool displayed a service going offline in colour.

The practical takeaways are to store target addresses in shell variables to avoid mistyped targets, timestamp commands and logs so results can be matched, and avoid changing settings mid-test. Traffic should be filtered as early as possible, for example with rate limits on ICMP and UDP at the router, and ISPs should be asked to apply router protection filters, since an upstream router can also take a network offline.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Everyday Numbers to Break Not So Everyday Software by Márk Módly
talks.teaser: Ordinary integers and floats become edge cases that break apps, APIs, and ops logic when types and limits are misunderstood.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that developers often treat computer arithmetic like school math, which creates exploitable gaps between specification, law, and code. It opens with a Swiss railway rule that caps trains at 256 axles, illustrating how rigid numeric thresholds in real systems invite creative circumvention rather than faithful compliance.

The core walkthrough moves through live examples in C and C++, Java, and JavaScript. Mixing signed, unsigned, and wider integer types makes a trivial sum evaluate to billions instead of zero. Floating-point rules produce missing exceptions, famously wrong decimal sums, and precision surprises when values are printed with higher accuracy. JavaScript’s safe integer ceiling means incrementing certain large values appears to do nothing, a pattern the speaker ties to denial-of-service scenarios and historical floating-point parsing failures.

The closing message is operational: integer overflow, type promotion, and float approximation are not academic quirks but common failure modes in production software. Reviewers and attackers alike should probe boundaries, inconsistent comparisons, and assumptions about exact decimals. The speaker frames the topic as material for developer security training rather than a single product bug class.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // A GREAT Sewing Workshop by Pierre Delcher
talks.teaser: Explores the February 2022 satellite modem outage via management-network intrusion, wiper malware, and hands-on firmware recovery.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the apparent mass failure of KA-SAT customer modems on 24 February 2022, the same day Russia announced its invasion of Ukraine, affecting tens of thousands of users and industrial deployments such as Enercon wind-turbine connectivity. It situates the outage against public procurement records showing Ukrainian government reliance on the service and later EU attribution of the activity to Russia, while noting how little was confirmed early on.

The middle of the session reconstructs a plausible attack path: entry through a Fortinet VPN into a TR-069 management network, references to Axiros ACS infrastructure, and discovery of a MIPS Linux wiper submitted from Italy that the team called Cosmic wiper—later publicly named Acid Rain—whose destructive behavior matches bricked modems. ViaSat’s late March statement about VPN bypass and remote deployment of destructive tools aligns with that timeline.

Without vendor firmware, the speaker acquires a production modem, maps its embedded architecture, and uses low-cost hardware probing—including deliberately shorting flash address lines with a sewing needle—to force a u-boot recovery shell. From there, a slow serial dump yields an unencrypted Linux image and bootloader knobs that can expose privileged services on the LAN. The closing point is how far open research can push a complex satellite incident narrative, while proprietary operator logs still limit full confirmation.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Spin That Steering Wheel by Domokos Nagy
talks.teaser: A live demo traces CAN bus recon, UDS service enumeration, and security-access flaws until a training ECU routine spins a steering wheel.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why in-vehicle cybersecurity matters alongside safety, referencing well-known automotive research and a “black box” mindset toward an unknown ECU. The speaker outlines an attack tree: understand in-car networking, focus on CAN, detach or bench the target, then layer Unified Diagnostic Services on top of the bus.

Theory covers ECU topology, CAN traffic noise, default versus extended diagnostic sessions, and how negative response codes leak which sessions, services, and routines exist. On a prepared two-wheel steering rig linked through a CAN interface to Linux and can-utils, the demo uses listening, ID enumeration, session probes, service scans, and routine-control attempts. Routine execution initially fails with security-access denials.

The live portion maps available security levels, studies seed behavior, respects brute-force timing limits, brute-forces a one-byte key space, then fixes routine-call message length and parameters for direction and speed. The wheel finally moves. Closing lessons stress weak entropy in early seeds, small key spaces, permissive attempt handling, and the need for testers who validate automotive security implementations before real-world impact.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Security Assesment of Embedded Firewalls - a Case Study by Csongor Ferenczi
talks.teaser: Walks through a teardown and memory analysis of an industrial firewall that ends in root command execution.
talks.summary:
Csongor Ferenczi describes an assessment of an industrial firewall based on a device first made in 2010. Such firewalls are needed because many industrial appliances are not built to be secure, and this one works transparently: it has a MAC address but no IP address. The assessment was part of a project to evaluate existing devices before building a stronger industrial firewall, with the goal of gaining root access.

The hardware work covered two Ethernet ports, a USB port, redundant power and a board with an FPGA that cuts USB off from the CPU. A debug header matched a JTAG pinout, but without a compatible tool or UART the hardware phase ended there, and the flash was not desoldered so the device stayed working. In software, most USB diagnostics were encrypted, but the configurator's network connection used port knocking before SSH. Its binary was too large for IDA, so a memory dump taken during diagnostics retrieval revealed a script path handed to a root shell. Swapping that path for a searchable string confirmed command execution as root, limited in output and command length; longer scripts went over USB.

With that access, the file system was dumped over USB, yielding scripts, configurations, custom binaries and keys, and the config encryption key was found to differ for each configuration. A live demo injected an ls command through a debugger to list the root folder. The takeaways are that obscurity does not protect embedded devices, that expert penetration testing matters, and that the vendor, notified more than a year earlier, had not replied, so the flaw stays open even if fixing it is architectural.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Pwned in Space by Paul Coggin
talks.teaser: Surveys the security risks facing satellites and spacecraft, from jamming and unencrypted links to past intrusions.
talks.summary:
Paul Coggin opens with his telecom and red team background and frames the talk as a baseline look at spacecraft security rather than ground systems. He notes that satellite operators are moving ground station services into public clouds, that companies propose placing cloud infrastructure in orbit, and that some plan data centers inside lunar lava tunnels. He asks how incident response and forensics would work once such systems are in space.

He then walks through the threat spectrum, from jamming and sensor dazzling, which stop when the source is removed, to directed energy and kinetic strikes that cause permanent damage and debris that could trigger a Kessler-style cascade. Space radiation can flip bits and break encryption sessions, which makes radiation hardening a cost and risk trade-off. Many satellite links remain unencrypted, so traffic can be captured passively with a specialized receiver. Examples include a US Navy UHF satellite that CB radio users exploited, leading to 39 arrests across nine states, and the Turtle malware, which reported back over satellite broadcast while commands came over a wired line. He also reviews reported satellite intrusions, including Landsat 7 in 2007 and 2008, a 2014 NOAA incident attributed to China, and a disputed 1999 Skynet case, along with two malware infections aboard the ISS spread by a USB drive and a laptop.

He closes with standards and guidance from bodies such as CCSDS and NIST, and suggests that software-defined satellites may make patching easier. For practitioners wanting a home lab, he points to NASA's core flight system, a 42 orbit simulator, and the Icarus tool for modeling denial-of-service against constellations.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Web3 + Scams = It's a Match! by Zoltán Balázs
talks.teaser: Surveys crypto and NFT scams, from pump-and-dumps and fake giveaways to a wallet-drainer website and hijacked social accounts.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how scammers exploit the hype around cryptocurrencies and NFTs to take people's money. It starts with the size of the market and then goes through pump-and-dump tokens and rug pulls, including a token tied to a popular TV series and an NFT project whose promoter allegedly stopped delivering on promised perks. Fake giveaways run by bots under popular Twitter posts are shown next, along with a fake withdrawal site that asked victims to send crypto before they could cash out.

The middle section covers account takeovers. Hijacked Instagram and Twitter accounts were used to push scam links, and the speaker suggests one Instagram case may have involved a support-desk social engineering attack. A company's Twitter account was reportedly compromised through admin access said to be sold on the dark web. The speaker then describes research that began in a Discord scam-alert channel: a site asked users to connect their wallet and confirm what looked like a mint, but the signature actually transferred their NFTs to the scammer. Searching the operator's GitHub history led to a less obfuscated copy of the script, which contained a back door sending high-value NFTs to the framework author. Other attacks covered included bookmarklets that steal Discord admin tokens and hardware wallet tricks such as requests for backup phrases.

The closing advice is practical: verify sources, never share seed phrases or private keys, prefer app-based two-factor authentication over SMS, use a password manager, and slow down before confirming any transaction. Keeping separate wallets for risky sites and for long-term storage also reduces exposure.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Automating Binary Analysis with Ghidra's P-Code by Gergely Révay
talks.teaser: Shows how Ghidra's P-code intermediate representation and scripting API can automate binary analysis tasks.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at automating reverse engineering with Ghidra, the open-source framework released by the NSA, with a focus on its intermediate representation, P-code. It covers the scripting options: Java is the native language and has the best development support, Python works through Jython or the Ghidra Bridge, and headless mode runs a script on binaries without the graphical interface. The flat API is kept stable across versions, while the wider SDK exposes nearly everything Ghidra itself uses, which is powerful but takes time to learn.

The core idea is that P-code expresses each assembly instruction as generic operations, so a script written against it can work across every architecture Ghidra's decompiler supports. Raw P-code maps closely to individual instructions, while high P-code, produced by the decompiler, exposes function arguments and variables that can be queried directly. Demonstrations include a script that lists imported functions as a quick triage step, and a second that scans a binary for COM usage, a technique malware uses to hide network communication, by finding calls to CoCreateInstance and their cross-references.

A third example reads the CLSID and IID arguments passed to that call from high P-code, avoiding manual backtracking to recover them. The identifiers can then be looked up in the Windows registry or online to reveal which COM component the binary uses. The takeaway is that Ghidra scripting and P-code suit repetitive analysis work, and the right tool depends on the task at hand.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // A New Default Value of OpenSSL could Multiply a DoS Potential by Szilárd Pfeiffer
talks.teaser: Shows how OpenSSL 3.0's default Diffie-Hellman settings make servers far costlier to hit with a key-exchange DoS.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from Diffie-Hellman key exchange, where each side performs a costly modular exponentiation. That step happens before authentication, so an unauthenticated client can send a crafted value and force the server to do the expensive work. The speaker stresses that this hits availability rather than confidentiality. The research began as a comparison of cryptographic libraries, which revealed large differences between OpenSSL 1.1 and 3.0.

The main finding concerns OpenSSL 3.0 defaults. TLS 1.3 Diffie-Hellman is enabled, the library uses large private exponents, and its default groups run from 2048 to 8192 bits. In a demo, generating 8192-bit public keys managed about three per second with long exponents, versus almost 50 with small ones. The speaker estimated the slowest default exchange costs 50 to 90 times more than in OpenSSL 1.1. Apache and nginx inherit these defaults unless named groups are set explicitly. A planned 3.0.6 fix switches to small exponents, but the default group list cannot change under OpenSSL's versioning policy, so the 8192-bit group stays.

Practical guidance: in TLS 1.3, set named groups explicitly, offer nistp256 and prefer x25519, and avoid large finite-field groups. For TLS 1.2, use well-known Diffie-Hellman parameters or adjust the private key length. The speaker published a command-line tool for changing private key size in parameter files. Asked about real-world abuse, he said he had heard reports of such attacks against large providers but had no details.
