talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Practical EDR Bypass Methods in 2022 by István Tóth
talks.teaser: Covers classic EDR evasion methods such as DLL unhooking, entropy reduction and proxying tooling outside monitored hosts.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how endpoint detection and response (EDR) products can be bypassed in practice. The speaker defines a bypass as either triggering no auto-prevention or raising no high-severity alerts, and notes that detection depends on each customer's custom rules. Because commercial products are hard to test legally, the speaker argues their strength rests partly on obscurity. The user-mode DLL injected into each process is presented as the easiest component to attack, since it runs with the process's own privileges.

Techniques shown include unhooking ntdll by restoring a clean copy of the DLL read from disk, which the speaker says still reduces EDR visibility substantially in 2022. Other methods lower the entropy of encrypted payloads by spacing out bytes, and resolve Windows API calls at runtime to avoid suspicious imports. These were combined in a custom loader for a Cobalt Strike artifact, which ran a beacon without alerts, though default payloads were now flagged. For kernel-callback detections, a load-library alternative avoided a hooked call. A Zoom DLL side-loading example used a version.dll placed in the application folder, and a simple window-clicking routine dismissed the trust warning.

The closing section argues for keeping tooling off protected hosts: a SOCKS proxy inside the implant lets operators run tools from their own machine, and reverse port forwarding supports an SMB relay attack, including a variant that routes through a Linux camera. The speaker concludes that default configurations can be bypassed with effort, but customized detections make bypass much harder, so defenders should tune rules beyond defaults.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // How to Kickstart a Security Program? by Ottucsák József
talks.teaser: Shows how a newly hired security lead can map obligations, find gaps and prioritise early work without alienating the business.
talks.summary:
The talk covers the first stretch of taking charge of a security program, drawing on the speaker's own experience moving into security leadership. The core problem is that frameworks and regulations describe what to achieve but not how to start, and new security leads often inherit legacy systems, unclear ownership and expectations nobody stated. Early steps suggested include asking for a written plan with 30, 60 and 90 day outcomes, reading wikis, policies and old issue trackers to see how things really work, and understanding why the company hired you in the first place.

Next comes mapping obligations and gaps. Contractual and legal requirements become a matrix that policies are built from, and gaps are found through frameworks, risk registers, threat modeling run without blame, and third-party audits, which the speaker doubts. Priorities go to high-risk items, fixes that free up time, and cheap quick wins. Delegating recurring operational work to the teams that own systems matters, and self-hosted tools carry upkeep costs, so reusing security features already in CI/CD pipelines reduces friction. Reports should serve both leadership and engineers, and repeated issues, such as cross-site scripting across products, can justify targeted training.

The closing advice centres on humility and sequencing: build foundations such as centralized identity before flashy technology, avoid overhauling everything on day one, and aim for security proportionate to real risk. Sharing lessons learned across the industry is presented as overdue. Suggested reading included The Phoenix Project and a CSO podcast.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // What are We Missing in Web Applications? by Mirza Burhan Baig
talks.teaser: Walks through business logic flaws in banking apps that let testers skip OTP steps and role checks scanners miss.
talks.summary:
The talk asks what web application testers still miss once scanners and framework defenses are in place. The speaker argues that business logic flaws, where a workflow step is skipped or a client-side value is trusted, are largely invisible to static and dynamic scanners and come down to design choices by developers. Common causes include excessive trust in the client, users who do not follow the intended sequence, and missing input validation on the server.

Several real cases from banking and insurance work are described. In one, a fraud detection system built on Oracle financials let a low-privileged analyst replay saved requests and responses from a higher-privileged user and see the same data, which led to a CVE published in 2019. In a mobile banking login, the one-time passcode was checked only on its first use, so the flow could be replayed past the OTP step. In a separate internet banking application, a saved successful response was reused after a wrong OTP, which opened the dashboard. The speaker says the banking issues were reported to the clients and fixed quickly.

For testing, the speaker recommends modelling each feature as a workflow, building threat models per module, capturing a legitimate flow, and replaying it with steps removed or with different user roles. Burp Suite extensions can automate role-based replay of workflows. For developers, the advice is to enforce access control and step ordering on the server and to ask where data goes and who can reach each endpoint. Online labs were suggested for hands-on practice.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Security in IoT - the Investigation of Bluetooth Low Energy by János Kepics
talks.teaser: Fuzzes Bluetooth Low Energy link-layer messages against smart locks, bulbs and trackers to see which ones crash.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the security of Bluetooth Low Energy, the variant many IoT devices such as smart watches, locks and cameras use. The speaker explains the stack's application, host and controller layers, and notes that the link layer, which handles advertising and connection setup, is written by chip vendors rather than application developers. Because little testing reaches that layer before pairing, the speaker argues it deserves attention, and walks through the sequence of link-layer messages between a peripheral and a central device.

To probe it, the speaker built a fuzzing engine on top of a Bluetooth framework. It generates weighted random values for chosen message types and fields, keeps seeds so runs can be reproduced, and wraps the data in link-layer packets sent through a low-cost Nordic dongle. Health checks and keep-alive scripts monitor each target during a run. Against a smart lock, a smart light bulb and an item tracker, two devices crashed and needed their batteries removed to recover, and one stayed in a connected state after repeated connection requests. The smart lock could only be unlocked again after a hard reset.

The speaker concludes that such findings should be reported to the Bluetooth SIG and to the chip vendor, since the flaw sits in code the manufacturer implements. Possible mitigations include randomised Bluetooth addresses or hardening the pairing process. Planned work includes making the fuzzer stateful, adding more detailed feedback from targets, and exploring AI-based approaches. The talk closes with a short aside on capturing BLE advertising packets using a cheap software-defined radio.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2022 // Cybersecurity Cannot Ignore Climate Change by Chloé Messdaghi
talks.teaser: Explains why climate change matters to security teams and how companies can prepare for its impact.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security teams can no longer leave climate change out of their risk discussions. The speaker, a strategist with an infosec background, first lays out the physical evidence: rising seas, longer droughts, more intense storms and wildfires. Projections cited include at least 1.2 billion people displaced by climate-related events by 2050, and one third of plant and animal species at risk of extinction within 50 years. Plastic pollution, and the links between deforestation, habitat loss and disease spillover, are also covered.

The middle of the talk turns to the current trajectory and to industry's role. The speaker notes that current pledges put the world on track for roughly three degrees Celsius of warming, well beyond the Paris agreement's goals, and that the technology sector uses large amounts of electricity, including for data centers. Climate-driven disruption can affect supply chains, remote work, the delivery of aid and access to water and power, and attackers may target those resources. Executives who avoid the subject leave organizations unprepared for these events.

The closing section offers practical steps. Suggestions include raising awareness inside companies, adopting ESG frameworks and annual sustainability reporting, and running scenario exercises that ask how higher temperatures would affect operations and staff. Individuals and events can track carbon footprints with public calculators, buy less, keep devices in use for longer and favor hybrid conferences. The speaker urges security professionals to fold these scenarios into their planning and incident response work.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Speeding Up Linux Disk Encryption by Ignat Korchagin
talks.teaser: Explains why Linux dm-crypt throttled disk throughput and how a synchronous patch recovers it.
talks.summary:
Ignat Korchagin, who works on performance and security at Cloudflare, starts by placing disk encryption within the storage stack. He compares self-encrypting drives, block-layer encryption such as dm-crypt, filesystem-level options and application-level encryption, noting the trade-offs each has in speed, visibility and exposure of keys in memory. Cloudflare chose open-source block-layer encryption for its servers.

When the encrypted servers performed worse than expected, the team benchmarked dm-crypt on a RAM disk to remove storage hardware from the picture. Throughput fell from over 1 GB/s on the raw RAM disk to roughly 150 MB/s encrypted, while the crypto benchmark suggested a worst case near 700 MB/s. Tracing the kernel code showed that dm-crypt queued each request several times, a design that dated back to the spinning-disk era. The fix was a patch with a runtime switch that bypasses these queues and routes crypto through a small synchronous module that defers to the kernel's hardware-accelerated AES implementation.

With the patch enabled, read and write throughput each reached about 300 MB/s, roughly 600 MB/s combined. On a production SSD, encrypted and unencrypted latencies converged, and a cache service's p99 response time spikes disappeared. The speaker cautions that gains appear mainly for small-block, high-IOPS workloads, that larger blocks saw some degradation, and that the approach depends on x86 hardware. The work was merged into mainline Linux starting with 5.9, and he advises benchmarking before enabling it.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Paste Wars: fighting for copypaste freedom by Ignat Korchagin
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of #Hacktivity2020 // Paste Wars: fighting for copypaste freedom by Ignat Korchagin.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Ignat Korchagin discusses the friction between password security best practices and web services that actively block copy-paste functionality in password input fields. While modern password security relies heavily on password managers generating long, complex, random, and unique passwords, blocking paste operations disrupts this security model and forces users into insecure habits. Korchagin analyzes the ineffective workarounds commonly used to bypass paste restrictions and introduces an OS-level tool, `passkb`, designed to simulate physical keystrokes and render client-side paste blocking obsolete.

### Key Topics
- **Password Complexity and Password Managers**: Passwords face attacks ranging from brute-force and dictionary attacks to client-side phishing and server-side breaches. To mitigate these, modern passwords must be long, unique, and random, necessitating password managers that encrypt credentials under a single master key.
- **Why Web Services Block Paste**: Citing investigations by Troy Hunt, the speaker notes common developer rationales for blocking clipboard paste: unfounded fears of clipboard malware (ignoring that keystroke loggers pose the same threat), misguided beliefs about stopping brute-force attacks, vague compliance claims, or organizational inertia.
- **Shortcomings of Browser-Level Workarounds**: 
  - Disabling clipboard/paste events in browser configuration (such as Firefox's settings) lacks portability, fails against other detection events, and breaks legitimate modern reactive web app features.
  - Browser extensions either inject JavaScript to neutralize paste filters or autofill fields directly via DOM manipulation. However, these extensions introduce security risks: they require broad permissions to read and modify all browsing data, run with network access, and present an attractive target for extension hijacking.

### Technical Details
To solve this cleanly, Korchagin presents an operating system–level approach that bypasses web-layer paste blocking entirely. Rather than attempting to suppress or manipulate the webpage's JavaScript filters inside the DOM, the user pastes their password into an external CLI tool called `passkb`.

- **Keystroke Simulation**: On Linux, `passkb` utilizes a special `uinput` (`winput` in transcript) device interface. On Windows, it leverages the `SendInput` API function.
- **Workflow**: The user launches the tool in a terminal, pastes their complex password into the CLI, and has a 5-second window to switch focus back to the target input field. The operating system then injects synthesized keystrokes directly into the field.
- **Security & Reliability Characteristics**: Because the tool runs as an independent OS process outside the browser, it has no network access and cannot read web browsing data. It can be sandboxed or jailed according to the Unix philosophy of doing one thing. Because the web application sees genuine typing events, it cannot detect or block the input with JavaScript paste filters.
- **Limitations**: The tool does not currently support macOS (help wanted) and does not target mobile platforms. From a usability standpoint, it requires running a terminal side-by-side with the browser, configuring Linux device permissions, and manually switching windows within the 5-second timer.

### Takeaways
Paste-blocking JavaScript on password inputs fails to improve security and instead degrades it by discouraging password manager adoption. Even official bodies like the UK government advise service operators never to block pasting in password forms. Korchagin urges web developers to cease blocking paste operations, encourages users to employ password managers, and invites open-source contributions to extend `passkb` across platforms.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // The 5G Battle by Róbert Moody and Bence Horváth
talks.teaser: Maps 5G threat actors from activists to state-backed groups and shows how intelligence can be shared across teams.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe how the 5G rollout has created a new threat picture for telecom operators. They sort the actors into three groups: anti-5G activists, whose beliefs are often fed by conspiracy theories and organised disinformation; well-resourced state-backed and criminal groups that target telcos and equipment vendors for interception, access or extortion; and corporate espionage actors who go after new technology and manufacturing know-how. The activist group, they note, has moved from online posts to physical attacks on towers in several countries, and telco staff have faced harassment.

To give stakeholders a common language, the team mapped each group's behaviour onto the MITRE ATT&CK framework. For activists, they walk through a lifecycle that runs from planning and target selection to information gathering, identifying weaknesses, building a following through petitions and social groups, and testing capabilities. For the higher-end actors, the focus is on defence evasion, persistence and covert command and control, along with insider bribery and fake base stations used to capture traffic.

The closing section proposes four teams working from the same intelligence: a grey team for cyber threat intelligence that sets priority requirements, red teams running intelligence-led tests, blue teams building detections from adversary methods, and a white team of senior management deciding on investment, public relations and when to involve law enforcement. The takeaway is that shared intelligence lets each function act on the same picture.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #Hacktivity2020 // DevSecOps in the Financial Services Industry by Stéphane Chmielewski.
talks.summary: Stefan Smilevski describes how Phenogy embeds security into agile DevOps for Luxembourg fintech amid tightening regulation. He argues integrated DevSec teams must coach developers, automate secrets with HashiCorp Vault, run SonarQube SAST and OWASP ZAP DAST in Harness pipelines, scan containers with Clair, express policy as Terraform compliance tests, and schedule kube-hunter or OpenUnison penetration hooks. He stresses iterative rollout, KPI-driven compliance, and continuous engineer training to keep pace with releases without siloed audit cycles.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Hacking Facial Recognition Systems by Alexander Polyakov
talks.teaser: Outlines a structured methodology for physical adversarial testing of facial recognition hardware and software combinations.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames facial recognition as a practical lens for broader machine-learning security. Traditional software flaws often involve malformed structured inputs; vision and audio systems instead accept unstructured sensor data, which enables evasion, poisoning, inversion, backdoors, and model extraction. The session concentrates on evasion and adversarial examples that fool models while staying hard for humans to notice.

A customer engagement aimed to pick dependable hardware and software pairings for a sensitive site, with emphasis on attacks that work in the real world rather than only on static images. The speaker describes a repeatable test plan: clarify attacker intent (lower confidence, avoid detection, or impersonate someone), map environmental limits (masks, glasses, bandanas, lighting, print color drift), pick optimization methods, and define success (misclassification rate, stealth, robustness, compute cost). Physical trials showed evasion is feasible; glasses and bandanas scored strongest. A shared “universal” attack then compared models, including how transferability depends on architecture, datasets, outputs, and ensemble training. Camera quality, color rendering, distance, and compression materially shifted outcomes; better cameras were not always safer.

Defense options depend on whether the buyer controls training, APIs, or devices alone, and none is universal—adversarial retraining is costly and often bypassed, architectural hardening can sap accuracy, and detection reacts after the fact. Practitioners should adopt a secure AI lifecycle: test, harden, monitor, and retest as threats evolve, while building joint expertise across security and data science teams.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Anatomy of Automated Account Takeovers by Tal Eliyahu & Begum Calguner
talks.teaser: Traces how criminals turn stolen credentials into automated account takeovers, from buying access to cashing out.
talks.summary:
The talk treats automated account takeovers (ATOs) as a profit-driven criminal business rather than a single technique. The speaker argues that the trend keeps growing because tools are cheap and easy to run, leaked credentials circulate within minutes of a breach, and some companies pay to recover customer data or struggle to catch fake accounts. Credential stuffing is used as the main example, although the research behind the talk reviewed more than 30 ATO methods.

The lifecycle is split into acquiring access, preparation, cashing in and cashing out. Access is bought from account shops, sometimes bundled with a digital mask that copies a victim's device and behaviour traits to pass fraud checks. Attack tools range from simple email checkers and configurable bots to scripted browsers run through residential proxies, and freelancers are hired to write custom configs. After a takeover, attackers apply for loans or credit, have cards sent to mail drops, and move money through mules, smurfing or peer-to-peer payments. Most takeovers last under 24 hours, often only minutes.

For defenders, the recommendations include unified authentication across channels, multi-factor designs shaped around real user flows, breach lookup services, password managers and credit freezes. The speaker also argues that companies should not rely on self-regulation alone, and that teams should define what they mean by bad bots before buying a tool to stop them.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Service Mess to Service Mesh by Rob Richardson
talks.teaser: Compares API gateways and service meshes with live Istio and Linkerd work securing and shaping Kubernetes east-west traffic.
talks.summary:
Microservices turn formerly internal calls into reachable endpoints, which makes east-west traffic hard to govern with an API gateway alone. The presenter frames a service mesh as infrastructure that observes, controls, and secures communication inside a cluster, typically by injecting sidecar proxies that terminate mutual TLS and consult a control plane before forwarding.

The talk walks from monolith-to-microservices history through north-south versus east-west traffic, then layers capabilities beyond baseline policy: topology discovery, health metrics, circuit breaking, canary and A/B routing, and dashboards. Istio is characterized as a broad, bundled stack; Linkerd as a simpler on-ramp that can grow via add-ons. Live segments install Linkerd on Kubernetes, validate the cluster, and use Istio’s Bookinfo demo to shift review traffic by percentage and headers.

Practitioners hear explicit trade-offs: roughly one and a half to two times more containers, larger clusters, and real operational cost. Mesh fits when workloads need strong segmentation (for example PCI or multi-tenant isolation beyond namespace labels), in-depth service security, or advanced routing; otherwise the overhead may outweigh the benefit.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Hacking the Hacktivity 2019 badge by Valerio Di Giampetro
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding #Hacktivity2020 // Hacking the Hacktivity 2019 badge by Valerio Di Giampetro.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Valerio Di Giampietro details his journey of accidentally bricking the Hacktivity 2019 conference badge and subsequently reverse engineering and reprogramming its hardware. The badge, initially configured to run MicroPython, features an ESP32-WROOM-32 module as its main dual-core processor and an Atmel ATSAMD21G16B ARM Cortex-M0 microcontroller as a co-processor. When Di Giampietro tried flashing an Arduino blink sketch, the IDE misidentified the badge as an Adafruit Circuit Playground Express (which uses a SAMD21 chip with four times more flash and RAM), wiping out the bootloader and rendering the badge unresponsive.

### Key Topics
- **Hardware Architecture**: The badge integrates an ESP32 (4 MB flash, 520 KB SRAM, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth) and an ATSAMD21G16B co-processor (64 KB flash, 8 KB SRAM). The SAMD21 handles USB connectivity, touch buttons, and RGB LEDs, and communicates with the ESP32 via UART and I2C.
- **PCB Reverse Engineering**: Lacking official schematics, Di Giampietro soldered pin headers, traced board layers using GIMP and a multimeter, and leveraged schematics and repository code from the Disobey 2018 badge designed by the same team.
- **Bypassing the Co-Processor**: Because the bricked co-processor left all its I/O pins floating as inputs by default, Di Giampietro bypassed it entirely to flash the ESP32 directly through exposed serial header pins using a TTL serial adapter.
- **Reflashing ATSAMD21**: Flashing firmware back onto the ARM co-processor required connecting to its Serial Wire Debug (SWD) pins using a Segger J-Link EDU Mini probe.
- **Arduino Integration & Optimization**: Transitioning away from bloated Atmel Studio tooling to an Arduino-based workflow, Di Giampietro resolved serial buffer overruns during flashing by implementing non-blocking serial communication and expanding buffer sizes.

### Technical Details
1. **Board Layout & Pin Discovery**: Tracing revealed crucial headers, including J9 (I2C bus connecting ESP32, SAMD21, and the 128x64 LCD), J10 and J12 (ESP32 GPIOs and bootloader pin), J11 (SAMD21 SWD pins: SWDIO, SWDCLK, RESET, VCC, GND), and J13 (ESP32 UART TX/RX).
2. **Direct ESP32 Flashing**: Di Giampietro pulled the bootloader pin low via jumper during power-up, validated the bootloader prompt via PuTTY, and flashed sketches from the Arduino IDE over TTL serial. This worked only because the unprogrammed SAMD21 did not drive the shared UART lines.
3. **Firmware on the SAMD21**: Attempting to develop a USB-to-UART bridge in Atmel Studio proved cumbersome due to multi-gigabyte installations, hundreds of boilerplate files, and complex clock tree configurations. Finding existing Arduino port code from the Disobey 2018 repository allowed Di Giampietro to flash an open-source bootloader using SWD/dfu-util.
4. **Bridge Performance Tuning**: The initial Arduino-based serial bridge dropped bytes during sketch upload. Di Giampietro resolved this by increasing the RX/TX serial buffer size from 64 bytes to 512 bytes and rewriting the bridge logic to be completely non-blocking, checking buffer readiness before read/write calls.

### Takeaways
Through hardware reverse engineering, SWD reflashing, and firmware optimizations, the bricked Hacktivity 2019 badge was transformed into a fully operational, versatile Arduino development board. Di Giampietro highlights two core engineering lessons: never remain stuck forcing an intractable path (such as struggling through Atmel Studio when simpler frameworks can be ported), and always utilize partial artifacts or documentation from related open-source hardware to accelerate debugging.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Stuxnet Attack by Dr. Mo Ashouri
talks.teaser: Revisits Stuxnet a decade on, walking through its zero-day exploits, USB spread and PLC sabotage of centrifuge motors.
talks.summary:
This Hacktivity 2020 talk revisits Stuxnet about a decade after its discovery in 2010, aiming to bring out details that are less widely known. It opens with background on uranium enrichment centrifuges and the programmable logic controllers that drive their motors, explaining why tampering with those controllers could cause physical damage. The worm existed in multiple versions and is said to have infected approximately 200,000 computers, though the exact figure is unknown. Its original target was Iranian nuclear facilities, but it spread to industrial sites in other countries.

The middle of the talk walks through the propagation and exploitation chain. Stuxnet used the MS08-067 flaw in Windows SMB to move across networks and shared folders, and a print spooler weakness let it drop files into the system directory through a malicious MOF file that ran with system privileges. Privilege escalation relied on a keyboard layout flaw that gave kernel-level code execution, along with a task scheduler checksum weakness. For air-gapped sites, the worm spread by USB drive using the LNK shortcut icon vulnerability CVE-2010-2568. The speaker's lab analysis of an infected drive found six files, four of them shortcut files that loaded a DLL to run the payload.

The final stage targeted Step 7 industrial control software, injecting DLLs into its project files so that code reached the PLCs and altered centrifuge motor frequencies. The worm also stored an encrypted configuration of about 1860 bytes holding C2 server URLs and activation and deactivation times. The talk closes by questioning whether infecting machines in the United States, Russia and India was worthwhile, given that uranium enrichment in Iran was not stopped. The practical takeaway is that Stuxnet showed isolated industrial networks could still be reached.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Making developers security aware. Lessons learnt. by Mateusz Olejarka
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from running appsec workshops for developers, covering communication, secrecy, testing limits, training and compliance.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why application security efforts aimed at developers often fall short. The presenter, a senior security specialist who co-authors a developer-focused AppSec workshop, opens with wartime stories: a 1940 airborne assault on a Belgian fort that succeeded through surprise and new explosives, and a bomber study that showed how survivorship bias skews conclusions. The core argument is that tools alone miss things and that people are the most important asset.

Drawing on more than 70 workshops, the presenter describes recurring problems. Security staff and developers communicate poorly, with slow replies and heavy jargon. Security is often seen as a secretive department that watches over others, and developers feel it is not their job. Penetration testing is treated as sufficient, although it covers only part of an application and may happen once a year while releases ship daily. The recommended response is to push security earlier, into design, threat modelling, code review and automated testing.

For training, the presenter argues it should be developer-oriented, work from source code rather than proxy tools, and keep participants actively involved. It should include many real breach examples, and be flexible, self-paced and online. Offensive exercises suit security champions who can use the skills at work, while broader teams benefit from defensive courses. Finally, compliance questionnaires do not make an application secure. Requirements should be written in language developers understand and created together with them. The talk closes by urging security staff to build direct relationships with developers and to secure management support.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Penetration testing VoIP UC nowadays by Moritz Abrell
talks.teaser: Demonstrates attacks on VoIP and unified communications, from desk phones and PBXs to softphones and Teams conferences.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how a modern voice-over-IP and unified communications setup can be attacked. It starts from a typical mid-sized company layout with desk phones, softphones, a PBX, an application server, an LDAP link to Active Directory, SIP trunks, remote workers, a conferencing system and a session border controller. The speaker introduces Wirebug, an open-source Python toolset he built because existing VoIP security tools are few and often outdated.

The demonstrations cover several attack paths. Spoofed LLDP-MED packets reveal the voice VLAN ID and grant network access to it. Media encryption keys carried in the SDP crypto attribute can be read from signaling traffic, which allows a captured SRTP call to be decrypted. A fake provisioning server got a desk phone to accept a new administrator password. Softphone calls were downgraded to unencrypted RTP by dropping key exchange messages. Unencrypted directory queries could expose domain administrator credentials to a man in the middle. On the PBX, registration responses allowed user enumeration and online password guessing. A session border controller was bypassed by changing the user agent string, and a reverse proxy forwarded unauthenticated registrations over TCP. In a Microsoft Teams conference, the media key was passed through Microsoft servers in plain form.

The speaker concludes that vendor "just works" defaults and manufacturer documentation often leave these systems exposed. He recommends treating VoIP and unified communications as part of the security concept and testing them in dedicated penetration tests. He stresses that the issues shown come from insecure configurations and implementations rather than new vulnerabilities.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Blue Team Over The Air by Besim Altinok
talks.teaser: Explains rogue Wi-Fi attacks such as Karma and Pineapple, and open-source tools that let defenders spot them.
talks.summary:
Devices that remember old wireless networks and reconnect automatically, especially to free networks without passwords, are easy targets. The speaker describes the risks this creates, including national security concerns, loss of privacy and data theft. He then walks through common attacker methods: open fake access points with tempting names, Karma-style replies to a client's probe requests, and Pineapple-style pools of collected network names used to open fake networks. Each leaves signs in the air, such as several network names appearing from unique MAC addresses or a growing number of probe responses.

On the defensive side, the talk presents an open-source project with modules for fingerprinting, monitoring, confusing attackers and active defence. Its first module targets Pineapple activity. It hops across channels, collects beacons, flags suspicious networks, then sends authentication packets to the attacking device so clients are not affected. A sensor tool called Pinocchio watches probe requests and warns users about nearby fake access points. A probe-request tracker can show which devices previously joined malicious networks, or match company or blacklisted network names to reveal who is likely exposed. A PCAP parser lets analysts run the same detection offline.

The talk ends with a trap-style tool that opens a fake enterprise access point and generates fabricated data to confuse wireless intruders. The practical takeaway is that Wi-Fi threats can be seen and countered by monitoring the air, not only by hardening the network itself.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Infra security automation in CI/CD: impossible is nothing. 1/2 by Davide Cioccia
talks.teaser: Explains why manual infrastructure pen tests stall CI/CD pipelines and how incremental security checks can keep pace with releases.
talks.summary:
The speakers, security engineers at ING Netherlands, describe why manual infrastructure security testing does not scale for a large, fast-moving environment. Each release moves through test, acceptance and production stages, and the acceptance stage can stall for about two weeks while manual pen testers review it. Devops teams ship several times a week, so results from a manual review are often out of date before they arrive.

They split the stack into layers: application code and its libraries, the system calls and operating system beneath it, and the infrastructure made of binaries, services, ports and files. Static analysis in the IDE and centralized incremental scans can cover the application layer, and software composition analysis can catch vulnerable open source libraries. Infrastructure, however, was only checked when machines were provisioned, and monthly vulnerability scans kept re-testing old machines without understanding what had changed. With roughly 2,000 applications and an estimated 20,000 machines, they framed the core question as how to assess the security of each infrastructure change on every commit.

The talk's first part sets up that problem and the terminology used later. The technical details and the framework built to run these checks as an integration test in the pipeline are handed over to a colleague. The speakers also outline roadmap items that were not yet implemented at the time. The main takeaway is that infrastructure checks need to be incremental and automated to keep up with frequent releases.

talks.teaser: Explains how communication, leadership and emotional intelligence can be practised to drive retention and performance.
talks.summary:
Scott Asai argues that soft skills, learned through practice rather than in a classroom, drive promotions and retention. He describes IT staff promoted from technical roles into management, where the job becomes leading former peers. Micromanagers, he says, cost companies more than most other factors.

On communication, he separates hearing from listening and urges people to clarify what they heard before responding. He notes that text and email strip out tone and body language, so video calls help. Leadership, he says, means getting things done through people. He recounts managing about 30 remote tutors, holding short weekly one-on-ones and asking how he could support each one under stress. Leaders who build trust earn the right to give hard feedback.

For emotional intelligence, he uses a thought, feeling and action loop, drawing on his own fear of public speaking. Reframing a negative self-statement, then practising and reviewing recordings of himself, helped him take on bigger talks. He closes by saying soft skills improve only through repetition, so listeners should practise on video calls and messages now.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Dissectiong and Comparing Different Binaries to Malware Analysis by Filipi Pires
talks.teaser: Walks through identifying a malicious PDF, from file-type checks to decoding obfuscated JavaScript and tracing its payload.
talks.summary:
Filipi Pires opens with a malware analysis workflow: decide whether an artifact is malware or a malicious document, choose static or dynamic analysis, report the findings, strengthen defenses, and turn indicators of compromise into threat intelligence. He frames the talk as fundamentals rather than a hacking showcase. Dynamic analysis runs a sample in a virtual machine or sandbox, and the resulting report still has to be interpreted by the analyst.

The first demo covers identification. The file command matches magic numbers from a signature database, so changing the leading bytes of a Python script changes how it is labelled and stops it running. The lesson is that file extensions cannot be trusted. The strings command has a four-character minimum by default, so a three-character ELF signature is missed unless the length is lowered. He also compares ELF and PE layouts, noting headers, sections where code can hide, and packers such as UPX that obscure them.

The main case is a malicious PDF. Its structure has a header, body, cross-reference table and trailer. A PDF triage tool flagged an OpenAction and five JavaScript entries. Following object references, the largest compressed stream decompressed to obfuscated JavaScript, and running it in an HTML page exposed a payload variable. That payload was Unicode-encoded, was decoded into an executable, and its network traffic revealed a command-and-control address. The takeaway is to combine several tools and carry the results into reporting and intelligence.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Machine Learning Evasion Competition by Zoltán Balázs
talks.teaser: Covers a competition where participants modify Windows malware so it evades machine learning detectors while staying functional.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces a machine learning evasion competition in which contestants receive 50 working malware samples and must modify them so that three machine learning detection models label them benign while they still run. Each sample can earn up to three points, the leaderboard ranks total bypasses first, and total model queries break ties. Droppers, self-extracting archives and multiple registrations are banned, and winners must publish a write-up. The speaker demonstrates the web platform and a newer API for submissions.

Lessons from the previous year's edition were also covered. Packing samples often broke files that were already packed, while adding sections or resources copied from Microsoft files evaded models but broke samples with self-checks. Appending overlay data was the approach that won that year, found by brute-forcing the models. Empty sections or large overlays were also noted as sometimes evading antivirus engines, and repeated sections or overlay data produced repeating patterns in a file's hash, which could make a binary look suspicious.

Hyrum Anderson then walks through an example solution. An offline attack runs a local copy of the EMBER model and uses discrete optimization over functionality-preserving file changes, implemented with the hyperopt library, to find variants that evade it. Those successful variants then seed an online attack against hosted models, which uses API queries, since the hosted models report only hard labels. Failed attempts are stored so they can be resumed, and contestants are advised to test each sample's behaviour before uploading. The closing point is that hosted models can learn from queries, so an evasion that works early may stop working later.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Bring your own demise. The corporate threat of mobile endpoints by János Pallagi
talks.teaser: Shows how personal smartphones with corporate access enable mobile kill chains from rogue Wi-Fi to credential theft and lateral phishing.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by contrasting old perimeter-heavy corporate networks with today’s cloud-centric, work-from-anywhere reality, where personal smartphones often hold the keys to email, collaboration, banking, and two-factor authentication. He argues that banning BYOD is rarely viable and introduces MITRE ATT&CK for Mobile as the map for the techniques he will demonstrate.

The core of the session is a condensed, simulated attack against a CFO’s iPhone on an outdated iOS build. Rogue Wi‑Fi and DNS spoofing of the company domain lead the victim to install a trojanized contact-tracing app that jailbreaks the phone and grants root. From there the walkthrough covers data theft from messaging apps, harvesting Wi‑Fi passwords and contacts, social pressure to open a banking app, keylogging and SMS one-time-password capture to bypass two-factor authentication, and sending a phishing message to a colleague as if from the compromised executive—with endpoint alerts shown but ignored for demo purposes. A brief Android follow-on illustrates how protection on the second device could have surfaced the lateral phish.

Takeaways emphasize that mobile threat protection can break the chain at many steps when logs are actually reviewed, that a large share of corporate access already comes from phones running unsupported operating systems, and that when full MDM is unrealistic, containerization plus monitored endpoint protection remains the practical path.

talks.title: #Hacktivity2020 // Perception vs Reality by Piotr Pobereźny
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning #Hacktivity2020 // Perception vs Reality by Piotr Pobereźny.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Piotr Pobereźny, a Senior Security Solution Architect at Qualys and former group CISO for two large insurance companies, addresses the disconnect between executive perception and operational reality in cybersecurity. While C-level leadership often assumes basic tools like antivirus, firewalls, and cyber insurance provide adequate protection, Pobereźny reveals that organizations manage an average of only around 12% of their total attack surface. The rest remains unmanaged due to complex hybrid architectures, visibility gaps, and inefficient legacy vulnerability management practices.

### Key Topics
- **Misaligned Patching Priorities:** Most enterprises focus patching efforts primarily on operating systems (ranked 11th in terms of vulnerabilities with public exploits) while neglecting software with significantly higher numbers of exploitable vulnerabilities multiplied by deployment volume.
- **Top Vulnerability Volumes:** Software presenting the highest volume of public exploits includes Adobe products (Flash, Reader) at number one, web browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Internet Explorer) at number two, and Intel graphics card drivers at number three—a component virtually ubiquitous across both workstations and servers.
- **Sensor-Driven Visibility vs. Scanning:** Moving away from heavy, periodic network appliance scans toward continuous, lightweight sensor and connector deployment (cloud, container, host) allows real-time asset discovery and vulnerability detection without consuming excessive host resources.
- **Prioritization and Remediation Integration:** Combining asset inventory, risk-based prioritization (via Real-Time Threat Indicators or RTIs), and built-in patch orchestration within a unified platform, replacing disconnected point solutions and static spreadsheets.
- **Executive Communication ("Dialects"):** Translating raw technical vulnerability metrics into executive-level operational, financial, and regulatory risk (such as GDPR infrastructure compliance percentages) mapped to recognized benchmarks.

### Technical Details
Traditional vulnerability management relies on manual flat exports (CSV, XML, Excel) that show flatlines where the incoming flow of vulnerabilities continually outpaces remediation. Pobereźny outlines an operational model built around four stages: comprehensive asset inventory, vulnerability detection, threat-based prioritization, and remediation.

Using an example of Windows workstations with over 100,000 confirmed vulnerabilities, Pobereźny demonstrates filtering with Real-Time Threat Indicators (RTIs)—such as active exploits, malware associations, and exploit kits. This filters the actionable remediation set down to 352 unique vulnerabilities representing less than 18% of the total scope, transforming an unmanageable backlog into an actionable plan. The solution supports direct patch deployment workflows—from scheduled maintenance windows (e.g., Patch Tuesday) to ad-hoc browser or driver updates—without needing external deployment tools. Additionally, unpatchable software reaching end-of-life (such as Apple QuickTime or older Flash versions) can be automatically identified for removal or migration.

### Takeaways
Pobereźny stresses that the target Time to Remediate (TTR) should approach zero rather than relying on Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), which often masks severely outdated vulnerabilities. To secure executive buy-in and appropriate budget allocation, security practitioners must stop delivering thousands of pages of raw CVE reports. Instead, technical data should be translated into high-level compliance and risk percentages tied to industry standards (like ISO 27001 or CIS benchmarks), clearly presenting residual business risk directly to decision-makers.

talks.title: Dave Lewis
talks.teaser: Argues that hackers belong in the security ecosystem and must communicate risk clearly to executives.
talks.summary:
Dave Lewis uses the image of sharks to argue that the security community focuses on the wrong things. Practitioners chase sensational stories, such as dark web labels and a high-rated flaw in a partly installed WordPress site, while neglecting core basics like patching, logging, network segmentation and user management.

A large part of the talk covers how hackers are perceived. He points to misconfigured Amazon S3 buckets, noting that public access is not granted by default and that such buckets are usually created by people outside security roles, so the gap is communication. He also contrasts paper ballots with election machines lacking audit trails, and describes a power company where he had five minutes to persuade a CIO by explaining financial and reputational risk.

Near the end, he recalls his own research in 2008, when vendors patched quickly, one within two hours, while another company threatened to sue him. He presents bug bounty programs as progress. His takeaway is that hackers should explain risk in terms executives understand, make security tools usable, and work with organisations rather than ridicule them.

talks.title: Dávid Török - My Adventures in Disabling Intel ME 12
talks.teaser: Shows how a researcher disabled Intel Management Engine on a newer motherboard by setting a hidden firmware configuration bit.
talks.summary:
Intel Management Engine is a separate coprocessor built into modern Intel chipsets. It runs its own proprietary firmware on a MINIX-based operating system, has broad access to chipset devices, and starts before the main CPU, so a failed firmware signature check keeps the machine from booting. The talk explains why its unlock levels make it an attractive attack surface and recalls earlier research into its firmware and login path.

A security firm had earlier found a stack buffer overflow in the firmware, reachable through a forged file in the chip's internal file system, which gave code execution and a route to the highest unlock level. On a newer motherboard that an existing open-source firmware cleaner could not handle, the speaker's earlier attempts with known offsets failed. Instead, the speaker compared Intel's firmware image tool XML files across releases, matching bit-field alignment to find a field once labelled as a high assurance platform bit. Setting it disabled the coprocessor, confirmed when the version query returned a default string. Applying it meant reading and reflashing the SPI chip with a clip and external programmer, and a pull request for the cleaner remains open.

The speaker stresses this is not a proper fix, since Intel could change the mechanism and closed components such as undocumented microcode remain. As a longer-term alternative, the talk points to fully open platforms like OpenPOWER, where board designs and microcode are open.

talks.title: František Střasák & Jan Fajfer - Increasing Efficiency of Encr. Traffic Analysis of People at Risk
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for František Střasák & Jan Fajfer - Increasing Efficiency of Encr. Traffic Analysis of People at Risk.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Researchers Frank Střasák and Jan Fajfer from the Civil Sphere Project at the Czech Technical University in Prague describe their work supporting people at risk—including journalists, human rights defenders, and lawyers—who lack commercial security teams. The initiative operates the "Emergency VPN" project, a free remote service where at-risk users route traffic to an OpenVPN server for three days of packet capture to uncover ongoing infections, malware traffic, or vulnerabilities. Because manually inspecting packets can take eight hours or more per three-day capture, the team explores machine learning and deep learning approaches to accelerate the triage of encrypted network connections.

### Key Topics
- **Emergency VPN Service**: Providing manual network traffic assessments for mobile devices owned by high-risk civil society members using OpenVPN profiles.
- **Encrypted Traffic Analysis Bottlenecks**: High manual effort required to investigate TLS/HTTPS connections and identify stealthy patterns such as periodic Command and Control (C2) or data exfiltration.
- **Impact of TLS 1.3**: The architectural changes in TLS 1.3, specifically handshake certificate encryption, which broke previous feature extraction methods relying on certificate metadata.
- **Deep Learning for Encrypted Flows**: Transitioning to raw TCP-layer network behavioral features processed by a 1D convolutional neural network inspired by ResNet.
- **Human-in-the-Loop Filtering**: Utilizing ML models not as autonomous endpoint blocks, but as filtering mechanisms to strip away 90%+ benign traffic so human analysts can inspect the remaining anomalies.

### Technical Details
Initially, the researchers generated flows using Zeek (formerly Bro) from network captures, aggregating flows sharing identical source IP, destination IP, destination port, and protocol into "SSL aggregations." They extracted 40 features primarily focused on plaintext TLS certificates (such as validity periods, SAN domains, and certificate chains), achieving roughly 95% accuracy using models like Random Forests and XGBoost. 

However, TLS 1.3 introduced handshake certificate encryption, rendering certificate-based features unavailable. To adapt, the team created a new feature representation independent of certificate data, focusing entirely on lower-level TCP/TLS behavioral patterns (bytes, packet counts, inter-arrival times/periodicity). They formulated sequences across flows within an SSL aggregation, zero-padding the sequence length to 250 across six feature channels. This input was fed into a convolutional neural network inspired by ResNet image classification architectures.

Trained on balanced datasets (80,000 malware samples from CTU-14/MCFP and 80,000 normal traffic samples), the CNN model achieved 94% accuracy, a 7% false positive rate, and a 3% false negative rate. In a simulated Android mobile infection test, the model flagged benign traffic (such as Inbox by Google) as false positives, but successfully captured the C2 communication to an IP address in China. Over 40 real captures, the model filtered out approximately 91% of traffic as benign.

### Takeaways
While modern encrypted traffic analysis via TCP metadata cannot act as a reliable standalone detector due to false positives, it serves as a powerful pre-filter for human analysts. By eliminating more than 90% of benign traffic, analysts can reduce review times drastically. Future improvements include training specialized models on native mobile traffic rather than desktop Windows datasets and segmenting models across operating systems and protocols.

talks.title: Kelly Shortridge
talks.teaser: Shows how blame, policy, and biases warp incident learning via systems thinking and security UX to make the secure path easy.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Alexander Pope’s framing that mistakes are intrinsic to human judgment, then argues that information security often fights that reality through punishment, ridicule, and fantasy fixes. It clarifies what “human error” actually means in incidents: subjective expectations, slips versus mistaken intentions, and the way hindsight bias and outcome bias rewrite whether a past choice looked reasonable when it was made.

The middle section dissects three familiar but weak responses: labeling people as the root cause (including PBKAC-style narratives and high-profile breach postmortems), leaning on policy violations, training, and discipline instead of workflow design, and seeking a single villain or violation to restore a “just world” sense of control. Examples span Equifax patching friction, Capital One discourse, aviation accident statistics, SOC alert fatigue, and sharp-end versus blunt-end accountability in complex systems.

The close shifts toward constructive practice: adopt a systems view that includes economic and social incentives, improve security UX and choice architecture so the secure path is the easy path, use defaults and thoughtful exceptions rather than iron-fist restriction, pick metrics that reflect real risk (not vanity counts), and pursue security chaos engineering with blameless learning cultures.

talks.title: Thomas Debize
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Thomas Debize - A Decade of Infosec Tools.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Thomas Debize presents an empirical study examining the landscape, lifecycle, and development practices of information security (InfoSec) tools over the past decade. While foundational utilities such as Nmap and THC Hydra have remained in active use since the late 1990s, the InfoSec community has seen a massive influx of modern tools driven by accessible Internet-wide scanning, social coding on platforms like GitHub, and growth in blue team defense and bug bounties. Debize evaluates thousands of tool publications and GitHub repositories to uncover hosting trends, maintenance lifespans, programming language preferences, dependency health, and vulnerabilities, concluding with a set of actionable recommendations for modern tool development.

### Key Topics
- **Data Sources and Tool Publication:** Analysis of metadata from four major InfoSec tool repositories and publication sources: Packet Storm, ToolsWatch, KitPloit, and NoWhere (leveraging structured data from the norse-corp / feed source). Over time, KitPloit emerged as a primary aggregator, while overall tool creation has trended steadily upward since 2010.
- **Hosting Dominance:** A review of hosting platforms (GitHub, Bitbucket, SourceForge, and Google Code) showing that around mid-2013, GitHub established overwhelming dominance as the single hosting platform for InfoSec software, raising minor concerns regarding platform dependency.
- **Repository Metrics and Maintenance:** Analysis of approximately 23,000 InfoSec repositories on GitHub to measure stars, forks, watchers, releases, and issue resolution. The findings show that tools average approximately 2.5 years of active maintenance, with strong issue-closing engagement.
- **Programming Languages and Dependency Ecosystems:** Identification of Python as the overwhelmingly dominant language, followed by shell, HTML, C, and JavaScript, with emerging growth in C#, Go, and Dockerfiles. A deeper dive into Python packages reveals heavy reliance on general libraries like `requests`, `beautifulsoup4`, and `lxml`, alongside security-specific modules like `scapy`.
- **Security Hygiene and Vulnerabilities:** Assessment of Python dependencies against vulnerability databases (via PyUp.io), exposing frequent use of unmaintained libraries (such as `pycrypto`) and pinned, outdated versions of packages like `django` and `requests` with known CVEs.

### Technical Details
- **Dataset Processing:** The study analyzed approximately 7,000 records from Packet Storm, 1,500 from ToolsWatch, 3,000 from KitPloit, and 1,000 from NoWhere using Dataiku (a French data platform) and automated GitHub API queries.
- **Repository Statistics:** The average GitHub InfoSec tool repository accrued roughly 1,000 stars (median: 200), an average tool size of 15 MB (median: 1 MB), an average of 70 pull requests total, and an average maintenance duration of 2.5 years (though some mirrored legacy projects, such as `samplicator`, date back to 1999 commits via backdated imports).
- **Top Repositories:** Leading repositories by stars and forks heavily feature offensive tools, including Metasploit, SecLists, Jadx, Ghidra, and mitmproxy, while high open issue counts frequently appear in defensive projects such as MISP.
- **Crypto Library Deprecation:** About 30% of surveyed Python tools requiring cryptography still utilized `pycrypto`, which has been unmaintained since 2013 and carries known flaws; Debize emphasizes migrating to `pycryptodome` or `cryptography`.
- **Version Pinning Risks:** Analysis indicated widespread strict pinning (`==`) in `requirements.txt` to vulnerable releases of `django` and `requests`, preventing security updates.

### Takeaways and Golden Rules for Modern Tools
Debize outlines practical guidelines for authors to ensure their security tools remain scalable, usable, and maintainable:
1. **Standard Argument & Input Parsing:** Use standard libraries such as Python's `argparse` rather than deprecated modules, and support input files processing one entry per line rather than only single targets.
2. **Architecture & Formats:** Adopt modular architectures (similar to Recon-ng) to facilitate community plugins; output data in structured formats like JSON or CSV (avoiding Excel formats); and enforce UTF-8 character encoding.
3. **Concurrency:** Use `concurrent.futures`, choosing multithreading for I/O-bound tasks and multiprocessing for CPU-bound operations.
4. **Enterprise Compatibility:** Provide tiered verbosity (info, warning, debug), support corporate proxy traversal (HTTP and SOCKS), and support Windows corporate authentication (NTLM and Kerberos).
5. **Packaging and Delivery:** Avoid rigid dependency pinning, publish packages to PyPI, provide pre-built binaries or Docker containers to aid both red and blue teams, and ensure network communications are properly encrypted.

talks.teaser: A walkthrough of Windows user privileges and access tokens that turn misassigned rights into full system compromise.

The presentation argues that Windows user privileges are widely assigned yet poorly understood as a privilege-escation path. After a short model of privileges, access tokens, and high-integrity shells, the speaker uses `whoami /priv` to show how token contents drive what an attacker can do.

The core surveys “god” privileges and concrete abuse: debug (including parent-process impersonation to reach SYSTEM or TrustedInstaller), backup and restore (file and registry overrides, service DLL swapping on WAP Push, SAM and Active Directory hash extraction, permission grants), take ownership on service registry keys, Act as part of the operating system with Kerberos and NTLM token forging, create-token tricks around Windows 10 version 1809 checks, load-driver abuse via a vulnerable third-party driver, and impersonate plus assign-primary paths including Juicy Potato-style COM reflection. Misconfigured service and application accounts are highlighted as common entry points.

Practitioners should map token-bearing accounts, grant only task-specific rights, and assume legacy builds remain exposed where Microsoft’s 1809/Server 2019 mitigations do not apply. Sensitive service accounts and unnecessary services matter as much as patching named potato-style chains.

talks.title: Zsombor Kovács - Cheaters for Everything from Minesweeper to Mobile Banking Applications
talks.teaser: Shows how Frida runtime hooks let an attacker alter Android game and banking app behavior, from minesweeper to blackjack.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a story about speaking to teenagers who only cared about game cheats, and uses that angle to introduce writing cheats for Android apps. It explains that an Android app relies on its runtime environment to reach hardware, local files and network endpoints. That layer can be attacked in several ways: intercepting traffic, patching the binary, editing files in the app sandbox, spoofing sensors such as GPS, or changing the runtime that wraps the app code.

The speaker compares three runtime manipulation tools. Xposed was the way to add permission controls and modules on rooted devices before Android built them in. Cydia Substrate is abandoned and only works on old Android versions. Frida is presented as the most capable option, with a scriptable API and a stable runtime. A typical workflow is to decompile an APK, find the relevant classes and methods, write a Frida script, and attach it to the running process. Obfuscated names can still be targeted by using their minified identifiers.

The demonstrations show several cases. A static AES key was recovered by logging the inputs to an encrypt method. A PIN check was brute-forced across 10,000 values by calling the app's own comparison function. A root detection routine was overridden so the device always looked clean. A minesweeper cheat read mine positions from a two-dimensional array, and a blackjack app had its deck enumerated, then rigged so the player received blackjack and bets could be stacked with a loop. The takeaway is that these changes needed little programming skill, and that checks performed on an attacker-controlled device, such as PIN screens or root detection, give weak protection, including in banking apps.

talks.title: Matthias Deeg - Bypassing an Enterprise-Grade Biometric Face Authentication System
talks.teaser: Shows how a printed photo can fool Windows Hello face login through its near-infrared camera.
talks.summary:
Matthias Deeg presents research he carried out with a colleague in 2017 on Windows Hello face authentication, the near-infrared biometric login included in Windows 10. Public information about its security was scarce, so the work took a black-box approach, testing the sensor and its image processing from the outside.

The researchers captured raw infrared frames with their own small tools and adjusted brightness and contrast in Python. Screens, glossy photo paper, inkjet printouts and an old cathode ray tube produced nothing the infrared camera could read, while a high-quality offset magazine print and a laser printout worked. An inexpensive USB infrared camera allowed the bypass on every Windows 10 version tested. On a Surface Pro 4, the attack worked on version 1607 but failed on 1703 and 1709 once the enhanced anti-spoofing setting was enabled. A live demo and a recorded video showed the attack.

The attack needs a frontal, eyes-open face image captured in near-infrared, and its success depends on the camera hardware and Windows build. Practitioners should use cameras that support enhanced anti-spoofing, enable that poorly documented setting, and re-enroll after enabling it, since older enrollments stayed vulnerable. Further ideas, such as a two-printout attack, had not yet succeeded.

talks.title: Csongor Tamás - Examples of Locality Sensitive Hashing & their Usage for Malware Classification
talks.teaser: Compares fuzzy hashing methods like ssdeep, sdhash and TLSH for finding ransomware samples similar to a seed corpus.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a practical bottleneck in malware research: building a fresh, relevant ransomware corpus. Collecting samples from news reports and hash lookups took months, and YARA rule matching, though common for finding related files, is slow and needs many similar samples to write good rules. The speaker proposed locality-sensitive hashing, where similar files yield similar digests that can be compared by a distance score.

Three fuzzy hashing schemes were compared: ssdeep, sdhash and TLSH. sdhash was judged unsuitable and its scores were poorly scaled. TLSH digests stay around 70 bytes, so a 300 million sample database needs roughly 30 GB, and comparisons take about a millisecond. On a daily feed of about 35,000 unlabeled binaries, three clustering approaches were tried; the best required a new file to be close to several group members, since closeness to a single member produced one giant group. Groups were checked manually through disassembly and sandbox reports.

Searches of a 477-sample corpus across 15 ransomware families were run against the 300 million sample database. Results differed by method: for one sample ssdeep found matches that TLSH missed, and for another TLSH found matches that ssdeep missed. The speaker concluded that fuzzy hashing can rapidly expand a corpus, but these methods can be deliberately evaded. Future work includes parallelization, broader family coverage and better LSH implementations.

talks.title: Alex Plaskett & James Loureiro - The Mate Escape
talks.teaser: Android Pwn2Owning explores Alex Plaskett & James Loureiro - The Mate Escape.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, James Loureiro and Alex Plaskett from MWR InfoSecurity share their experience competing in Mobile Pwn2Own 2017. While other teams targeted the Samsung Galaxy S8, James and Alex focused on the Huawei Mate 9 Pro in the browser category. Given tight deadlines (two to three man-months) and increasing platform mitigations against memory corruption, they pursued an exploit chain based entirely on logic vulnerabilities. Their strategy allowed them to pivot out of Google Chrome and achieve full remote code execution without user interaction.

### Key Topics
- **Target Selection & Attack Surface**: Modern Android devices ship with massive pre-installed bloatware—around 200 OEM apps on Samsung and Huawei devices. These proprietary applications offer a wide, poorly audited attack surface with elevated permissions.
- **Logic Bugs vs. Memory Corruption**: While memory corruption requires defeating mitigations like ASLR, sandboxing, and lacks cross-device stability, logic bugs are architecture-agnostic, reliable, and harder to detect. However, logic chains often require many bugs, deep application context, and are harder to automate or fuzz.
- **Automation & Tooling**: MWR used internal scripts to decompile APKs in bulk, grep for dangerous keywords (e.g., `install`, `update`, file I/O), and JEB for reverse engineering. They prototyped graph-theory tooling to trace reachability from exported intents to dangerous sinks (such as `DexClassLoader`). Dynamic tools like Frida and Xposed assisted in tracing behavior and prototyping.

### Technical Details
The full exploit chain against the Huawei Mate 9 Pro relied on chaining several logic issues across multiple components:

1. **Browsing & Whitelist Bypass**: A victim visits a malicious link in Chrome, which invokes a browsable intent registered to the Huawei Marketplace application under the `hiapp://` protocol schema. Although Huawei enforced a domain whitelist (`hiapp.hicloud.com`, `vmall.com`, `huawei.com`), the check used a flawed regex (`.*`) and lacked HTTPS enforcement, allowing navigation to malicious content via HTTP/DNS spoofing.
2. **Intent Proxying via JavaScript Bridge**: The loaded webview exposed a native Java bridge object (`window.hispace` / `hiAppSpace`). An exposed method, `launchApp`, processed user-supplied URIs with `Intent.parseUri` and `setPackage`. By utilizing the `android-app://` URI schema with embedded intent extras, the researchers turned browsable intents into arbitrary exported intents across any application on the device.
3. **Pivot to Huawei Reader**: Using this intent proxy primitive, the exploit targeted the Huawei Reader app (`com.huawei.reader`). Although low-privileged, the app contained multiple unvetted interfaces, including a webview bridge with a `doCommand` function.
4. **Directory Traversal File Write**: Through the Reader's online download feature, an unvalidated JSON `fileName` parameter allowed path traversal (`../../`). This gave an arbitrary file write primitive anywhere writable by the app, though it could not overwrite existing files.
5. **Arbitrary File Deletion via MD5 Path Traversal**: To replace an existing binary, the researchers exploited a cache-cleaning deletion feature that checked for failed open attempts. The app constructed deletion targets using an MD5 hash of the filename appended to the failure path. By pre-calculating the MD5 hash of a path with traversal sequences (`../../plugin/dfservices/classes.jar`), they induced the deletion of an existing plugin JAR file.
6. **Arbitrary Code Execution via DexClassLoader**: Huawei Reader implemented plugin functionality that loaded JAR files from an SD card directory using `DexClassLoader`. After deleting the original JAR and writing a malicious `classes.jar` via path traversal, navigating to a `.txt` file triggered the plugin loading routine. The loaded payload executed a BusyBox binary to spawn a remote reverse shell.

### Takeaways
- Chaining multiple low-severity logic flaws across OEM applications can defeat modern sandbox protections without relying on traditional memory corruption.
- Pre-installed vendor apps remain a critical vulnerability vector due to inconsistent security audits and risky patterns like dynamic code loading (`DexClassLoader`) from shared or exposed directories.
- Defending Android ecosystems requires strictly validating browsable intents, sanitizing inputs in JavaScript bridges, and eliminating insecure custom scheme parsers.

talks.title: Inbar Raz - Under the Hood - The Automotive Challenge
talks.teaser: Explains why cars are hard to secure, covering buggy supplier code, in-car networks, and past vehicle research.
talks.summary:
Inbar Raz opens by explaining why automotive security is so hard to get right. A modern car is assembled from parts made by many suppliers and runs a very large amount of code. The speaker estimates roughly 10,000 known bugs and 50,000 unknown bugs in a newly rolled-out car, and cites a survey of automotive software developers in which most did not believe their industry was knowledgeable about secure development. The talk then describes the in-car architecture: dozens of electronic control units connected over several network types. The CAN bus has no sender authentication, so anyone with access can impersonate devices, and infotainment units now behave like full computers running Linux or Android.

The middle of the talk covers the attack surface and past research. Any connection to the outside world counts, including GPS, remote keyless entry, the diagnostic port, USB, SD cards and cellular links. The speaker walks through several cases: a 2015 remote takeover of a car over the internet, a Tesla key-cloning study that broke a 40-bit key, a Tesla attack that went through the owner's phone, and infotainment and BMW findings. A cheap OBD dongle bought online can query and change some car functions. Because cars stay on the road for up to fifteen years and rarely receive remote updates, old software often remains in service.

The closing section compares the economics of cybercrime in IT and automotive. Mitigations already exist in computers, but cars lack them, and the speaker says attacks on cars have been proven but not yet seen at scale. Standards for connected vehicles, autonomous fleets and ECU consolidation could change that. The takeaways are layered defence with detection, bringing dedicated security expertise into design, and recognising that regulation in the US and Europe may push manufacturers to raise their security levels.

talks.title: Zoltán Balázs - Ethereum Smart Contract Hacking Explained like I’m Five
talks.teaser: Explains Ethereum and smart contracts in plain terms, then walks through famous hacks like the DAO and Parity wallet bugs.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Ethereum and smart contracts for an audience with little blockchain background. It explains how mining solves hard puzzles, how public transactions are signed by wallets, and how Solidity code is compiled to bytecode that runs on the Ethereum Virtual Machine. A live walkthrough shows buying a CryptoKitties collectible through the MetaMask extension, and the speaker notes that the approval screen did not clearly show which function and parameters a user was authorising.

Several incidents follow. The DAO lost roughly 250 million dollars in 2016 to a reentrancy flaw, because funds were sent before the balance was updated. The community's hard fork produced Ethereum Classic, where the attacker kept the funds. In 2017 a shared multi-signature wallet library in Parity had an unprotected initialisation function reached through delegatecall, which let an attacker take control of wallets. Later, an accidental call to kill that library left about 300 million dollars permanently locked. A separate integer underflow in a scam contract cost about two million dollars.

The conclusion is that deployed contracts cannot be patched easily, so secure coding is hard and developers need outside help. Practical advice includes using safe math libraries against overflow and underflow, testing on test networks, and practising with tutorials and capture-the-flag style challenges.

talks.title: Rodrigo Branco - How Offensive Security is Defining the Way We Compute // Keynote Speech
talks.teaser: Argues that exploit mitigations should be judged by evidence from real exploit work rather than vague claims of raising the bar.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens with a disclaimer that the views are personal, then focuses on how exploit mitigations are designed and judged. Threat modeling is presented as a mature practice, while mitigation design lacks a comparable process and claims of "raising the bar" go unquantified. The speaker proposes three tests: a mitigation aimed at a bug class should hold against at least three real instances where bypass is impossible; mitigations should be judged together with the ones they depend on; and designers should understand exploitation, either by writing exploits or by pairing with someone who does.

The middle section examines missing data. Write-ups rarely record time spent, failed attempts or reusable tooling, and mitigations tend to become legacy instead of being retired. Vendor exploit statistics are cited as useful but hard to verify without raw data. The speaker also covers attempts to formalize exploit primitives and notes conflicts with established guidance: LangSec's push to parse input early differs from advice to validate input close to its use. Memory encryption without authentication is described as only probabilistic protection, showing that implementation details can matter as much as architecture.

The closing argument is that formalization can move exploit work from art toward engineering and bring in more people. The main takeaways: demand evidence for mitigation claims, understand the problem before proposing a fix, and let offensive research guide defensive investment.

talks.title: Paolo Stagno - A Drone Tale: All Your Drones Belong To Us
talks.teaser: Walks through attacking a DJI Phantom 3 via Wi-Fi, firmware, SDK and GPS spoofing, plus the drone's forensic traces.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the attack surface of a DJI Phantom 3 drone. The speaker describes the aircraft's architecture, with the ground controller acting as a Wi-Fi access point for the drone and a separate system for the camera. Services were largely filtered after a hardening step aimed at an illegal modification market, and the default Wi-Fi password was a practical weak point. Classic Wi-Fi attacks were shown: disconnecting the controller triggers the return-to-home behaviour, and the WPA key could be cracked with a dictionary.

The middle section covers how the speaker moved from limited access to root. The mobile app's no-fly zone updates were unsigned, so the data could be edited. A hidden downgrade option let the speaker reach the file system over FTP, which exposed configuration files with credentials and allowed telnet to be re-enabled. The SDK account check was bypassed by patching the Java bytecode, and the custom TCP-based flight control protocol was reverse engineered, partly using earlier community findings. GPS was presented as the main remote vector: replaying spoofed signals with a software-defined radio could make the drone believe it was elsewhere, trigger no-fly zone restrictions, or force a landing. Possible receiver-side checks against fake signals were also discussed.

The final part covers forensics. Flight data is held in an onboard memory on the aircraft, while text logs on the phone are uploaded to vendor servers and media stays on the camera. Combining these sources can rebuild flight paths and events. Anti-forensic options were noted, including overwriting old log data and flying without the onboard memory. The talk closes with counter-drone measures and plans to reverse engineer the custom binaries further.
