### Overview
Róbert Neumann, a security researcher on the Special Investigation Team at Forcepoint, presents an investigation into a widespread point-of-sale (POS) malware campaign characterized by extremely small (~4 kilobyte) assembly-based binaries. The investigation began following Forcepoint's discovery of Udpos (which used DNS data exfiltration) and public reports on PinkKite malware (a 4–6 KB POS malware utilizing double-XOR encryption and clearing houses), both evoking older malware families like TinyPOS and AbaddonPOS. While researchers initially anticipated only a handful of samples, the team collected over 1,500 unique samples, discovering that the overwhelming majority acted as modular downloaders while fewer than 40 were actual final payloads.

### Key Topics
- **Staged Infiltration Architecture**: The attack relies on modular components: initial tiny loaders/downloaders, multi-stage fragmented shellcode, reconnaissance tools (Scouts), and memory scrapers.
- **Obfuscation and Anti-Analysis**: Attackers utilize custom code-push obfuscation, fake API calls, junk instructions, randomized version info, XOR decryption wrappers, and basic execution-skipping techniques rather than heavy anti-debug or anti-sandbox mechanisms.
- **POS Reconnaissance**: Profiling victim environments using targeted Scout tools comparing processes against an extensive list of over 300 POS software names.
- **POS Ecosystem Vulnerabilities**: Legacy hardware and operating systems (Windows XP-based POSReady 2009 and Windows 7-based POSReady 7), weak remote access configurations, and unencrypted magnetic stripe Track 1 and Track 2 data in memory.

### Technical Details
- **Downloaders (Tiny Loaders)**: Averaging ~4 KB, these samples decrypt themselves using a fast DWORD brute-force XOR routine at the entry point without storing the decryption key. They connect to C2 servers using dual IP address configurations (often duplicating constants due to developer laziness) and frequently cycling port numbers (incrementing by 1 or 2 per campaign). The downloader fetches fragmented shellcode in chunks of a few hundred bytes, which reassembles in memory.
- **Shellcode Execution & Profiling**: Once staged, shellcode resolves API names dynamically and performs process filtering using truncated 4-character process strings. It collects running process lists and relays them to C2 infrastructure. If the victim is non-viable, it executes progressive sleep loops (minutes to hours) rather than terminating immediately.
- **Scout Modules (Type A & Type B)**: Type A maps running processes, attempting to open each and logging success (`OK`) or failure flags (`EOF`). Type B gathers the PC name, maps the local network (`net view`), and cross-references running processes against a static list of 327 distinct POS application names matching only the first 6 characters.
- **POS Memory Scraper Module**: The final payload operates without binary-level encryption because targeted POS endpoints rarely run security software. It conducts multi-threaded memory scraping to locate and extract Track 1 and Track 2 magnetic stripe card data. The extracted track data is XOR-encrypted prior to C2 exfiltration to bypass DLP systems. Code evolution shows updates between January and September to refine memory read buffer sizes (down from ~400 KB chunks) and increase sleep intervals to avoid read exceptions.

### Takeaways
- Attackers do not need complex, bloated codebases; a ~4 KB assembly-written binary is lightweight, highly modular, fast to recompile or modify, and avoids runtime dependencies.
- The pre-compiled database of 327 distinct POS process signatures demonstrates multi-year development and persistent targeting across commercial POS vendors.
- POS exploitation remains prevalent due to legacy OS platforms reaching end-of-life, delayed EMV/chip adoption compared to magnetic swipe transactions, unencrypted memory architectures, and compromised remote administration tools.

talks.title: Jack S (linkcabin) - Becoming the Quiz Master: Thanks RE
talks.teaser: A researcher reverse-engineers pub quiz machine firmware, exposing archives, plaintext player data, and ways to emulate games off-premises.
talks.summary:
Curiosity about British pub quiz machines—and whether one could run outside the pub—drives a research path that avoids buying hardware by downloading vendor firmware from a public support site. The deliverable is a zip-based update chain where setup.exe decrypts nested, password-protected archives and exposes a custom batch-style install language, SHA-256 package checks, and archive passwords sitting in configuration.

Reverse engineering maps a Windows 2000 base with a WindShell overlay that kills and starts processes, talks to a local web server using custom monetary commands, enforces reboot-fraud checks, and ships router-probing code aimed at TP-Link gear for bundled connectivity. Firmware also carries plaintext SQLite data: on the order of 6,000 UK and Ireland pub locations and 17,000 player rows with leaderboard payout PINs, plus cleartext dial-up style credentials behind archive passwords framed as the main defense.

The speaker runs setup for behavioral decryption, parallels these packaging habits with malware developers, patches game credit logic to emulate titles under DirectX, and notes TLS-backed remote game updates amid an ancient OS surface. Practitioners auditing embedded entertainment systems should treat passworded archives, debug strings, and local control planes as review targets, and expect IoT-scale privacy impact when location and payout metadata ships in the clear.

talks.title: Joxean Koret - Pigaios: A Tool for Diffing Source Codes against Binaries
talks.teaser: Presents Pigaios, a tool that matches functions in C source code to compiled binaries using AST artifacts and machine learning.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common reverse engineering problem: a team holds source code for a program but cannot build it, and needs to map its functions onto a compiled binary. The speaker describes trying to rebuild an old source release, where missing headers, libraries and outdated compilers blocked the build, and how manually matching functions by strings and neighbouring code does not scale.

The middle of the talk explains how Pigaios works. Source files are parsed with the clang Python bindings, which produce a syntax tree even when code has errors or cannot be compiled, while binaries are read with IDA. Both sides yield comparable artifacts such as string constants, loop, condition and switch counts, and called functions. These are stored in SQLite databases and matched first with strict queries that return few results with almost no false positives. Further matches come from iterative heuristics based on call graphs, neighbouring functions and rare string constants. The speaker explains why compiler-optimised output differs from source-level control flow, and why a hand-written scoring function was replaced by a multi-classifier ensemble of decision tree, gradient boosting and random forest models that produces a similarity ratio.

The talk closes with demos: matching a small program, then a BusyBox source tree against a MIPS binary, where the tool reported many matches. Planned work includes importing structures and enumerations into IDA and sharing prebuilt databases of open-source projects. The project was published during the talk. The takeaway is that artifact-based diffing of source against binaries is workable, while reliable parsing of compiler-specific C dialects remains the hardest part.

talks.title: Julien Thomas
talks.teaser: Explores how Android's permission model can be bypassed through shared user IDs, package updates, and app virtualization.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the limits of Android's permission system and the UID-based model beneath it. The work grew out of a software VPN project, where the team could not reliably determine which installed apps were allowed to reach the internet. The speaker outlines the change at Marshmallow, when dangerous permissions moved from install-time grants to runtime requests, and explains how UIDs protect files while kernel-level group IDs gate network and other resources.

A live demo on a Nougat phone showed two apps that requested nothing gaining access to contacts and calendar after one was updated to define a custom permission and share a user ID with the other. The talk then covered several cases: permissions granted through shared user IDs that the system never displays, a flag mismatch between pre- and post-Marshmallow API levels, a revocation flaw that leaves group IDs in place, and a permission-definition update that silently grants dangerous permissions. Google treated some reports as working as intended, fixed others, and left some pending.

The speaker also argued that UID-based isolation gives users little visibility, since shared user IDs and app virtualization let one app control another and reach its data without the user knowing. Play Protect would likely struggle to flag this. The takeaway is that kernel enforcement is robust, but security apps should not rely on the package manager's view of permissions and need their own checks.

talks.title: Roland Kamarás - Locky: anti-analysis techniques used by the ransomware
talks.teaser: Shows the layered anti-analysis tricks Locky ransomware uses to hide its payload from reverse engineers and sandboxes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Locky, a ransomware family spread through phishing emails with malicious Office macros. The macros fetch a downloader, which retrieves the encryption payload from a command-and-control server and loads it into memory. The speaker walks through the outer 32-bit executable, which is packed in an NSIS installer whose script is padded with junk lines and builds Windows API names from substrings before calling them.

The encrypted payload sits behind several decryption layers. The speaker counts eight in total, with each stage differing mainly in its length and XOR key values, and shows how an assembly trace can recover those parameters. The embedded DLL is then decrypted with a simple XOR keyed by a Unicode string. Its imports are resolved by matching a modified CRC32 checksum against export tables, and it is mapped into a suspended process through shared memory using direct system calls. Control is redirected by changing the entry-point register of the suspended thread.

The speaker then compares Locky with Hockey, a Hungarian ransomware family that looks similar at first glance. Unlike Locky, it is written in Visual Basic .NET, uses Hungarian identifiers, hard-codes its RSA public key instead of fetching it remotely, and asks victims to contact an email address rather than use Tor. The conclusion is that the techniques themselves are well known, but their combination shows deliberate effort to frustrate static analysis, debugging and automated sandboxes. The talk also notes that copycat families often reuse the behaviour of successful ransomware.

talks.title: Kirils Solovjovs - Tools for effortless reverse engineering of MikroTik routers
talks.teaser: Presents tools for jailbreaking, unpacking and analysing MikroTik RouterOS devices and their proprietary file formats.
talks.summary:
RouterOS runs on a Linux kernel, but its startup scripts and binaries are proprietary, so researchers need a jailbreak before they can examine a device. The speaker recalls an older built-in login backdoor and contrasts an earlier jailbreak method, which relied on a VirtualBox appliance and netboot, with a newer one. The script-based jailbreak works from any Linux machine regardless of CPU architecture, can run remotely and is much faster, though it does not recover lost passwords.

The toolset also downloads older RouterOS packages by probing candidate URLs, unpacks NPK package files into ordinary folders, and collects kernel sources and configuration files. The talk explains the NPK layout and the boot sequence, in which a loader starts services and a watchdog reboots the router if the loader fails. Decoders for support output files reveal configuration, memory and log data. A crafted support file was shown to trigger cross-site scripting in the vendor's web interface, which was fixed within about a day. Other scripts parse the binary configuration store and recover the admin password, which is reversible from a static key. A backup-file weakness that allows files to be written under arbitrary names was also demonstrated, though it requires admin credentials.

The main takeaway is that these tools let researchers inspect and interoperate with devices they own. The speaker said the new jailbreak and backup tools would be published on GitHub after the event.

talks.title: Mehmet Ince - A heaven for Hackers: Breaking Log/SIEM Products
talks.teaser: Shows how researchers breached log and SIEM products through source review, SQL injection and unauthenticated command execution.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at log management and SIEM products, which gather logs from firewalls, web application firewalls, databases and servers into one place. Because they hold broad privileges across a network, they are attractive targets. The speaker describes one risk where a WAF forwards full HTTP requests, including session cookies, to the SIEM, so anyone who reaches its console can read them. The research method starts with the documentation and product features, then gets a trial or access, and then compares source code between old and new versions to find what changed in security fixes.

Each case is handled separately. In an AlienVault USM build, the older release used PHP unserialize where the newer one used a different decode, and a session check accepted requests based on a user-agent value. This led to SQL injection that evaded the built-in WAF by swapping in a different function. The attacker pulled an administrator session token from the database, then used the product's own response actions and a policy triggered by failed SSH logins to run operating system commands. In a second product, default admin credentials worked, a query endpoint allowed database access, and stored host passwords were encrypted with a static key shipped inside a bundled library. In a third, a Python API endpoint lacked its authentication annotation and passed POST data into a command line call, allowing unauthenticated command injection. The speaker also showed that an attacker could delete their own entries from the local log database.

The main takeaway is that these products need strict access control, no default or static secrets, and isolation of their components. Teams that run them should treat them as high-value assets and monitor for changes to their configuration and logs.

talks.title: Haroon Meer / keynote
talks.teaser: Argues that generic security products fail against determined attackers and shows cheap, people-driven defenses like canary tokens.
talks.summary:
The keynote opens by revisiting an earlier argument that penetration testing was not moving customers forward. It then points to growing complexity, with the Linux kernel expanding from about 10,000 lines to roughly 20 million, and to peripheral hardware that runs its own processors. Enterprises are still slow to notice intrusions, and the speaker cites industry reports of attackers living on networks for 200 to 300 days before discovery.

The middle section argues that most generic, boxed security products fail against a determined opponent, since attackers study and bypass them. Good defense, the speaker suggests, often means quick, imperfect internal hacks that are cheap and still useful. Examples include canary tokens, which are bait files or links that report back when opened, and a simple alert whenever someone is added to the domain admins group. The speaker also points to companies whose security engineers write libraries and infrastructure that developers use, rather than only issuing checklists.

The closing argues that people matter more than process and technology, and that security teams should be measured by what they enable rather than what they block. Organisations are urged to hire strong engineers and treat enterprise security as an engineering problem. Red teamers are encouraged to move toward the defensive side, where the harder and more interesting problems remain unsolved.

talks.title: Bálint Varga-Perke (Buherátor) - Corrupting Ancient Spirits
talks.teaser: Penetration Testing Oracle Forms details Bálint Varga-Perke (Buherátor) - Corrupting Ancient Spirits.
talks.summary:
Oracle Forms is a long-established Oracle technology for building enterprise database front ends, still found at banks and government offices. Its client-server traffic is a serialized, event-driven protocol wrapped in RC4, so ordinary web testing tools struggle. The server holds the user interface state, so editing or replaying a single request breaks the session, and injected bytes desynchronise the client and server keystreams.

Earlier attempts included a Burp extension that reused the vendor's Java classes for serialization, which proved fragile, and approaches that tried to set cipher state through a debugger or a patched client. What worked was stripping encryption from the client by patching the vendor's jar, then running a man-in-the-middle proxy that handles plaintext messages and re-encrypts them for the real server. The cipher use also had weaknesses: no integrity checks, keystream reuse between directions, and a short key exchange that makes passive decryption practical. In a demo against a login form, an automated scan with a post-request macro found a SQL injection login bypass.

The practical advice is to focus on vulnerability classes that matter in a Java-based client rather than running irrelevant scanner checks, define insertion points manually, and use a single scanning thread. Because much of the application logic is generated PL/SQL, source review is worthwhile where code can be obtained, and authorization deserves close attention since it is often handled poorly. Where possible, enable HTTPS instead of relying on the built-in encryption.

talks.title: Leigh-Anne Galloway - Money makes money: How to buy an ATM and what you can do with it
talks.teaser: Explains how a used ATM was bought and moved, and how its software, hardware and vault can be attacked.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Leigh-Anne Galloway discusses her experience acquiring a physical ATM for research and exhibition purposes at InfoSec 2017 on behalf of Positive Technologies. Coming from an incident response and payment card investigation background without prior ATM hardware experience, she explores the market landscape for purchasing ATMs, the intense logistical challenges of handling heavy cash machines, and the physical, hardware, OS-level, and network attack surfaces present in modern automated teller machines.

### Key Topics
- **History and Market of ATMs**: Tracing ATM development from John Shepherd-Baron's 1967 prototype in Enfield (Barclays) to modern deployment of roughly 3.8 million units worldwide, Galloway outlines key manufacturers such as NCR and Wincor Nixdorf.
- **Procurement Paths**: Galloway evaluated four avenues for obtaining a machine: grey market (eBay listings, medical used-goods liquidators), black market inquiries, a wildcard road-trip option importing an ATM from Russia to the UK, and legal procurement through ATM maintenance companies such as Testlink or SPC International.
- **Logistics and Physical Handling**: Freestanding ATMs weigh between 700 and 1,000 kilograms (near a ton) due to reinforced steel vaults with concrete and steel fibers. Moving, powering, and storing an ATM posed extreme challenges, including destroyed concrete floors, outdoor power rigging, and courier lift limitations.
- **Attack Vectors and Security Flaws**: Examination of brute force physical attacks, operating system vulnerabilities, application control bypasses, hardware tampering, and network exploitation.

### Technical Details
- **Procurement Specifics**: Galloway purchased a refurbished freestanding machine from maintainer Testlink for approximately £3,200 (including VAT). She emphasizes understanding the distinction between "tested" units (no component guarantees) and "refurbished" units (every component refurbished), as well as ordering necessary internal cash cassettes holding roughly 1,800 to 2,000 notes per cassette across four denominations.
- **Operating System Attacks**: ATMs predominantly run Windows XP (with newer models moving to Windows 7). Galloway demonstrated bypassing kiosk mode interfaces via hotkey combinations and keyboard navigation to reach the underlying OS and file system, noting that disabled mouse pointers can be easily circumvented with keys. Software-level malware frequently targets XFS (Extensions for Financial Services), which utilizes an open API. Application whitelisting controls can frequently be bypassed using vulnerable whitelisted executables.
- **Hardware & Physical Attacks**: While vaults are heavily fortified, front facades are often made of weak plastic that can be cut through with basic household drills or bare hands to access internal PC cabling (such as USB connections). Galloway also highlighted connecting embedded systems (e.g., Arduino, Teensy) directly to the dispenser or PC inside the rear service area (via lockpicking without cosmetic damage) to issue direct dispensing commands. Network access vectors include intercepting unencrypted 3G/4G or leased-line infrastructure, deploying malware via OS update channels, or compromising VPN credentials.

### Takeaways
Acquiring and compromising an ATM does not require elite or prohibitive skill, but handling the physical logistics and weight of the machine represents the biggest real-world obstacle. Galloway highlights that ATM security relies heavily on the physical bulk of the vault rather than robust internal computing protections, and points out that responsibility disputes between hardware vendors and banks often leave older hardware inadequately secured despite config-level hardening possibilities.

talks.title: Travis Goodspeed - Some Thoughts on Literate Disassembly and Symbol Porting
talks.teaser: Explains how to run reverse engineering as a maintained project using text symbol files, version control and CI.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that reverse engineering projects should be built and maintained like software projects. It starts from a common pattern: an analyst accumulates names, comments and function boundaries inside a single disassembler database. That works for a small, one-off target, but it becomes hard to share with teammates, hard to compare across firmware versions and tied to one tool. Opening someone else's database can show only a few names, or fail on licensing.

The proposed alternative is plain text. Symbols are kept in simple flat files of address and name pairs, in formats that disassemblers and GNU ld can read, and each guess is marked so it can be filtered out before anything is linked against. Version control records who named what and when. The speaker describes porting symbols between firmware revisions with a small tool that matches byte-identical functions while ignoring linker relocations, then fixing the few functions that changed by hand. Structural patterns, such as a module's address range or the Thumb function prologue, can label large parts of an image in one pass, though these hold only for some programs. Emulation can exercise embedded code on a development machine, and headless Binary Ninja scripts can validate imports in continuous integration.

The main takeaway is to choose one file format, use clear file names, write down findings, and add tests that run against every target version. Keeping the project clean lets a new collaborator catch up quickly, and keeping the data in text lets it move to other tools and targets later.

talks.title: Costin Raiu / keynote - APT Paleontology in the age of cyber
talks.teaser: Walks through Kaspersky's APT hunts, from a Silverlight zero-day caught with YARA to the Wild Neutron espionage group.
talks.summary:
Costin Raiu, who leads the global research and analysis team at Kaspersky, frames advanced persistent threat investigation as paleontology. Analysts often hold only a few fragments of a campaign, so they keep collecting samples, tracing lateral movement and mapping command-and-control domains until the full picture takes shape. He used the Regin espionage platform as an example: his team began tracking it around 2008 and 2009 but published only in 2014, once the scattered early samples formed a complete structure.

Three investigations follow. The first began with a Russian seller offering exploits to the surveillance vendor Hacking Team. Raiu noticed that the seller's Silverlight exploit code left debug strings behind and wrote a YARA rule to match them. Months later the rule flagged a Silverlight exploit used against a victim in Laos, which Microsoft confirmed as a zero-day. The second covers the Wild Neutron group, which avoided government targets and went after law firms, Bitcoin companies and investment-linked businesses. Its tactics included watering-hole sites, stolen code-signing certificates, a Java zero-day, a versioned backdoor and an SSH-based tool for bulk data theft. Attribution stayed unresolved, with several apparent false flags.

The talk closes by returning to the seller's unsold iOS zero-day. Raiu argues that anyone can do this kind of hunting by learning YARA, a rule language he still uses most days and which Apple has built into macOS antivirus. He also argues that defenders should give their own networks as much attention as offensive research.

talks.title: Dániel Komáromy
talks.teaser: Argues that defenders protecting mobile and embedded products start at a structural disadvantage against attackers.
talks.summary:
The keynote challenges the view that large companies get breached only because they do not care. Drawing on years of product security work at a chip maker, the speaker argues that attackers hold the edge in mobile and embedded systems. Defenders have little telemetry on local, proximity and carrier-network attacks, so they cannot see what is being exploited. Exploit prices have also kept pace with rising target difficulty, so the cost of attacking has not really gone up for attackers.

The middle of the talk looks at why defenders' usual advantages erode. Products are often assembled from black-box components supplied by others, such as a phone's baseband or a car's key-fob chip, and vendors inherit their flaws. Examples include a remotely reachable baseband interface on iPhones, an outdated key-fob chip still shipping in cars, and poor early-boot entropy that made a car's onboard Wi-Fi passwords easy to crack. Other problems include debug interfaces that work as back doors, long product tails that keep old bugs alive, misaligned patch cadences, and disclosures that give attackers reusable older bugs.

The closing advice is to choose priorities and state known gaps openly instead of chasing rare research showcases. The speaker warns that obscurity and firmware encryption can slow fixes and create safe havens for attackers. Security work should also run in parallel with development rather than being squeezed in after a product is finished.

talks.title: Kelly Shortridge - "The Art of Explanation: Behavioral Models of InfoSec"
talks.teaser: Applies behavioral economics such as prospect theory to explain why defenders and attackers make irrational security decisions.
talks.summary:
Kelly Shortridge uses the familiar Keynes observation about financial markets to frame security defenders as people whose irrational habits can outlast their uncompromised status. The talk introduces prospect theory, which holds that people judge outcomes against a reference point, feel losses more strongly than gains, and overweight small probabilities.

Applying that model, the speaker argues that attackers act from a gain-seeking posture and tend to be risk-averse, while defenders sit in a loss posture and take risky bets to return to their baseline. This helps explain why simple, high-certainty controls such as two-factor authentication and Microsoft's EMET see low adoption, while flashy anti-APT products sell well. The talk also covers time inconsistency, the fast intuitive versus slow deliberate thinking described by dual system theory, and how group decisions can amplify biases through groupthink and escalation of commitment.

For practitioners, the suggested responses include raising attacker costs by eliminating low-hanging fruit, reducing the value of a breach through segmentation and separated data stores, and using data and individual accountability to counter bias. The speaker closes by calling for more empirical research on defender behavior and more sharing of unbiased metrics.

talks.title: Vladimir Katalov - iOS Acquisition Methods Compared
talks.teaser: Compares ways to extract data from iPhones and iPads, from local backups to iCloud, and what each method reveals.
talks.summary:
The talk compares the main ways a forensic examiner can extract data from an iPhone or iPad, and what each one reaches. The speaker opens with the kinds of information a modern phone holds, such as messages, browser history and keychain entries, and stresses preserving the device as seized. Leaving a powered phone switched on, blocking remote wipe and keeping it isolated from networks are presented as the first practical steps.

Three acquisition families are compared. Local iTunes backups are the easiest route but depend on the passcode or on a pairing record saved on a previously trusted computer, and an encrypted backup password is tied to the device itself, so breaking it is slow. Physical imaging of the memory chip is described as largely impractical on modern 64-bit hardware, since it generally requires a jailbreak. The speaker also warns that passcode-guessing boxes often fail and can wipe keys after repeated attempts, so they are risky to use.

Cloud acquisition, through iCloud backups and synced data, is presented as the most common approach today. It needs an Apple ID and password or a valid authentication token from a paired computer, and two-factor authentication complicates access. Synced content can include photos, Safari tabs, the reading list, contacts, calendars and the iCloud Keychain, which the speaker says always requires two-factor protection. The closing advice is to work through a checklist of passcode status, credentials, physical access and jailbreak state before choosing a method, and to enable two-factor authentication on personal accounts.

talks.title: Csaba Fitzl, Miklós Desbordes-Korcsev
talks.teaser: Shows how to automate buffer overflow exploit generation in WinDbg and how to debug obfuscated browser exploits.
talks.summary:
The speakers start from a pain point: turning a crash into a working exploit for a basic stack buffer overflow is slow, since offsets, bad characters, jump instructions and shellcode all have to be found by hand, and the debugger is restarted after every mistake. Their Python module drives WinDbg through the PyKD library to automate that flow for two Windows applications. It finds the offset, filters bad characters, locates jump instructions in loaded modules, can bypass ASLR when a module lacks the flag, and uses Metasploit for shellcode. A demo on Minishare runs the whole chain and saves a ready-to-run Python exploit.

The second part covers reverse engineering browser exploits hidden in obfuscated JavaScript. Pulling the script out of the page breaks its references to DOM objects, and anti-debugging checks can change behaviour, so the speakers instead let the sample run in the native browser. WinDbg scripts hook evaluation functions, log each session to its own file, and stop at the crash or before the shellcode runs. Attaching to the right browser process and handling different symbols across Internet Explorer, Edge and Chrome are called out as the main hurdles. A demo recovers deobfuscated strings from a multi-stage exploit sample.

A pointer-chain tool is also released to find chains of pointers from a register or stack value to a target address, useful when building ROP-based exploits. The speakers note that the same techniques serve defenders analysing malicious browser code. Source code and a tutorial on the methodology are promised after the conference.

talks.title: Dmitry Chastuhin, Dmitry Yudin –Getting access to the SAP server via SAP Management Console
talks.teaser: Researchers detail chaining SAP Management Console authentication weaknesses with process crashes to gain remote command execution.
talks.summary:
Two ERP-focused security researchers describe how they pursued remote command execution against SAP, beginning with reverse engineering the large disp+work dispatcher binary in IDA Pro and abandoning that path when debugging multi-process request handling proved too costly. They shifted to SAP Management Console (sapstartsrv), which exposes administrative HTTP methods including OS execute but normally requires OS credentials.

By analyzing sapstartsrv authentication, they identified a trusted internal connect path with hard-coded usernames and a shared-memory check for the password. Misconfigured dispatcher profile settings that left sapstartsrv in a bad state could leave shared memory uninitialized so the effective key became predictable, allowing OS execute calls with the hard-coded account. Alone that was local; they added remote denial-of-service race conditions against JSTART and the Internet Communication Manager so those components restart and recreate the vulnerable conditions, then looped execute attempts until Management Console accepted the weak key.

Practitioners should treat ancillary SAP binaries and consoles as high-value attack surface, expect exploit chains rather than single critical bugs, and harden even issues that look non-exploitable at first glance.

talks.title: ROUNDTABLE DISCUSSION
talks.teaser: Industry, university and nonprofit panelists discuss Hungary's IT talent shortage and why so few women enter computing.
talks.summary:
The moderator opens a roundtable on the shortage of IT professionals in Hungary, noting that a similar discussion was held a year earlier. The panel, drawn from a software company, a university, a cybersecurity firm and a girls' coding nonprofit, focuses on why women and girls are underrepresented in computing. Several speakers argue that gender stereotypes form early, and that girls who are enthusiastic at eight to ten years old often lose interest by fourteen, when career choices begin.

The nonprofit's founder describes its free Saturday sessions for girls aged eight to eighteen, where volunteer developers from partner companies mentor groups of about fifteen. Over two years, around 1,000 girls took part, and a survey found roughly 85 percent wanted to keep programming. A university representative says the faculty puts about 200 new IT graduates on the market each year, and the speakers agree that finding qualified staff is the main obstacle for employers. One speaker cites Israel's army, which trains about 1,000 cybersecurity specialists a year, as a model of close industry and military cooperation. Charts of the aging IT teacher population are also shown.

Toward the end, the panel discusses the digital education strategy, the pay gap between IT teachers and other teachers, and the difficulty adults face in judging the value of paid retraining courses. Community colleges and free online courses are offered as routes for people who missed earlier qualifications. The discussion closes with the view that lasting change needs structural decisions, and that the results of such decisions may only show after about ten years.

talks.title: Sergej Proskurin, Tamás K. Lengyel
talks.teaser: Shows how hypervisor-based malware analysis on Xen hides its presence from anti-analysis checks.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why malware analysis run from a hypervisor is needed, since debuggers and in-guest monitors can be spotted by malware that fingerprints its environment. The speakers walk through common checks such as hypervisor CPUID bits, vendor strings, disk size, uptime and memory size, and show how a test program flags a default setup. They explain that CPUID responses can be filtered on the fly and that copy-on-write storage and memory sharing can address disk and RAM checks, while noting that memory sharing weakens over time and can open cross-VM Rowhammer risks.

The harder problem is monitoring with multiple vCPUs, where breakpoints hidden through EPT permission changes create a race condition. The speakers describe the alternate p2m subsystem, which provides several memory views that can be switched at runtime, and gfn remapping, which points a guest page at a shadow copy that only appears during execution. They also cover a breakpoint-length quirk in the Intel manual that could let malware detect the monitor, and early Linux system call tracing on ARM, where stealthy single-stepping is still missing.

Remaining gaps include I/O emulation, timing instructions and debug events. The ARM work includes a Google Summer of Code project that extends alternate p2m to ARM and a TLB-partitioning approach for single-stepping. The takeaway for practitioners is that stealth depends on hypervisor internals, and that hypervisor-level features such as CPUID trapping and memory views can hide analysis, though much of this is still in progress.

talks.title: Aleksandar Nikolic
talks.teaser: Shows how closed-source Linux binaries can be instrumented with Dyninst to get fast, coverage-guided fuzzing like AFL.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a primer on guided fuzzing, contrasting blind mutation with coverage feedback. It covers AFL's core ideas: compile-time instrumentation, a shared-memory bitmap that records edge transitions as a fitness signal, and a fork server that keeps process creation cheap. The speaker then reviews ways to fuzz closed-source binaries, such as Pin- and DynamoRIO-style dynamic instrumentation, which is slow, and AFL's QEMU user-mode mode, which must instrument either only the main binary or every linked library.

The core of the talk is a small tool built on the Dyninst static rewriting framework. It instruments each binary once, adds AFL-compatible coverage hooks and a fork server, and can target individual functions or libraries. Control-flow recovery in mixed code and data is heuristic, and Windows support is weak. In a live comparison on a PNG library, native AFL ran at roughly 2,600 executions per second, QEMU mode at 600 to 700, and the rewritten binary at about 1,700, with coverage growing during the run.

The last part covers bugs found over the past year. A month or two of runs on a twelve-core machine against an Oracle document-filtering SDK and HP KeyView produced thousands of crashes, leading to automated triage and roughly 20 patched Oracle bugs. Examples include an XML integer overflow that needs precise byte conditions, a stack overflow from a tiny unknown-format input, and a TIFF heap overflow. Takeaways: speed matters, good corpora carry over between parsers, and narrow instrumentation keeps fuzzing focused.

talks.title: Zoz - Data Demolition: Gone in 60 Seconds
talks.teaser: Compares thermal, kinetic, explosive, and electric ways to destroy rack storage in under sixty seconds against capable adversaries.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from waste-stream and trash-picking history: discarded printers, drones, and live seizures can expose secrets when encryption keys remain on captured hardware. The stated goal is a one-rack-unit kill switch that eliminates magnetic and solid-state media in about sixty seconds, without sprinklers, collateral gear damage, or risk to nearby staff, while assuming state-level or well-funded forensic opponents.

Industrial degaussing, shredding, and burning set the baseline; the speaker then walks platter metallurgy and Curie temperatures before testing thermal paths (plasma cutting in roughly forty seconds, oxygen-fed aluminum combustion, thermite slurries, pre-packed thermite and thermate, copper thermite, and large molded charges), kinetic nail guns through spinning platters, and damped high-explosive work including oilfield perforators, parametric OpenSCAD enclosures, a reverse-engineered nitromethane-aluminum mix called Felix, annular and radial shaped charges, and supermarket shaving cream as blast cushioning. SSD-oriented electric attacks cover exploding bridgewires, ground-reference spikes that delaminate board traces, and inductive crush demos on cans as a scale metaphor.

Closing guidance favors plasma cutting and oxygen injection thermally, nail guns for less capable threats, contained Felix charges with side containment, and high-voltage ground spikes for flash chips, while noting uncertain military SSD recovery limits. A Bluetooth out-of-range laptop demo with detonation cord in an optical bay underscores that powered-on checks at borders do not prove tamper-free devices.

talks.teaser: See how radio replay and weak keystroke protection can put wireless keyboards and mice at risk.
talks.summary: The speaker describes an analysis of five wireless desktop sets, covering hardware and firmware inspection, radio testing, and the tools used. The talk demonstrates how weak data protection and replay handling can expose keystrokes or enable unauthorized input, including keystroke injection on some tested devices. Attendees learn the attack conditions, the vendors’ responses, and why the speaker recommends avoiding the tested vulnerable products.

talks.title: Levente Buttyán, András Szijj, Zsolt Szalay - Hacking cars in the style of Stuxnet
talks.teaser: Shows how a compromised workshop diagnostic PC can use a proxy DLL to intercept and alter a car's OBD traffic.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that attacking a car through the diagnostic software on a workshop PC is easier than the remote attacks that dominate car-hacking research. The speakers, from the Budapest University of Technology and Economics, frame this as a Stuxnet-style approach: infect a poorly maintained PC that is often connected to the internet, then manipulate the application that talks to the vehicle over the OBD port. They note that remote attacks need a specific exploitable bug for each interface and brand, which makes them hard to scale.

For a proof of concept, the team examined a widely used third-party diagnostic application against an Audi TT used for teaching. The application's DLLs were not effectively checked for signatures, so the team loaded a proxy DLL ahead of the original, which let them log, replay and modify messages before passing them on. They reverse engineered the proprietary cable protocol, including its message format, a checksum, and XOR-based encryption driven by a static table, and recomputed checksums after each edit. An inexpensive clone cable passed the license check. Using replayed and modified messages, they switched off the airbag while the software kept showing it as on.

The takeaway is that the application's protections, such as signing and obfuscation, were not sufficient. The speakers recommend verifying every third-party component with signatures and CRCs before loading and periodically during runtime, and using proper cryptography rather than simple XOR. They close by raising an open question about IoT devices managed from PCs, where an infection could remove itself and leave the devices compromised.

talks.title: Váradi Tamás– Tárcsás zárak nyitásának eszközei és módszerei
talks.teaser: Shows how disc detainer locks are identified, how their discs work, and how a specialised pick is used to decode them.
talks.summary:
The talk covers disc detainer locks, which can be recognised by a circular keyway with a rectangular or butterfly-shaped cut and by their key profiles. The speaker explains how the internal discs and spacer rings determine a lock's complexity, and how the number of notches and their angles reveal how many discs a lock has. He recounts the history of the method, beginning around 2007 when a young Finnish picker claimed he could decode Abus Granit locks. The manufacturer responded by sending him locks to open, and his solution became the basis for the decoding approach presented.

The method works from the back of the lock. All discs are first turned to the end position, then each one is manipulated in reverse. The pick's tip is under half a millimetre thick so it can move between the discs without disturbing them. The tool is scaled in 18-degree steps, which the speaker's group subdivided into tenths. They found that false cuts allow a much narrower movement of a disc than correct cuts, which makes the two distinguishable. Once a lock is opened, its key code can be read directly, because such keys are cut from the code rather than from an existing key.

The speaker contrasts these locks with cheaper Chinese disc locks, whose plastic sleeves give unreliable feedback, and with newer designs that place a rotating disc at the top or middle, which requires a three-part tool. He stresses steady practice on many different locks, and notes that opening locks is prohibited in Hungary. He closes by saying that the Abloy Protec has not yet been opened publicly.

talks.title: Márk Vinkovits - I play Jack of Information Disclosure - How to do threat modeling via playing cards
talks.teaser: A session contrasts report-driven threat modeling with OWASP card games that pull developers into finding flaws in a web shop.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by challenging doom-and-gloom views of security and frames threat modeling as something ordinary teams can do when the goal is to harden real software, not to produce unreadable paperwork. He walks through ENISA-style definitions—threat agents, business-meaningful assets, and paths through weaknesses—and stresses scope, purpose, and audience, especially developers who need clear technical language instead of battle reports that land in spam folders.

Classical threat modeling steps are familiar on slides, but published advice often boils down to vague brainstorming, impractical attack enumeration, or risk write-ups that architects might mock and developers cannot act on. The alternative is gamification with OWASP Cornucopia and Elevation of Privilege: suit-based cards describe concrete abuse cases, players compete by severity, and each play must map to the system under review. Using a deliberately weak online store and a shared data-flow diagram, the room works through authentication, authorization, validation, cryptography, and general issues such as enumeration, missing rate limits, privileged config access, injection, integrity of updates, plaintext secrets, and insider abuse.

After the game, developers capture findings in their normal ticketing flow; product owners and senior engineers then prioritize by customer impact and exploit difficulty. The closing message is that document-heavy modeling widens the security–development gap, while the card-driven workshop produces shared context, notes developers understand, and backlog items they can fix—without drilling into endless low-level detail during the session itself.

This talk aims to demonstrate that graph databases and the typical program representations developed in compiler construction are a match made in heaven, allowing large code bases to be mined for vulnerabilities using complex bug descriptions encoded in simple, and not so simple graph database
queries.

talks.title: Glenn Ten Cate - OWASP Security knowledge Framework
talks.teaser: Shows how the OWASP Security Knowledge Framework guides developers through requirements, checklists and continuous integration checks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with an analogy between aviation and software security. Airlines rely on long training, checklists, manuals, in-depth testing and quick sharing of incidents between operators and manufacturers, and the speaker argues that software development should work the same way. He points to the large number of web application breaches and to the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard, a checklist of web security controls, now in its 3.0 revision, with levels meant for everything from simple to critical applications.

The main part is a walkthrough of the Security Knowledge Framework, an open source web application. Its knowledge base holds around 200 items, each explaining an attack and its mitigations, and its code examples cover PHP and .NET, with Python and Java in progress. In the pre-development view, a team selects planned features such as file upload or forms and receives the matching attack vectors and a downloadable report before any code is written. After development, the ASVS checklist is answered control by control, and each "no" answer is linked to a knowledge base item that explains the impact and the fix. The speaker describes running this as a workshop, reviewing code with the development team on screen.

The closing section covers continuous integration for the framework project itself. Travis CI builds each commit, Coveralls tracks unit test coverage, and a code quality service grades the code, so a developer sees problems within minutes. The speaker stresses that automated scanners still need manual validation and that expert penetration testing comes last. He ends by asking practitioners to contribute code examples, checks and project help.

talks.title: Áron Szabó - Post-kvantumkriptográfia: prím kérdések = príma kérdések
talks.teaser: Explains quantum threats to RSA and elliptic curves, then walks through hash-based signatures as a practical post-quantum option.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with lessons from classical cryptography failures: MD5 collisions later used to forge a code-signing certificate in the Flame malware, weak random number generation in OpenSSL and Android, and a Sony PlayStation signing flaw caused by bad randomness. It also warns that open-source code is not automatically audited, pointing to the Heartbeat bug that sat unnoticed in source code for years.

For post-quantum threats, the speaker explains how Shor's algorithm would break factoring and discrete-logarithm schemes, while Grover's algorithm roughly halves the strength of symmetric keys, so key sizes must grow. A small worked example factors 15 through period finding. He warns of harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks against hybrid key exchange and says forward secrecy needs rethinking for long-lived data.

The second half focuses on hash-based signatures, which rely only on simple hash functions. The speaker walks through parameter choice, generating private keys from random values, hashing them into a public key, then creating and verifying a signature and embedding it in a certificate structure. He notes IETF and RFC drafts and guidance from an EU working group. The main limit is that each key pair signs once unless combined into Merkle trees, so the approach fits narrow uses such as voting or public administration rather than general web servers.

talks.title: joernchen of Phenoelit - Your Web app, those hackers & you
talks.teaser: Shows recurring web app flaws like predictable password reset tokens and argument injection, and how developers can prevent them.
talks.summary:
The talk examines recurring flaws in web applications and the habits that let them reach production. The speaker, who focuses on Ruby on Rails, starts with password reset flows, which often break in surprising ways. In one case, MySQL treated a numeric zero as matching a string token, letting an attacker reset another account. In an ownCloud case, reset tokens were built from a predictable time-based identifier, and PHP type casting made the value even easier to guess. A third example, a Rails challenge modeled on Discourse's reset code, let a user-supplied session key choose which account was reset.

The middle section moves to other classes of bugs. A Git-backed wiki's search passed user input to git grep as separate arguments, so a query beginning with a dash could inject the -O option and run a shell command, even though shell metacharacters were blocked. GitHub's SSH frontend was another case, where a crafted username injected environment variables into a second SSH process. The Debian OpenSSL case, where a fix for an uninitialized variable weakened key generation, shows why scanner output needs checking.

The closing advice is aimed at developers. Treat each disclosure as free audit work: find the root cause, add a regression test, search for the same pattern elsewhere, and confirm the fix with the reporter. Follow public vulnerability mailing lists, and use threat modeling with trust boundaries to question assumptions about user input and the environment.

talks.title: Balázs Bucsay - Chw00t: Breaking Unices' chroot solutions
talks.teaser: Shows how chroot-confined processes escape on Linux and BSD systems, and why chroot should not count as a security boundary.
talks.summary:
The talk examines chroot, a long-standing Unix mechanism that confines a process to a directory tree. The speaker traces its lineage from Version 7 Unix through FreeBSD jails, Solaris containers and Linux containers, then argues that chroot was never meant as a security feature. For anyone who still must use it, the talk lists hardening steps: keep directories root-owned, avoid privileged processes inside, use distinct user and group IDs, close open file descriptors before the call, change the working directory first, and never mount procfs.

Attack scenarios are grouped by what the attacker already has: a shell, code execution inside a confined service, or only file system access such as an FTP account on shared hosting. Escape methods include changing the working directory before calling chroot, keeping a directory descriptor open across a second chroot, passing a descriptor over a Unix domain socket, mounting the host root partition, and reaching the init process root through procfs. A ptrace-based method attaches to a process outside the jail and is shown live. Results differ by system: on one BSD variant several techniques caused a denial of service, and a procfs-based technique triggered a kernel panic on DragonFly BSD. Nested privileged Linux containers were also shown to allow escape.

The practical takeaway is that chroot should not be relied on to contain an attacker, and that configuration mistakes such as a writable passwd file or writable shared libraries used by setuid binaries give an easy path out. The speaker's open-source tool, which implements the techniques, is available on GitHub, and the speaker invited testing on additional Unix variants.

talks.title: Axelle Apvrille - Fitness Tracker: Hack in Progress
talks.teaser: Shows how a popular fitness tracker can be tricked into logging fake steps and how its sync protocol was probed.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the popularity of entry-level fitness trackers, with sales estimated between 40 and 70 million units, and asks whether their step counts can be faked. Steps come from a three-axis accelerometer, and the speaker shows how a tracker mounted on a desk fan can log steps while the wearer sits still. Earlier researchers had done the same with a tracker on a car wheel. Some step-reward and betting platforms pay out for step goals, which gives attackers a clear motive.

The research then moves to the software side. The speaker wrote a small Python utility that talks to the tracker through a Bluetooth dongle, lets it synchronize data and makes its LEDs blink. The packet formats were reversed by hand, and the synchronized data sent to the vendor's servers was shown to be encrypted. Using the device channel, the speaker injected a short string of up to 17 bytes that came back in every later reply, even after a reset. This relies on a flaw reported to the vendor, which treated it as a bug. The tracker's output was also tested as a random number source with statistical suites, and it showed weaknesses.

The talk closes with its limits. The injection was a proof of concept with no real payload, and getting code to run on the synchronizing computer was left for future work. Replaying recorded step traffic with corrected counters failed, which suggests the encryption involves more than a simple counter. Probing the hardware was the next planned step, and the speaker expected a firmware update to close the flaw.

talks.title: Felix 'FX' Lindner - keynote speaker
talks.teaser: Rethinks what hacking means, who gets to judge it, and how disclosure, policy and the security industry shape each other.
talks.summary:
The speaker, Felix 'FX' Lindner, opens by describing how their security consulting work involves testing systems in aircraft, medical devices and cars, and then asks what hacking really means. They argue that the word depends on intent, and that people who take up hacking must accept the consequences, since connected technology now affects many people beyond the hacker. They describe how the culture moved from a meritocracy among friends to one driven by fame, money and competition.

Turning to organisations, the talk looks at why penetration tests are often unwelcome, since a damaging report can cost executives bonuses, which makes security spending hard to justify. It contrasts bug bounties with full disclosure, recalls how public pressure once pushed vendors to fix flaws, and argues that today vulnerabilities are often treated as a PR issue while compliance becomes box-ticking. The speaker also compares the NSA's surveillance reach with Google's data collection and says international policy advisers are largely drawn from large vendors.

The closing section argues that adding more security products often adds more code that can fail, and that reducing network connections and the number of computers is a better first step. The speaker stresses that availability and manageability matter in industrial settings, where a delayed packet can cause problems, and ends by saying that the work matters.

talks.teaser: Walks through famous malware blunders by virus authors and OS vendors, and the lessons each side should take away.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at well-known mistakes in the history of malware, where both virus authors and operating system developers made errors that let infections spread for years. It starts with the 1986 Brain virus and the growth of Windows malware, which the description puts well above 200 million samples.

The speaker then goes through individual cases. These include the SQL Slammer worm of 2003, which spread across networks, and macro viruses that moved through Office documents. Other examples are a file-destroying program whose plain delete routine left files recoverable when no significant disk writes followed, a bitcoin-mining botnet idea that did not pay off, and the 2005 Sony audio CD rootkit. The talk also covers Windows autorun behaviour, a 2012 botnet that infected hundreds of thousands of machines, and a 2008 malicious JavaScript in PDF files that exploited Adobe Reader. For each case, the speaker explains who contributed to the problem and how long it took for the fix to arrive.

The closing section draws the lessons together. Operating system vendors need to respond faster once weaknesses are known, users need security awareness and timely updates, and antivirus makers should rely more on proactive detection than on signatures alone. The speaker's point is that these recurring mistakes can only be avoided if every party learns from them.

talks.title: Váradi Tamás, Zánthó Csaba
talks.teaser: Lamellás vs. csapos zárak biztonsága examines Váradi Tamás, Zánthó Csaba.
talks.summary:
The talk takes up a common question: is a pin tumbler lock (csapos) or a lever lock (lamellás) safer for a home? The speakers sort locks into four grades by resistance to attack. Basic locks open within seconds, protected locks with anti-pick features hold off an unprepared attacker but fall to a skilled one in about five minutes, high-security locks use unfamiliar mechanisms, and unpickable models have no publicly known method.

Much of the talk explains why pin tumbler cylinders can be picked. Manufacturing tolerances mean the holes and pins never line up perfectly, so often only one pin binds at a time and can be set on its own. Lever locks share this weakness, with a single lever often holding the bolt. Makers answer with complex keyways, extra levers and replaceable cores, and magic-key decoding fails once a single lever loses its spring. Premium cylinders need special tools made for one lock type and long practice.

For home use, the speakers advise choosing mid to upper-tier locks, since a higher price usually means better quality, and replacing old locks that may be decades out of date. A good lock should hold a skilled attacker for at least 30 minutes and leave clear signs of tampering. Safes can take hours to manipulate, and the door, frame and surrounding wall matter as much as the cylinder, because a system is only as strong as its weakest part.

talks.title: Zsombor Kovács, Gergő Köpenczei - Advanced Tracing and Monitoring of Android Applications
talks.teaser: Shows how to trace Android app methods and their parameters by instrumenting smali code, without a debugger.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe reverse engineering Android apps that rely on heavy and poorly documented cryptography. Their usual options were decompiling the APK to approximate Java, running a static analyzer to locate classes tied to certificate pinning, login or storage, enabling debugging and attaching a jdb console, or hooking OS API calls. Each approach still left them searching through a large, unfamiliar codebase.

They built a Python tool, called D-Logger in the talk, that unpacks an APK, converts it to smali, and inserts log statements at every method entry, invoke and return, including parameter and return values for primitive types, strings, byte arrays and intents. The modified app is repackaged and resigned so it runs on a device or emulator, and the output appears in logcat, grouped by class and method. The talk covers register limits, the method count ceiling and unsupported object parameters.

In the demos, a small encryption app showed its encrypt call and key directly in the log, and a larger open-source password app produced far more output. A companion module converts the log into HTML that can be linked to decompiled JD-GUI sources. The tool is passive: it traces but cannot intercept or change behaviour. Practitioners would take away a faster way to map security-relevant code paths in apps without a debugger, though synchronized blocks can crash instrumented apps and need blacklisting.

talks.title: Ruchna Nigam - Android Packers: Separating from the Pack
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Ruchna Nigam - Android Packers: Separating from the Pack.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Ruchna Nigam, a malware analyst at Fortinet, presents an examination of Android runtime packers and their evolving role in mobile malware analysis. While packers were initially designed for legitimate purposes like code protection, tamper-proofing, and DRM to prevent tampering with published applications, those same defenses become anti-analysis mechanisms when applied to malware. Nigam details the anatomy of Android runtime packers—comparing them to executable Russian nesting dolls that unpack and run nested executables in memory—and evaluates four specific packers: Panxi, LIAPP, Bangcle (referred to phonetically as Benkel), and APKProtect. She demonstrates practical unpacking methodologies, highlighting the challenges packers pose for automated security scanners and detection pipelines.

### Key Topics
- **Runtime Packer Concepts**: Comparison of runtime packers to Russian nesting dolls and desktop analogues like UPX in Windows malware, where an outer wrapper decrypts and executes Dalvik executables in memory.
- **Packer Analysis (Four Tools)**:
  - **Panxi**: An analyst-friendly packer analyzed purely statically. It relies on a wrapper application, loads a native library (`nsecure`), checks integrity via an AES-decrypted digest file (`diesd`), and decrypts the target application payload (`clex`) with simple XOR and Base64 before launching it via `DexClassLoader`.
  - **LIAPP**: A publicly hosted packing service that does not scan submissions for malware. It obfuscates original classes and uses anti-debugging mechanisms. A demonstrated unpacking approach uses an Android emulator, GDB server/client, memory inspection to locate an optimized DEX file via its magic number, and tools like baksmali/smali to extract readable code. A 'level two' variant includes anti-VM checks that crash on emulators.
  - **Bangcle (Benkel)**: A widely publicized runtime packer. While its cloud service scans and rejects known malware, it remains vulnerable to unknown threats. It employs native library decryption, obfuscated Dalvik-to-JNI mappings, hooked `ptrace`, disabled stack backtracing, and anti-debugging tricks.
  - **APKProtect**: An armor-style packer that breaks analysis tools like `apktool` and `dex2jar`. It employs complex string obfuscation involving swapped bytes, reflection-based Base64 decoding, XOR operations, and DES encryption.
- **Malware Usage & Detection**: Real-world sightings of these packers protecting malicious payloads (including SMS-sending malware) and the difficulties involved in detecting packed threats.

### Technical Details
- **Dynamic Unpacking via Memory Dumping**: Nigam demonstrates attaching GDB server to an emulator process. Because the primary application process blocks debugger attachment via anti-debugging routines, she identifies spawned child tasks and attaches to the final task where the payload is completely unpacked in memory. Inspecting `/proc/<pid>/maps` reveals temporary files and memory segments containing the magic bytes for an optimized DEX (`odex`) file. Once dumped from memory, `baksmali` converts the optimized DEX to Smali files, which can then be decompiled into Java source using a Java decompiler.
- **Static Analysis & Crypto Reversal**: In Panxi, exports from `nsecure` (`verify_digest` and `decrypt_x`) revealed AES decryption and XOR keys directly in plaintext. Conversely, APKProtect required reversing nested layers: extracting a hardcoded XOR key to generate the Base64 API string, invoking decoding via Java reflection, and applying DES decryption where the key (`safeguard`) was exposed via the Androguard-based sandbox Andrubis.

### Takeaways
- Detecting packed malware based purely on visible static signatures (such as static wrapper class names or shared library names) yields unacceptable false-positive rates because legitimate applications share the same packer artifacts.
- Dynamic memory dumping remains a highly effective, generic unpacking technique against modern packers, provided analysts can bypass anti-debugging and anti-VM safeguards.
- Antivirus and malware analysis pipelines must strike a careful operational balance between resource-intensive dynamic analysis (running samples in sandboxes/emulators to observe behavior or dump memory) and time-consuming manual reverse engineering of emerging packers.

talks.title: Gábor Németh - Fruitful Solutions - What To Use a Bank-Card Sized Computer For?
talks.teaser: Shows how a bank-card sized Raspberry Pi computer is used for education, hobby electronics, servers and industrial projects.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the Raspberry Pi, a credit-card-sized, low-cost open source computer running Linux, originally designed to get children learning to program. It traces the device back to early home computers and the 2012 launch, then compares the hardware generations: the power draw of the smaller model against the larger one, the extra USB ports and the reshaped composite video output, and the 2014 compute module used inside embedded products. The GPIO pins, the camera connector and the supported buses are shown as the way to attach sensors, relays and displays for physical projects.

The software side covers Raspbian, a Debian-based distribution with a graphical desktop, plus Scratch and Python for programming and any tool available on Debian. The examples range from a media player that turns an old television into a smart TV, to a file and torrent server, a time server fed by GPS, and a thin client. Other cases include a solar-powered wildlife camera, beehive weight monitoring, passenger information in buses, a camera rig for 3D photogrammetry that cut capture time from several weeks to half an hour, and a ruggedised telescope controller shipped to Chile where power is unreliable.

The talk closes with Banana Pi as a compatible alternative offering a SATA connector and gigabit Ethernet, and notes that Android and penetration-testing distributions such as Kali Linux also run on these boards. The main takeaway is that a cheap, low-power board can cover many roles at once. The speaker invited the audience to try the demo units at the booth and to take part in the EU Code Week programming events from 11 to 17 October.

talks.title: Gábor Molnár - Handcrafting ASCII Flash Files for Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Shows how a JSONP callback flaw let attackers run Flash files on a major platform, built from only ASCII characters.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a cross-domain weakness in the JSONP API of a large web platform, where the callback name parameter was not checked against the expected CSRF token. The speaker explains why JSONP is used to get around the same origin policy, and how an attacker who controls the callback name can pull data from another domain. Because the API prefixed its responses with an empty JavaScript comment, plain HTML injection did not work, but a crafted Flash file used as the callback could run in the target's domain context.

The constraints made the exploit hard. On one endpoint the callback filter allowed only the lower half of the ASCII table, and browsers rejected zero bytes in the name parameter, which blocked the first working version. The speaker therefore built a minimal loader and a Flash file made only of permitted bytes. This meant tuning DEFLATE compression inside a ZIP container, designing Huffman tables by hand so that the encoded output stayed within printable characters, and avoiding uncompressed blocks and negative offsets. The issue was reported through a bug bounty to Adobe, and a separate researcher later published a tool that compressed any Flash file into an ASCII form.

The talk closes with the vendor's fix and its weakness. The check for JSONP compatibility could be bypassed by omitting a closing parenthesis. The practical lessons are that JSONP callbacks need strict validation, that a Content-Type header is not a reliable defence when a browser renders content as Flash, and that legacy plugins can turn small filter gaps into serious cross-origin access.

talks.title: Philip Young - Smashing the Mainframe for Fun and Prison Time
talks.teaser: Walks through a 2012 breach of a Swedish government mainframe and the z/OS attack techniques that enabled it.
talks.summary:
The talk is a primer on IBM mainframes for people new to the platform. It explains z/OS concepts such as logical partitions, TSO sessions, data sets, Unix System Services and RACF, the central database that controls access and stores password hashes. JCL job control and REXX scripting are introduced so the later attack details make sense.

The main case study is a 2012 breach of a Swedish government mainframe run by a third-party contractor. The attacker abused a web server CGI weakness to run commands, submitted JCL through an exposed FTP interface, and used a setuid-root REXX script to reach root. He then planted root-shell backdoors and SSH keys that survived account deactivation, and copied the RACF database for offline password cracking. An operator's notice of unusual workload first exposed the intrusion.

The speaker then demonstrates tools he has built for mainframe testing, including an Nmap patch and screenshot script, an Ettercap module that captures TSO logins from 3270 traffic, a user enumeration script, and an EBCDIC-aware netcat replacement. He warns that password guessing can lock out entire user populations. The talk closes by pointing to the free Hercules emulator as a way to practise safely and by urging more researchers to examine the platform.

talks.title: Tamas K. Lengyel - Virtual Machine Introspection to Detect and Protect
talks.teaser: Covers Xen-based virtual machine introspection for cloud workloads: isolation, guest memory interpretation, and hypervisor traps.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that common cloud security assumptions—ephemeral instances, host AV, and network IDS alone—leave defenders without real isolation between protected workloads and their tools. It positions virtual machine introspection as a way to relocate the security stack outside the guest, using the hypervisor to see virtual hardware, interpret guest state, and actively control execution.

On Xen, the speaker walks through moving protections into segregated security domains with XSM policies, Linux kernel changes for secondary control domains, and libVMI plus Rekall for paging-aware memory analysis on live guests. Demos on Windows 7 under Xen 4.4 list processes and modules from outside the VM, trace kernel activity and heap allocations to spot file access and thwart DKOM-style hiding, and hijack user-mode execution to launch programs without an in-guest agent.

The same stack supported a DARPA Cyber Fast Track cloud IDS prototype and will ship as open tools (including the Drogön release). Takeaways: interposition via VM exits, CR3 traps, EPT violations, and debug events enables coherent monitoring; VMI still has blind spots such as compromised hypervisors, virtual DMA, and out-of-band management processors.

talks.title: Komáromy Dániel - Enter The Snapdragon!
talks.teaser: Qualcomm's product security team shares how it hunted, fuzzed and hardened Android kernel bugs at scale.
talks.summary:
Qualcomm's product security team explains how a rise in public Android kernel exploits, from one in 2011 to three in 2012 and many more in 2013, drove a new response. Many of those exploits were simple, such as an exposed mmap interface giving user space access to kernel memory. The team's work spans attack intelligence, root cause analysis with patching, and feeding findings back into secure development.

A manual audit by about 11 engineers over roughly two months covered about 12 million lines of kernel code and found 266 zero-days, mostly information leaks, plus 93 high and three critical issues. Manual review proved unscalable. Nine checkers written for a graph-based static analyzer, queried in a Gremlin-style language, took about four weeks and found around 100 zero-days at roughly 30% false positives. A port of the Trinity syscall fuzzer to Android and ARM, focused on ioctl handlers, found more than 20 zero-days and now runs in production.

Hardening covered removing /dev/mem and /dev/kmem after refactoring code that depended on them, seeding early entropy from a hardware RNG, broadening stack protector coverage, and blocking RWX pages on ARM. PaX-style features were limited on ARM because domain support is missing. For discovery, the team uses an in-house web-monitoring tool and a kernel tracing tool to triage obfuscated exploits. The closing message is that getting fixes onto phones through device makers and carriers remains the slowest step.

talks.title: Benjamin Tamási
talks.teaser: Shows how a CCTV video recorder's hidden telnet service and firmware-stored password hash let an attacker gain root access.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at closed-circuit television recorders, the DVRs that store footage from security cameras, and how a widely used model can be compromised. It starts with a recorder whose admin password had been forgotten, where a simple default code opened the web interface. The speaker then found an undocumented telnet service on a second port and noted that weak default passwords were common across the devices they had examined.

The main technique was firmware analysis. The firmware file was a renamed archive containing a U-Boot image with a 64-byte header, and stripping that header with dd made it mountable as a compressed filesystem. The password file held an unshadowed DES hash for root, which was cracked quickly with hashcat and then used to log in over telnet as root. The speaker showed that binwalk, with its extraction option, could automate these steps. A separate account file in the configuration directory could be deleted to reset the admin password on reboot, and debug ports on the board offered console root access without any firmware work.

The impact is that a shared master credential exists across the vendor's products, so an attacker on the local network could wipe recorded footage or clear logs. The speaker argued that vendors should avoid master passwords, remove the hidden telnet access or tie it to a physical reset control, and consider custom firmware where vendors will not change their builds.

talks.title: Dr. Leitold Ferenc Horváth Botond
talks.teaser: Compares how endpoint tools and firewalls catch botnet command-and-control traffic, using replayed and live malware samples.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at defending against command-and-control (C2) traffic, the channel malware uses to contact its operators after infecting a machine. The speaker argues that no defense stops everything, so spotting and blocking C2 communication matters, and that endpoint protections and firewalls do not always handle it well. The work compares several defensive products on how they treat this traffic, and the talk also demonstrates what those products can do.

The team tested in two ways. In the first, recorded traffic from users was replayed against the protections, so every product received the same input. The limits are that only the captured exchanges were covered, and that protocols where the same message cannot be sent twice are hard to test this way. In the second, live malware samples were run in a test setup on Linux and Windows clients, which produces real traffic but takes more preparation. The samples included Zeus, a botnet family used to steal credentials, whose configuration file, executable and drop zone were examined.

Product verdicts were compared with the majority opinion across all products, since the true label of each sample was not always known. Over the test period, one product showed a stretch where it failed to identify the traffic and later recognized it, which the speaker linked to a communication problem with its backend servers. The takeaway is that a single product's verdict should not be trusted alone, and that repeated testing over time reveals gaps that one-off checks miss.
