talks.title: Tamás Jós, Attila Bogár - is BitTorrent really providing anonymity?
talks.teaser: Shows how BitTorrent trackers, DHT nodes and magnet links leak peer IPs, persistent node IDs and download history.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether BitTorrent actually provides anonymity. The speakers start with the history of peer-to-peer systems, from early file sharing and the Arpanet to Skype and Facebook's update distribution, then explain how a torrent file works. It holds tracker information, file names and a SHA-1 hash of each piece, and the info hash identifies the torrent. Magnet links expose that info hash and the trackers as plain text, and a small tracker can run in about 90 megabytes of disk space.

To show what an observer can learn, the speakers built a proof-of-concept logger that monitored the network without downloading content. Over the study they collected around 16,000 torrents and roughly 140,000 peers, then enriched the IP addresses with reverse DNS and GeoIP data. Tracker announces reveal uploaded and downloaded totals, and on private trackers a passkey ties activity to one account. In the DHT, each client has a persistent random node ID, which let them link a user across home, work and mobile addresses. They also found users who started a torrent client before their VPN, so the same node ID appeared under a new IP. Routing attacks on the DHT were described as possible in theory, though attempts to disrupt it had not succeeded in practice.

The speakers also described rights holders monitoring torrents and sending letters to IP owners, including one cam-recording download that cost 2500 euros. Their conclusion is that BitTorrent is not anonymous. Users should choose what they download, start the VPN before the torrent client, and remove the torrent client from autostart. Employers and governments should expect this traffic to be traceable.

He shows how Etsy raises attacker cost by pruning unused certificate authorities, quarantining Java browser plugins on jump boxes, forcing silent browser updates at SSO, pushing ad blockers, and reframing awareness around reporting phishing. He closes with goal-oriented attack simulations that mirror how adversaries actually reach crown jewels.

talks.title: Lajos Muha, Dr. - Interpretation of the Act on Information Security
talks.teaser: Explains how a Hungarian information security law defines electronic systems, scope, and risk-based security classes.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through Hungary's law on securing the electronic systems of state and municipal bodies, seen from one of its drafters, a cybernetics engineer. The speaker explains why the law avoids the label IT and adopts the term electronic information system, meaning devices, procedures, software and people working together rather than just linked hardware. The scope reaches beyond state institutions to national finance, national data assets and critical systems, so one system can fall under several authorities at once.

Protection is framed as keeping data and every system component confidential, intact and available in a closed, risk-weighted way, with logical, physical and administrative controls treated as equally important. The speaker argues that prevention alone is not enough, so detection of attacks and a structured incident review, covering cause, responsibility and fixes, are also required. The law asks organisations to assign components to security classes using a risk assessment that weighs likely damage against probability, with five damage classes modelled on a shorter American document.

The speaker stresses that the law prescribes outcomes rather than specific methods, so organisations may use any recognised risk analysis, while the five damage classes are fixed. Implementing regulations had not all appeared when the talk was given. The main takeaway for practitioners is to judge confidentiality, integrity and availability separately, so that one property does not force unnecessary spending on the others, and to keep the chief executive accountable for the overall result.

talks.title: Ákos Maróy, Tamás Bodoky - Anonim whistleblowing using the GlobaLeaks platform
talks.teaser: Explains how the open-source GlobaLeaks platform supports anonymous tips over Tor, and the practical risks sources still face.
talks.summary:
Ákos Maróy presented alone, as his co-presenter could not attend. He opened with the nature of whistleblowing and historical cases such as Daniel Ellsberg and the Pentagon papers, Frank Serpico's fight against police corruption, and Mark Felt, the anonymous source in the Watergate affair. He argued that whistleblowers often pay heavy personal costs, and that freedom of information requests and typical internal reporting forms give little protection to the person reporting.

The core of the talk was GlobaLeaks, an open-source submission platform developed by an Italian group. The server runs as a Tor hidden service, so sources reach it through a Tor browser without exposing their IP address. Each submission receives a random code that lets the source return later for a two-way exchange with journalists while staying anonymous. The platform can encrypt stored data and strip metadata from uploaded files, since names, machine details and organisation information often remain inside them. Maróy described a Hungarian instance called Modular Leaks, and noted that an earlier version was used in Bulgaria in a case he linked to a government falling.

He walked through the steps a source takes: install the Tor Browser, open the onion address shared on printed materials, upload documents, and keep the code. He stressed that technical anonymity does not cover every risk, since metadata, workplace monitoring and the small pool of people who could be suspected of leaking all remain dangerous. The takeaway for practitioners was that the tooling protects the channel, but sources still need careful handling of their own behaviour.

talks.title: András Fehér, Csaba Otti
talks.teaser: Shows how two face recognition access systems can be fooled with infrared photos and a plaster mask.
talks.summary:
The talk comes from an independent testing group at a university-based biometrics institute, which evaluates security products under realistic conditions rather than relying on vendor datasheets. The speakers argue that face recognition is spreading quickly as a contactless access method, yet vendor figures for false acceptance and false rejection often do not match what happens in the field. They explain why many surveillance and access devices work in the infrared band, and how lighting, eyewear, partial face coverings and changing expressions affect matching.

For the live demonstration, two volunteers were enrolled in a face ID access device. The team then built a low-cost infrared camera from a web camera with its infrared filter removed, captured infrared images of both volunteers, adjusted them in image editing software and printed them. One device accepted a printed photo once the image and lighting were tuned, while the speakers reported that another device did not accept the paper image in their tests. They also made a plaster mask from a volunteer's face, registered it, and it was accepted after chalk makeup was applied, though differences in skin reflectance limited how closely the mask matched a real face.

The main takeaway is that a claim of perfect security does not hold up, and that each device has to be checked individually because no generic solution was found. Practitioners should map the real risks of biometric access control, test how a device behaves under realistic lighting and spoofing conditions, and treat vendor claims with caution.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Balint Varga-Perke, 'Buherator' - Heureka - The Suspicious Thing Is That It's Not Suspicious.
talks.summary: Bálint Varga-Perkő releases Heureka, a C++ Lego toolkit for exercising host antivirus and HIPS products beyond VirusTotal signature scans. He contrasts vendor hundred-percent marketing with RSA-style failures, then scores free, mid-tier, and enterprise suites on trivial persistence tasks finding roughly forty percent detection each. Live Hacktivity demos show Symantec, Avast, F-Secure, Kaspersky, and ESET missing raw Metasploit callbacks, download-execute chains, keyloggers, and injected explorer DLLs. He argues products behave like lazy station police, urges training reputation whitelists, and open-sources Heureka so buyers and researchers can compose their own behavioral test campaigns.

talks.title: Charlie Miller - Mobile Threats
talks.teaser: Compares iOS, Android and desktop attack costs to show why mobile threats are rarer than headlines suggest.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by questioning alarming mobile security headlines, arguing that most describe researcher demonstrations rather than attacks criminals actually run. It explains that code reaches a device either through malware a user chooses to run or through exploits that fire without user intent. Defenders can mostly make exploitation harder, limit what code can do, restrict persistence, and detect it afterwards.

The speaker contrasts iOS and Android. iOS requires code signing for every binary and library and relies on Apple's review and removal process, which makes persistence after a reboot hard. Android lacks mandatory signing, so an app can pass review with no permissions and fetch exploit code at runtime. Two personal cases are described, in which apps were pulled from each store after the speaker's research. The jailbreakme 3 exploit is walked through as an example of an iOS chain combining a browser memory bug with a kernel bug to disable code signing. Malware volumes and browser traffic shares suggest desktops remain the easier target, while mobile attack surfaces such as SMS, baseband and NFC are rarely abused in practice.

The talk argues that bigger everyday risks are lost unlocked phones, user jailbreaking, and Android fragmentation, where carriers and manufacturers slow updates while iOS versions spread quickly. For organisations, it recommends focusing on MDM controls such as passcodes, encryption and remote wipe rather than costly defenses against rare exploits. The closing point is that the picture could change if PCs become as hard to attack as phones, and that determined state actors are the main concern for mobile exploitation.

talks.title: Domonkos Tomcsanyi - GSM - have we overslept the last wake-up call?
talks.teaser: Demonstrates low-cost RTL-SDR sniffing of GSM, tracking a subscriber's temporary ID, and recovering A5/1 keys to decrypt a call.
talks.summary:
The talk by Domonkos Tomcsanyi reviews the state of GSM security and argues the protocol is weak enough that people should test it themselves. It traces the history from early theoretical attacks on A5/1, through published rainbow tables, to sniffing work built on software-defined radio and the osmocom-BB firmware that could follow hopping channels. Cost and scarce documentation are presented as the main barriers for newcomers.

Tomcsanyi proposes RTL-SDR dongles, which cost about 15 dollars, as an affordable receiver, and notes their limits: only downlink capture, no support for hopping cells, and a need for frequency calibration. The attack has four stages: finding the victim's cell, matching a phone number to its temporary subscriber identifier by sending silent SMS and correlating paging messages, analysing the cell's system information to locate known plaintext, and recovering the keystream. Kraken, with two terabytes of rainbow tables, produces a candidate key that a second burst verifies.

A live demonstration captured a phone call with an RTL-SDR stick, parsed the bursts, recovered the key and played back the decrypted speech. The speaker reported that cloud hardware ran the cracking faster than a local machine, and that two of three Hungarian operators he tested use non-hopping cells. He closes by urging attendees to repeat the process on their own equipment so pressure builds on carriers to fix the protocol.

talks.title: Csaba Krasznay - Cyber soldiers in the world -- how to become a military hacker?
talks.teaser: Surveys how states from the US to North Korea recruit hackers into military cyber units, and compares four national models.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how national militaries build cyber units and why they turn to the hacker subculture for people. The speaker, who holds a PhD on cyber warfare and the link between hacker culture and the military, says a NATO video about cyber defence prompted his research. He opens with recent examples: the NSA hiring large numbers of cyber experts, a Pentagon programme meant to fund hackers more quickly, and defence contractor job listings asking for reverse engineers and penetration testers.

The middle of the talk surveys several countries. China is described through military academies and civilian universities that teach information warfare, with hacker celebrity and nationalism presented as recruitment drivers. South Korea runs cyber warfare courses at a university for future soldiers, while North Korea is described through reported unit structures and a claim by a former professor of more than 3,000 hackers. Russia is presented as a largely opaque case with few official details. The UK announces an offensive cyber capability alongside a reserve unit of IT experts, and Germany and Estonia are contrasted as defence-focused. Hungary's ministerial order is also described as emphasising defence.

The speaker groups these examples into four models: a US-style approach that mixes offence and defence and recruits civilian experts, a Russian and Chinese approach built on state-linked talent, a developing-country model relying on nationalist hacker groups, and a European model focused only on defence. He closes by asking hackers to decide whether they will cooperate with the military or with government.

talks.title: Dmitriy Chastuchin - Injecting evil code in your SAP J2EE systems
talks.teaser: Demonstrates chaining SAP deployment manager weaknesses into a backdoored Java server and stolen administrator credentials.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the security of SAP's software development infrastructure, focusing on the Software Deployment Manager, a Java component that installs and updates applications on the SAP application server. The speaker argues that SAP systems hold financial and HR data and are increasingly reachable from the internet, yet they are often neglected. He also cites rising yearly patch counts as evidence that vulnerabilities keep appearing.

The main attack path starts with the deployment manager's login. The client sends a hash of the password, which the server compares with a hash stored in a configuration file, so an attacker who obtains that hash can log in without knowing the password. The hash can be read through an exposed SAP Lock Viewer service that lets a remote user register and read arbitrary files, or through a file traversal flaw. The client's hash function is then hooked at runtime using the Java attach API and the JavaSnoop tool. Once logged in, an attacker can deploy a backdoored application and gain a shell on the Java server. From there, the encrypted credential store and its key file can be read and decrypted with a custom tool, which yields administrator credentials for the system. A live demo walks through this chain.

The closing section lists mitigations: restrict access to the secure store and key files, apply the relevant SAP notes, and run regular security assessments that include code review and network segregation. The practical message is that ERP systems need the same ongoing scrutiny as other business-critical services.

talks.title: Vaagn Toukharian
talks.teaser: A spider-driven layer-seven GET flood hammers slow endpoints, then Apache modules and QA workflows show how to harden apps.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames denial of service from volumetric crashes through resource consumption at the network, device, and application layers, with emphasis on layer seven and business-logic abuse such as cart stuffing. It contrasts blind GET flooding and distributed botnets with slower attacks and WebSocket drains, then introduces a Qualys-built approach that still uses GET requests but adds pre-attack crawling to list resources, measure transfer speeds, and filter out high-variance URLs so stress targets the slow, stable quadrant of the distribution.

The demonstrated tool crawls to a chosen depth, exports XML for other workflows, and visualizes crawl graphs. On a local Concrete CMS instance, parallel clients pushed CPU to roughly one hundred percent with only a handful of threads. The speakers position the same utility as offensive load generation and as a QA aid to find CPU or database hogs, while noting load-balancer rate limits can be ridden under thresholds.

Defense covers horizontal scaling, commercial scrubbing services and their tuning pain, and hands-on tests on a four-core Apache host that hit about ninety-eight percent CPU without extra modules. They evaluate ModSecurity, IP-based limiters, mod_qos, mod_bwshare, mod_evasive, and honeypot blacklisting, favoring mod_evasive for broader slow-attack coverage with simpler setup, and outline future work on parallel degradation metrics, load-balancer skew, and genetic SQL wildcard payloads.

talks.title: Charlie Miller
talks.teaser: Shows how CAN bus messages were injected into two 2010-era cars to control steering, braking and gauges.
talks.summary:
This talk covers car hacking research by the speaker and a colleague who was not present, done on two 2010-model cars, a Ford Escape and a Toyota Prius. It explains why the work was harder than normal software research, from sourcing cars to working on their wiring by hand. It then introduces the electronic control units and the CAN bus that links them, where every unit sees every message and senders are not verified.

Using an OBD-II cable and a Python library the team wrote, they injected CAN messages to change the speedometer, apply the brakes and turn the steering wheel, the latter by sending several messages so the car believed it was parallel parking. Ford tests also killed the engine, disabled lights, sounded the horn and tightened seat belts. A Toyota acceleration test kept the engine running after the pedal was released and blew out the inverter. Diagnostic security access was bypassed by reverse engineering mechanic tools to recover secret keys.

The researchers published a paper of about 100 pages with their tools, captured data and ECU firmware dumps so others could check their own vehicles. The key takeaway is that more electronics mean more things an attacker can affect, and the implicit trust placed in CAN traffic is a weak point.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Vivek Ramachandran - Cracking WPA/WPA2 Personal and Enterprise for Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Explains how WPA and WPA2 personal and enterprise networks are cracked, from handshakes to rogue access points.
talks.summary:
The talk covers attacks on WPA and WPA2 in both personal (pre-shared key) and enterprise (802.1X with RADIUS) modes, beginning with why WPA was designed as a stopgap for WEP-era hardware. It explains how a passphrase is stretched into a key and how the four-way handshake exposes enough values to test passphrase guesses offline. Captured handshakes are checked against a wordlist, so the attack only succeeds when the passphrase appears in that list.

Speed is the next focus. Precomputing master keys for a specific SSID turns each check into a lookup, and rented cloud instances make large wordlists affordable. The speaker also shows AP-less capture, where a rogue access point that answers a client's probe requests for a remembered network collects a usable handshake without knowing the key. Other cases include WPS PIN brute forcing with Reaver, which older firmware without lockout is vulnerable to, and an insider abusing the shared group key to spoof traffic.

For enterprise networks, a rogue WPA2-Enterprise honeypot with a fake certificate captures PEAP MS-CHAPv2 challenge-response exchanges when clients accept any certificate or trust any certificate authority, and those responses can then be dictionary attacked per user. The takeaways are to avoid WPA-Personal for shared environments, since any insider who knows the passphrase can decrypt others' traffic, to use long random passphrases, to pin trusted server names in client profiles, and to consider EAP-TLS where certificate management allows.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - András Kabai - Hunting and exploiting bugs in kernel drivers
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Hacktivity 2012 - András Kabai - Hunting and exploiting bugs in kernel drivers.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Hacktivity 2012, András Kabai explores hunting and exploiting vulnerabilities within Windows kernel drivers for local privilege escalation (LPE). While modern operating systems enforce strict separation between user mode (Ring 3) and kernel mode (Ring 0), third-party device drivers (such as those installed by antivirus or firewall software) frequently introduce vulnerabilities. Because Ring 0 code executes with unrestricted system and hardware access, successfully exploiting a kernel driver allows an attacker operating from a restricted user account to completely compromise the underlying operating system.

### Key Topics
- **Windows Driver Architecture:** The speaker examines the Windows Driver Model (WDM), which superseded VxD. When loaded, a driver uses `IoCreateDevice` to register a device object and exposes symbolic links that user-mode applications open via `CreateFile`. Communication is handled using I/O Request Packets (IRPs) sent through `DeviceIoControl`.
- **IOCTL Handling and Transfer Types:** Drivers process I/O control (IOCTL) codes targeting specific driver functions. The talk contrasts standard `METHOD_BUFFERED`—where the kernel I/O manager manages user/kernel buffer copying—with `METHOD_NEITHER`. In `METHOD_NEITHER`, raw user-space pointers are passed directly to the driver, frequently resulting in arbitrary memory overwrite vulnerabilities if parameters and pointers are not rigorously verified.
- **Tooling and Discovery:** Common tools for finding and analyzing drivers include Windows Driver Kit (WDK), WinObj (Sysinternals), Driver View, and IRP Tracker. For vulnerability research, Kabai highlights IDA Pro for reverse engineering alongside fuzzers such as ioctlbf, IOCTL Fuzzer, and Kito.
- **Exploitation Mechanics:** The presentation discusses "write-what-where" conditions, Kernel Patch Protection (KPP) limitations (which monitor dispatch tables but miss local function pointer overwrites), and staged shellcode execution.

### Technical Details
Kabai demonstrates an end-to-end local privilege escalation on a 32-bit Windows system using a vulnerable demonstration driver:
1. **Lab Setup:** Kernel debugging requires two machines connected via virtual serial ports configured using `bcdedit` (replacing legacy `boot.ini`). In the presenter's setup, two Windows VMs run on a Linux host.
2. **Vulnerability Analysis:** Disassembling the target driver (`dump_drv` function) shows stack-allocated variables followed by an array of function pointers. Although the driver uses `ProbeForRead` to verify user buffer readability, it performs a `memcpy` without verifying the input buffer length, creating a buffer overflow that can overwrite the function pointer array without triggering stack cookie protections.
3. **Crafting the Exploit:** The exploit script, written in Python, crafts an input buffer that satisfies a 4-byte "magic key" check and specifies an offset (setting the second DWORD to 0) to invoke the first function pointer. Python natively allocates executable memory for variables in user space, allowing Kabai to point the overwritten kernel function pointer directly to user-mode memory holding kernel shellcode.
4. **Token Stealing Execution:** The kernel shellcode accesses the current thread's `_KTHREAD` structure via `FS:[0x124]`, locates its `_EPROCESS` structure, and traverses the `ActiveProcessLinks` doubly linked list. It searches for the System process by checking for a UniqueProcessId of `4`. Once found, it copies the System process token and overwrites the attacker process's token before restoring registers and cleanly returning to kernel mode. Launching `cmd.exe` from the elevated process demonstrates full `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` privileges.

### Takeaways
Kernel driver exploitation remains a practical and impactful avenue for privilege escalation, especially during penetration testing when restricted user access has already been obtained. While remote kernel attacks are considerably more difficult, local driver vulnerabilities are prevalent in third-party software. The presenter notes that once analysts understand kernel structures like `_EPROCESS` and `_KTHREAD`, kernel exploitation relies on standard binary exploitation concepts.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Gábor Szappanos - Journey to the bottom of a black hole
talks.teaser: Dissects the Black Hole exploit kit, from how its source code leaked to how its browser exploits delivered malware.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the Black Hole exploit kit, described as the leading web threat of the previous two years. The speaker outlines its server-side design: a PHP and SQL back end with an admin panel, rental pricing, and a traffic direction system that serves exploits matched to a visitor's browser and operating system. The kit could also block addresses belonging to analysis labs and check its payloads against antivirus products. The analysed build was version 1.0.2, whose source code leaked in 2011.

Much of the talk covers how that code was obtained and read. The speaker traces the theft to a weak admin password, which a basic dictionary attack recovered quickly, after which a c99 shell backdoor was uploaded to the server. The code was protected with ionCube, so the analysis relied on decoders and educated guesses about obfuscated function names. Language settings, time zone, character encoding and date format were used to suggest a Russian origin, with a warning that such clues can be planted. The delivery chain then runs from email lures through redirects on hacked WordPress sites to a sequence of Java, PDF, Flash and Windows exploits.

The closing part shows Hungary with one of the highest infection rates in the statistics displayed, and Java as the most targeted attack surface. The speaker argues that users rarely know Java is an attack vector, so they should install updates promptly and refuse unexpected prompts to download and run a program.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - László Tóth Ferenc Spala - Think differently about database hacking P.
talks.teaser: Shows post-exploitation and network hijacking of Oracle and MS SQL sessions, including credential theft from the OCI client driver.
talks.summary:
The talk moves beyond SQL injection to ask what an attacker can do once they are already positioned around Oracle databases. The first part targets the Oracle OCI client driver: by hooking the functions that receive connection parameters and execute statements, the speakers showed that a user's username and clear-text password can be captured from the next query they run, and that credential material stays in memory after logout. A Metasploit extension automated this during a live demo on a Windows client.

The network section revisited TNS poisoning, which abuses the unauthenticated registration messages an Oracle listener accepts to redirect a share of client connections through an attacker's proxy. Their Python proxy then hijacks an established session, so queries run under the victim's identity; in the demo this was a DBA account. They also published a Metasploit module that supports service identifiers longer than the six characters the public proof of concept handled. With a privileged session, they showed how a debugging command could disable auditing, run operating system commands, and load a payload into Oracle's process memory.

The same hijacking approach was applied to Microsoft SQL Server through a TDS proxy, where a client that opens several connections lets an attacker take over one of the spares. Metasploit modules then ran queries and xp_cmdshell through the hijacked thread. The main lesson is that database clients, listeners and connection paths are part of the attack surface, and that a database's own controls can be bypassed once an attacker reaches the process or the wire.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Judit Varga - Amy Farrah Fowler, or the geek girl's case with the tiara
talks.teaser: Traces how the geek girl stereotype formed, from homeschooling and typewriters to TV sitcoms, and why girls leave science.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the geek girl, starting with how the terms geek, nerd and hipster have changed meaning over time. Drawing on interviews with women in geek circles, the speaker argues that geek culture has become less gendered, yet girls still often feel they must choose between being geeky and being feminine.

The historical section traces how girls were steered away from science. In past centuries, homeschooling taught boys mathematics and physics while girls learned embroidery and languages, and new technologies such as the telephone were seen as threats to morals. The typewriter was first marketed to men and flopped, then to middle-class women, becoming a symbol of a modern, fashionable working woman. Using Marshall McLuhan's idea that each invention extends a bodily function at some cost, the talk reads that shift as both upward mobility and loss. Television sitcoms are then examined, with The Big Bang Theory's Bernadette and Amy Farrah Fowler presented as feminine scientists, unlike earlier shows that portrayed science girls as unattractive loners.

The closing section covers the leaky pipeline: about 60 to 70 percent of girls enter technology-oriented schools, but only 30 to 40 percent remain in science. Losses cluster in childhood, adolescence, college and job entry, when feedback from teachers and parents matters. Suggested fixes include visible role models with clear practical goals, hands-on programs such as a project where girls around twelve built and documented games in C or C++, corporate social responsibility awards, and spaces like hackerspaces where girls can socialise with similar peers.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Zoltán Balázs - Zombie Browsers, spiced with rootkit extensions
talks.teaser: Shows how malicious browser extensions can act as a botnet client, hide from users and evade antivirus detection.
talks.summary:
The talk examines malicious browser extensions as a persistent foothold on victim machines. The speaker downloaded publicly available malicious Firefox extensions from Mozilla's add-on site and found that over ninety percent were built to spam Facebook. The speaker argues they can be far more dangerous: they poll a master server for commands, run on Firefox, Chrome and Safari across several operating systems, and slip past firewalls and application whitelisting because they use ordinary HTTP and plain JavaScript.

The demonstrations begin with a fake YouTube page that persuades a Safari user to install a fake Flash plugin, after which the attacker runs arbitrary JavaScript in the browser. Further demos show installing extensions through remote code execution, hiding them from the extension list with a Firefox configuration flag, and concealing a Chrome extension with a custom stylesheet. The browser is also used as a proxy to reach an internal web application and test it for SQL injection. Other examples include distributed SHA-1 password cracking through Chrome Native Client, a Flash configuration that grants webcam access, and altered currency rates shown on a Hungarian news site.

Antivirus products did not detect the sample extensions, and the speaker doubts behavioral detection would help. Recommendations include that antivirus vendors analyze and block public malicious extensions, that Mozilla refuse installs from outside its official store, and that website operators bind sessions to the client IP. Users should keep banking on a separate operating system, and companies should control which extensions are installed, for example through Group Policy in Chrome.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - András Veres-Szentkirályi - USB = Universal Security Bug?
talks.teaser: Shows how a cheap AVR microcontroller can move data out of a locked-down Windows PC using only keyboard LED signals.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at moving data out of a tightly restricted computer with no network link, data loss prevention controls, and only a keyboard, mouse and display allowed. The speaker builds a custom USB device around a cheap ATmega328 microcontroller running a software USB stack, so the chip can present itself as a keyboard. Along the way the speaker points out that USB's voltage levels and timing make it a poor fit for hobbyist hardware, so the design relies on workarounds rather than a compliant implementation.

Getting code onto a Windows 7 machine was the first hurdle, since the default shell offers only batch files and the old debug tool caps executables at 64 kilobytes. The workaround was to encode a binary as base64 inside a Visual Basic script that rebuilds the file, with the keystrokes typed by the device. A small PNG was delivered this way and opened correctly. For the return path, the keyboard's Num Lock and Caps Lock LEDs carried two bits per frame, with Scroll Lock acting as a clock. The stolen file was stored in the chip's EEPROM and read back by shorting two pins to trigger a hex-output mode. An audio modem and an SD card over SPI were also tried, and the SD card conflicted with USB timing.

Measured throughput was slow: about 10 bytes per second when typing and about one byte per second over the LEDs. The speaker concludes that PS/2 ports are no safer than USB, and that allow-listing USB identifiers does not stop a keyboard-emulating device. The prototype lacks encryption and integrity checks, and a packaged version could use more storage and be made smaller.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Miroslav Stampar - Spot the Web Vulnerability
talks.teaser: Walks through real PHP code examples showing how common web injection flaws arise and how to fix them.
talks.summary:
The talk is aimed at both defenders and attackers who read web application source code, and it focuses on the vulnerability classes that attackers exploit most often. To ground this, the speaker counted names of public vulnerabilities in a large exploit database and found that SQL injection, followed by cross-site scripting and various file inclusion flaws, dominated the list, with WordPress and PHP applications heavily represented. The talk then defines the main classes: SQL injection, cross-site scripting in persistent and non-persistent forms, local and remote file inclusion, file disclosure, directory traversal and remote code execution.

The core walks through real-world PHP examples, each tied to the application it came from. Several show filters that looked sufficient but were not, such as an escaping routine that ignored numeric input, an HTML encoding call that left single quotes untouched because the quote flag was missing, and a prepared statement built by concatenating the query. Others cover an insert statement with an unchecked field, a WordPress comment URL stored unfiltered, a shout box whose tag stripping could be bypassed with a null byte, and a settings file that user input could write into executable PHP.

The closing section lists remedies: validating input with anchored regular expressions, casting numeric values to integers, sanitizing with proper escaping functions, encoding output, and using PDO prepared statements where the query text and parameters are passed separately. The speaker stresses that prepared statements only protect when variables are bound rather than concatenated.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Alexander Kornbrust
talks.teaser: Shows how a database can spot SQL injection error messages and lock accounts or sessions automatically before data is stolen.
talks.summary:
Alexander Kornbrust argues that many web applications are vulnerable and cannot be fixed quickly, and that attackers can extract database contents within minutes using off-the-shelf SQL injection tools. Human responders are too slow, especially at night or on weekends, so he proposes letting the database itself detect an attack and react automatically.

The approach relies on error triggers: Oracle's error trigger and SQL Server's event notification can fire when a known SQL injection error appears, such as a UNION column-count mismatch, an unclosed quotation mark, or the division-by-zero error produced by sqlmap. The trigger can rebuild the offending statement, check that the error came from the application server, and then lock the database user and terminate its sessions. He also described honey data: unused tables named like real ones, where any select can lock the user. False positives, such as a name containing an apostrophe, can be reviewed by a manager on duty, who can re-enable the account.

He closed by framing the response as a management decision, trading availability against data theft, and noted that scoping accounts per application, blocking IP ranges or countries, and treating Tor-origin traffic as a stronger signal can limit the impact. He had not yet built a SQL Server proof of concept and was not aware of the approach working on other databases. His advice is to start with notifications on a test system before enforcing blocking in production.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Tamás Váradi
talks.teaser: Live demonstration walks through file, foil, and self-impressioning keys for unknown locks without destructive entry.
talks.summary:
The session introduces impressioning as a non-destructive lock-opening method within lock picking, with a live attempt to file a working key for an unknown lock while the audience follows the work under magnification. The speaker notes that Hungarian law treats many of these tools as restricted, and stresses that success depends on practice and lock knowledge rather than exotic gear; everyday items such as a strong magnifier, quality Swiss or German files, pincers, and pliers suffice.

The core theory contrasts an ideal lock—which could not be opened this way—with real cylinders that suffer production tolerances, wear, and misalignment, so only one pin binds under tension at a time. File impressioning prepares a blank to a dull, homogeneous edge, inserts it with tension, reads binding marks, and files incrementally until the lock turns; the talk covers mark enhancement with UV or smoke, timing on the order of competition limits, and the rule of filing only while marks remain. Variants include foil impressioning (aluminium shaped inside the lock, often unusable after withdrawal), soft materials such as adhesives eroded by pin movement, and self-impressioning tools built like contour copiers or commercial high-security sets.

Practitioners should expect skill-sensitive work: poor filing can break blanks and complicate the job, and advanced tools are lock-specific and costly. The presentation closes by pointing attendees to a nearby lock-picking workshop for hands-on practice.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Shakeel Tufail
talks.teaser: Walks through threat modeling software with data-flow diagrams and trust zones, illustrated by the Sony breach.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that software security matters more each year because software now runs most organisations, and that flaws caught late are expensive to fix. The speaker used the Sony breach as a case study. Attackers entered through a little-known web application server, escalated privileges, and reached a database holding millions of customer records. They scheduled jobs that wiped logs on reboot while a denial-of-service attack drew attention away from the data theft. The speaker argued that the SQL injection used to pull the data was avoidable with input filtering and parameterized queries.

The middle of the talk set out a hands-on threat modeling method. Teams list their assets, then sketch component and data-flow diagrams on a whiteboard, mark trust boundaries, and decompose the design to find weak points. Threats are matched to those points using STRIDE and DREAD, and attack trees and abuse cases are built from them. The speaker described ambiguity analysis: interviewing each developer separately, because developers on one financial client's application drew the authentication mechanism in different ways. In one architecture review, most of the protocols carrying data between components were unencrypted.

The closing advice was to revisit the model whenever code changes, rank findings by risk, and pair each finding with a concrete fix rather than handing over a scan report. The speaker recommended OWASP's OpenSAMM as a framework for building security into each phase of development.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Joe McCray - Big Bang Theory
talks.teaser: Pentesting high security environments examines Hacktivity 2012 - Joe McCray - Big Bang Theory.
talks.summary:
This demo-driven session runs on a lab setup with a wireless access point, a Snort-based intrusion detection box, and vulnerable ASP.NET applications, one of them guarded by a web application firewall. The speaker starts with the basics of testing a parameter for SQL injection, showing how simple arithmetic on the parameter can reveal injection even when the application suppresses its error messages. From there he moves through error-based enumeration of database and table names, union-based injection with column counting, and inference and time-based blind techniques.

The demos then turn to defenses. Re-enabling a disabled command-execution feature on the database server sets off the IDS, which the speaker uses to argue that signature products mostly catch noisy, simple attacks. He shows how a WAF built on outdated rule sets can be probed and sidestepped, and points to default exclusions copied between products, rules written for old Windows and IIS versions, and a file-read logic flaw on a contact page that a scanner had rated as low. He also describes getting past 802.1x network access control by spoofing a printer's MAC address, and an exploit that evaded a host intrusion prevention signature after a single keyword change.

The closing message is that understanding how a defense decides what to block is usually more useful than buying more products. Tools are only as good as the people who configure, tune and monitor them, so staffing and training matter as much as the purchase.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - László Biró
talks.teaser: Explores how amateur radio links and TCP stacks can backstop internet access when centralized providers or exchanges fail.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames information assurance as getting data to end users, not only collecting it. It traces distribution from early wired telegraph and spark wireless through broadcast media, arguing that highly controlled central outlets become single points of weakness for news, emergency services, and military-style links with different cost and reach tradeoffs.

The core proposal chains amateur digital radio to familiar networking stacks. Telegraph-style on-air encoding, AX.25 and historical X.25 over PC sound cards with Fourier decode, and later TCP over the same audio path are walked through, including Hungary’s meter-band repeaters and roughly 200 bit per second class links when eight symbol states are used. Lessons from Egypt’s shutdown and from Hungarian internet exchange choke points illustrate how BGP might prefer backup edges when primary paths vanish.

For practitioners, the talk sketches a minimalist kit—open-source BGP on portable media, a dual-band radio, and cabling—to mesh local networks for mail-grade traffic, optionally bridge internationally, and consciously limit bandwidth for bulky web content. It notes firewall and data-diode bypass risks, distribution through hundreds of willing Hungarian operators, and unresolved legal questions around protected material while expressing hope for a live national radio backbone within about a year.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Tevesz András
talks.teaser: Antivírus program hatástalanítás examines Hacktivity 2012 - Tevesz András.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at weaknesses in ESET antivirus found during penetration tests, where its password protection and self-defense features stopped the tester from disabling the product or running payloads. It opens with a Microsoft Security Essentials example, where a process-killing script from the Metasploit scripts folder could shut the scanner down. On ESET, the speaker reports that the scanner quickly removed the Meterpreter payload and that access was denied when trying to launch it.

The middle of the talk covers how ESET's self-defense is layered: registry protection, a kernel driver reached through a device control interface with a few IOCTL calls, and a service paired with a GUI process. Stopping the GUI and then the service in the right order lets the tester change settings such as exclusions. The speaker also reimplemented the unlock-code routine, which relied on a CRC32-based calculation, so codes could be generated on the client side without the vendor. Those codes are reusable and tied to a machine name. Injecting code into the protected process's address space was then used to disable the driver checks and self-defense.

The closing part discusses possible fixes. These include vendor-signed license responses using RSA-based codes that the client verifies, validating trusted images through the crypto API, and checking every loaded module and binary for a valid signature. The speaker notes that some binaries were not signed and that self-defense checks did not cover every component, which is why protections fall once a method is known.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Bucsay Balázs
talks.teaser: Examines PayPass NFC flaws and shows how open-source tooling on a Raspberry Pi can read contactless card data at close range.
talks.summary:
The session centers on Mastercard PayPass, Hungary’s dominant contactless payment option, and a known class of weaknesses whose novelty lies in reproduction with inexpensive open-source stacks rather than commercial terminals. After brief scene-setting on prior UK research and the Barclays scandal, the speaker walks through payment-card evolution—from embossed numbers through magnetic stripe and chip (ISO 7810, 7812, 7816, EMV)—and explains how PayPass layers NFC (ISO 14443) on EMV, contrasting the stronger M/Chip path with Magstripe PayPass that mirrors track data and CVV handling (including CVV3 variants banks may implement loosely).

Relay attacks abroad and NFC’s short nominal read range set up discussion of extended-distance capture reported elsewhere. The practical thread covers painful libnfc versioning, a FreeBSD-aligned toolchain, and modifying a Java EMV reader so the PC/SC stack talks to the contactless card instead of only the reader’s internal chip—mirroring behavior on newer readers.

A live demo on Raspberry Pi with pcscd reads primary account number, expiry, and related fields from volunteer cards, with censored and full-display modes. Takeaways stress user judgment on risk, backward compatibility keeping Magstripe PayPass readable, limits on contactless transaction counts without PIN, and that NFC cardholder data paths are not encrypted in ways PCI DSS would expect on open channels—without advocating fraud.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Balázs Bucsay
talks.teaser: Examines how contactless bank cards communicate over NFC, and what open-source tools reveal about their weaknesses.
talks.summary:
The talk examines contactless payment cards, using MasterCard PayPass as the main example, and asks whether the technology can be trusted. The speaker traces the path from embossed and magnetic stripe cards to chip cards under EMV, then to RFID and NFC. He covers the relevant standards, the 13.56 MHz frequency and the usable range of about 4 to 10 centimetres. Earlier cases are recalled, including the Mifare card broken in 2007, the London Oyster card, and a UK relay attack that let a small payment appear as a much larger one.

The core of the work is reading a PayPass card with open-source tools. The speaker modified an existing Java EMV reader so it addresses the card directly, rather than going through the reader hardware. He then ran it live on cards from two banks. The demo read data from one card that worked, including the primary account number and expiry date. He also explained that magnetic stripe data remains on these cards for compatibility, that the CVV3 value may be static on some cards, and that small payments can go through without a PIN or signature. He noted that the PCI DSS requires encryption for cardholder data over open networks, while NFC is not encrypted.

The main takeaway is an understanding of what a contactless card exposes and how it can be read. The speaker stressed that the talk was about how the technology works, not a guide to misuse, and he left the judgement of its trustworthiness to the audience.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Krisztián Schäffer
talks.teaser: Explains how security code review finds vulnerabilities, using a MySQL authentication bug caused by a memcmp return-value mismatch.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Hacktivity 2012 presentation, code auditor Krisztián Schäffer discusses the role and practice of security code reviews and code auditing within software development. He notes that security code review is often treated like an unwelcome byproduct of development or a neglected quality assurance activity, particularly in commercial business applications where speed and low cost are prioritized over code quality. In contrast, large open-source projects like the Linux kernel, Firefox, and Google's Chromium integrate code review directly into their development lifecycles. Schäffer breaks down code review into three primary areas: vulnerability research, security code auditing methodologies, and building a security culture through quality assurance.

### Key Topics
- **Code Review in Practice:** Examining peer review systems (such as Chromium's Gerrit-based model) where developers read delta changes, debate security and typing implications, and require supervisor approvals before committing code.
- **Vulnerability Research vs. Weaknesses:** Distinguishing between actual exploitable vulnerabilities and underlying code weaknesses. Schäffer emphasizes that code auditors should focus on finding and eliminating bad patterns rather than spending excessive time proving whether an issue is immediately exploitable.
- **White-Box Auditing vs. Black-Box Testing:** Comparing the strengths and trade-offs of black-box testing (behavioral testing, simulating attackers with limited time, building client trust) versus white-box code auditing (root-cause identification, better developer feedback, deep structural visibility).
- **Auditing Methodologies:** Exploring practical code reading strategies, including control-flow sensitive and data-flow sensitive analysis, threat modeling with business stakeholders, developer interviews, and static analysis tools.
- **Metrics and Security Culture:** Implementing metrics such as lines of code reviewed per hour (LOC/h), defect density, and detection rate, alongside secure coding standards and developer training.

### Technical Details
- **MySQL Authentication Bypass Case Study:** Schäffer analyzes a major bug involving MySQL authentication and the C standard library `memcmp` function. The code compared password hash blocks using `memcmp` and assigned the return value to a `my_bool` type (defined as a signed `char`). While `memcmp` returns an integer (zero for a match, non-zero for differences based on byte comparison), casting non-zero results (such as multiples of 256 or values where the lower byte truncates to 0) into a signed byte can cause a non-zero integer to evaluate to zero, incorrectly bypassing authentication roughly every 256 attempts. He critiques automated tools (like Clang static analysis and Splint) and explains how static analyzers either missed the bug or suggested casts that silenced warnings without fixing the root cause.
- **XML Injection via Session Cookies:** An example from an authorization module demonstrated an XML payload constructed by concatenating user session cookies directly with string addition (`+`). This allowed attackers to craft session cookie values containing injected XML tags to request unauthorized actions or resources.
- **Java Class Loading Flaw:** A Java zero-day example illustrated fallback code where, after failing standard permission checks, the code attempted an alternative class-loading path, inadvertently allowing an app to load unauthorized classes.
- **Custom Crypto Experiments:** The speaker references an example where custom, poorly understood code generation tools were introduced into a cryptography module, violating standard security principles against unapproved tools and experimental cryptography.

### Takeaways
- **Audit Speed and Metrics:** Reviewing more than 400 lines of code per hour significantly reduces the likelihood of finding subtle security bugs. Teams should track defect density and detection rates.
- **Don't Waste Time on Exploitability During Audits:** If a dangerous pattern or weakness (such as raw string concatenation into XML) is identified, flag it for remediation immediately rather than spending audit time proving exploitability.
- **Pair Auditing as Training:** Sitting down face-to-face with developers to review code acts as an effective, hands-on secure coding training session.
- **Early Static Analysis:** Static analysis should be integrated early; running it late produces unmanageable volumes of warnings, whereas using it incrementally educates developers on typing and coding standards.
- **Adherence to Approved Tools:** Security-sensitive components (especially cryptography) must rely strictly on well-understood, approved tools and established coding codices rather than experimental approaches.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Váradi Tamás
talks.teaser: Shows how impressioning opens pin-tumbler locks by filing a blank key, using binding pin marks as a guide.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces impressioning, a non-destructive lockpicking method that produces a working key without the original. The speaker explains that manufacturing tolerances mean that when the cylinder is under rotational tension, only one pin binds at a time. Each binding pin can be located and marked on a blank key, so the marks show where filing is needed. Before starting, the speaker noted that Hungarian law restricts possessing such tools for people who are not authorised to use them.

The core method is to polish the blank key's cutting edge to a uniform, non-reflective finish with a fine, well-cut file. The key is inserted and rocked back and forth under light tension, so the binding pins leave small bright marks on the blank. The key is then filed to the depth matching each marked pin, checked, and filed again until the marks change and the lock opens. The speaker stressed that file quality matters, recommending a Swiss No. 4 cut, and that UV light, soot or wax coatings can make the marks easier to see. A volunteer worked on a key on stage during the demonstration, and the speaker showed magnified images of the marks and the finished key.

The speaker also covered alternatives. Aluminium foil or soft fillers such as two-part epoxy can be used on a prepared key so pins erode the material, though such keys usually cannot be removed intact. Custom impression tools exist for specific lock types, but they are costly and fragile, and a commercial set can reach thousands of euros. The talk closed with an invitation to a two-day lockpicking workshop and a pointer to a follow-up talk on weak, inexpensive locks common in Hungary.

talks.title: Hacktivity 2012 - Sir David Pepper - Cyberspace and Beyond
talks.teaser: Maps the main threat actors, from criminals and spies to hacktivists and states, and how organizations must change to respond.
talks.summary:
Sir David Pepper frames cyberspace as an evolutionary arms race in which attacks and defences keep forcing each other to change. He argues that the main pressures come from the real world of motives and organisations rather than from the technology itself. He sorts threat actors by their purpose: cybercrime aimed at money, espionage by states and companies, hackers and hacktivists driven by fun or ideology, cyber terrorism, which he says has not yet happened but should be planned for, and state-on-state cyber warfare. As examples he cites the denial-of-service attacks on Estonia and the Stuxnet attack on control systems.

He then turns to victims and defenders. Criminal groups and intelligence services both run sophisticated, trust-based organisations, and individuals, especially older or less technical users, need deeper habits of distrust rather than basic rules alone. For companies and governments, a technical fix is only the start. Boards and senior leaders must treat security as their own responsibility, plan how they will respond to an attack, and follow the same policies they set for staff. Staff education, information sharing between companies and collaboration across borders are also essential.

Drawing on the experience of his former agency, which had to redesign its skills, processes and culture after the internet changed communications, he warns that organisations which only buy technology will fall short. He closes by suggesting the struggle is unlikely to end and may last as long as cyberspace itself.
